documents.title: 根据崩盘预警行动：预警要有多准，转为现金才划算？
documents.description: 假设投资者有一个崩盘信号，有时正确、有时误报。把避开崩盘带来的收益与误报期间错过的增长相比较，找出仅仅打平所需的命中率。
documents.body: A crash warning has to be right often enough to pay for the false alarms, and the required accuracy rises the longer you stay in cash and the faster markets rebound. Because nobody knows a signal’s future hit rate, a written allocation that you can hold through a fall usually serves crash fear better than switching in and out. Every warning is a bet with two outcomes Headlines about bubbles, recessions and “the next 2008” arrive every year. For someone with savings already invested, each one raises the same question: should I move to cash until it passes? A warning can turn out right, in which case cash avoids a loss. It can also be a false alarm, in which case the investor sits in cash while markets keep rising and then has to decide when to buy back. FINRA’s guidance on market timing warns that an investor who sells after a fall “very well might miss a subsequent recovery and rally.” A timing strategy therefore needs two decisions to go right: when to get out and when to get back in. This guide prices those two outcomes with one simple, editable model. It does not ask whether a crash will happen; it asks how accurate a warning would have to be for acting on it to beat staying invested. The model: ordinary years, crashes, rebounds and time in cash An existing CAD 100,000 balance is followed for 25 years. Ordinary years return 6%. A crash year falls 25% and the year after rebounds 25%, so a crash and its rebound together leave the market about 6.25% lower than before. The investor receives six warnings. After each one, they hold cash earning 2.5% a year for two years and then reinvest. Two warnings are followed by a crash, four are false alarms, and one crash arrives with no warning at all. The correct warnings are generous: the cash period begins just before the crash year, so the investor avoids the whole fall. Real warnings are rarely so precise. An investor who moved to cash a year too early, or returned a year too late, would do worse than the model shows. Two right calls out of six did not pay for four false alarms Staying invested ends at about CAD 249,302 . Acting on every warning ends at about CAD 239,344 , about CAD 9,958 less , even though the investor avoided two of the three crashes. The episode chart shows why. Each correct warning left the cash holder about 12.1% ahead of the invested path over that two-year episode: two years of cash at 2.5% against a 25% fall followed by a 25% rebound. Each false alarm left them about 6.5% behind : two years of cash against two ordinary 6% years. Four small losses outweighed two larger gains. The unwarned crash hit both investors equally; no signal catches every fall. The ending values do not depend on the order of the episodes. Growth multiplies year by year, so the same set of years gives the same result in any sequence. The chart’s order is arranged only for display. The break-even hit rate is about 37% here, and it moves fast Under the defaults, a warning has to be right about 37% of the time just to tie with staying invested. With three correct warnings out of six, acting on them comes out about CAD 31,334 ahead; with one, about CAD 59,446 behind. The line chart shows how steep that trade-off is. The heatmap shows what drives the break-even rate: Time in cash. With a 25% crash, the required hit rate rises from about 10% for one year in cash to about 37% for two years, 56% for three and 74% for four. Each extra year out costs a year of ordinary growth on every false alarm, and after a correct warning it means missing the rebound. Crash size. For two years in cash, a 45% crash needs about a 14% hit rate; a 35% crash about 21%. Larger falls reward correct warnings more. Small crashes. With a 15% fall and a 25% rebound, staying out two years or more is “not reachable”: the rebound more than recovers the fall, so even a correct warning leaves the cash holder behind. The one-year case looks attractive only because the model lets a correct warning sidestep the crash year exactly and return in time for the rebound. That requires knowing the timing of both the fall and the recovery. Why a hit rate cannot be planned on The model treats the hit rate as known. In practice it is the unknown that matters most. A signal that looked accurate in past data may have been fitted to those few episodes; markets and economies change; and crash warnings are often clustered, so an investor who acts on one may already be in cash when the next arrives. The OSC’s GetSmarterAboutMoney site cautions that trying to time the market often leads to losses when prices drop and opportunity costs when they rise, and that selling in a downturn locks in losses. Staying invested is not a promise of recovery by any date, and a long recovery can test even a patient investor. Moving to cash in a non-registered account can also realize capital gains, so tax can make each switch more expensive than the model shows; the fund-switch break-even guide estimates that cost. Trading fees, spreads and deferred sales charges on some older fund purchases add to it. Ways to respond to crash fear without a timing bet Check that the allocation matches the loss you could live through. The risk-profile stress test turns a stock share into a dollar loss. If a 30% fall in the equity portion would force you to sell, the allocation may be too aggressive, and changing it once is different from moving in and out. Hold spending money outside the market. Cash needed within a few years belongs in savings or short-term deposits, not in equities you hope to time. Rebalance on a rule. A balanced fund or a written target mix sells some of what has risen and buys what has fallen; the rebalancing guide shows the drift during a crash. Keep new contributions going. Contributing part of each paycheque continues through declines; FINRA describes dollar-cost averaging as a way to limit the effect of a significant decline on purchases, though regular investing cannot prevent losses on money already invested or guarantee a profit. Staging an existing lump sum is a separate decision, compared in the phased-investing guide . If you do act, write the rule first. State what will trigger a move, how much, and when you will return, then test it here with your own assumptions.
documents.keywords: Acting on crash warnings: how often must a warning be right before moving to cash pays off? Give an investor a crash signal that is sometimes right and sometimes a false alarm. Count the gains from avoided crashes against the growth missed during false alarms, and find the hit rate needed just to break even.

documents.title: 2026 年配偶及子女抚养费的税务处理：付款人扣除什么、受款人申报什么，以及为何子女抚养费优先
documents.description: 这是一份关于 1997 年 4 月之后订立的法院命令或书面协议下抚养费联邦税务处理的实例指南：为何子女抚养费既不可扣除也不须课税、配偶抚养费何时填在第 22000 行和第 12800 行、令付款不足变成失去扣除额的优先规则、一次性付款与付给第三方的款项、分居之年与第 30400 行之间的选择、对 RRSP 额度的影响，以及 CRA 关于谁在扣除抚养费的统计。六张图表及一个可编辑模型。
documents.body: Under orders and agreements made after April 1997, child support is paid from the payer’s after-tax income and arrives tax-free. Spousal support stated separately in the order is deductible by the payer on line 22000 and taxable to the recipient on line 12800, but each year’s payments count first as child support, so a payer who falls behind loses the spousal deduction until all child support is caught up. The deduction is worth the payer’s marginal rate and the tax is the recipient’s, so the net federal effect depends on the gap between their two brackets. Two kinds of support, two tax results When a couple separates, an order or agreement usually sets two kinds of payments. The tax rules treat them in opposite ways: Under Folio S1-F3-C3 (¶3.13), any amount the order does not identify as solely for the spouse or former spouse is a child support amount . A single global figure “for the family” is therefore treated entirely as child support, with no deduction. Spousal support has to be stated separately to be deductible. The date matters because orders made before May 1997 followed the older rule, under which child support was deductible and taxable too. Such an order moves to the current rules if the child support is changed after April 1997, if a new order between the same people changes the total, if the order names a date from which the new rules apply, or if both parties sign Form T1157. The election cannot be reversed. This guide models current-rule orders only. When spousal support is deductible Under the Income Tax Act definition of a support amount (subsection 56.1(4)), as CRA explains it in the Folio, a payment is deductible to the payer and taxable to the recipient only if all of these apply: It is paid under a court order or written agreement . A written agreement is generally signed and dated by both parties; emails alone may not be enough (¶3.31). Registering the order or agreement with CRA is required to claim the deduction. It is an allowance payable on a periodic basis : a set amount fixed in advance and paid, for example, monthly. Payments at intervals of more than a year, or a sum for a fixed term that looks like a property settlement, may not qualify (¶3.38–3.43). The recipient can use it as they see fit . Payments to third parties are covered below. The two people were living separate and apart because of the breakdown of the relationship when the payment was made. Spouses are treated as separated only after 90 consecutive days apart (¶3.7–3.9). Payments made before the order or agreement count only if made in the same or the preceding year and the document says they are considered paid under it (subsections 60.1(3) and 56.1(3)). Amounts paid on top of what the order requires, such as gifts or pocket money sent directly to children, are not support and are left off lines 21999 and 12799. Legal fees to obtain a separation or divorce are not deductible by either person. A recipient may deduct fees to collect overdue support or to establish or increase it on line 22100. Interest on arrears is not deductible by the payer but must be included by the recipient (¶3.65). A worked year Take a former couple with an order made in 2025. The payer has CAD 110,000 of employment income; the recipient has CAD 35,000 and the children. The order requires CAD 1,000 a month of child support and CAD 1,500 a month of spousal support, and the payer pays all CAD 30,000 in 2026. The CAD 18,000 deduction stays within the payer’s 20.5% band (CAD 58,523 to 117,045), and the inclusion stays within the recipient’s 14% band, so the two federal returns together pay CAD 1,170 less than if the spousal support were not deductible. Provincial tax adds a similar effect at provincial rates. The first chart shows how the saving and the added tax change with the amount: each moves at the marginal rate of the person concerned, so the net effect shrinks or reverses when the recipient has the higher income or the support pushes them into a higher bracket. Family law usually takes this into account. The Federal Child Support Guidelines set child support from the payer’s income on the basis that it is not deductible, and the Spousal Support Advisory Guidelines are expressed in gross, pre-tax amounts that assume deductibility. This guide does not calculate how much support is owed. The priority rule: short payments are child support first If the order sets both kinds of support, CRA treats every payment in a year as child support until all child support for that year and earlier years is paid. Only payments above that count as spousal support and can be deducted. Under the paragraph 60(b) formula, the Folio shows the shortfall reducing the deduction dollar for dollar (Example 1). With the CAD 30,000 owed in the default case: a payer who pays CAD 24,000 has paid all CAD 12,000 of child support and CAD 12,000 of spousal support; the deduction is CAD 12,000, saving CAD 2,460 instead of CAD 3,690; a payer who pays CAD 10,000 has paid only child support, deducts nothing, and owes CAD 2,000 of child support that is added to the next year’s child support before any spousal support can be deducted again; a payer with child support arrears from earlier years must clear them first in the same way. The rule applies separately to each recipient: arrears owed to one former partner do not cut the deduction for support paid to another (Folio Example 4). It does not apply where child and spousal support are under different orders with different recipients. CRA’s page on the amount to claim or report includes an example where a payer who stopped paying after three months cannot deduct any spousal support, while the recipient is still shown as reporting the spousal part of what was paid. The model applies the Folio’s formula to both returns, so if a real case has a shortfall, check the treatment with CRA or a tax professional. Lump sums, retroactive payments and third-party payments Lump sums are generally not periodic and so not deductible or taxable, especially a sum paid to settle future obligations or released rights. Exceptions are arrears of periodic amounts that fell due after the order or agreement, an advance of future periodic support under a court order, and retroactive periodic support for a period before a court order. A lump sum under a written agreement for a period before that agreement does not qualify (Folio ¶3.44–3.46). A recipient of a qualifying retroactive lump sum of CAD 3,000 or more may be able to ask CRA to tax it as if received in the earlier years (Form T1198). Payments to third parties , such as rent, a mortgage or medical bills paid directly, are deemed paid to the recipient (subsection 60.1(1)) but still need to be a support amount. For specific-purpose payments to count, the order or agreement must say that subsections 60.1(2) and 56.1(2) apply, or clearly state they are taxable to the recipient and deductible by the payer. Payments for a home the payer lives in are excluded, and payments toward buying or improving the recipient’s home are limited to 20% of the original loan principal each year (¶3.50–3.61). Repaid support : a recipient who repays support under a court order that they earlier reported can deduct the repayment on line 22000 in the year of repayment or either of the two following years. The year of separation: deduction or line 30400 A payer generally cannot claim the amount for an eligible dependant (line 30400) for a child they must pay support for. In the year a couple separates, though, a payer who meets the line 30400 conditions for the child, for example because the child lived with them before the separation, can choose: deduct the spousal support paid on line 22000, or enter zero there and claim the personal credits (line 30400 and, for that child, lines 30425 and 31800). They cannot have both for the same year. The line 30400 credit for a child with no income is CAD 16,452 at 14%, or CAD 2,303.28. The deduction is worth the payer’s marginal federal rate on the spousal support paid. At CAD 110,000 of income, that is 20.5% until the deduction carries the payer below CAD 58,523, so the deduction wins once spousal support passes about CAD 11,235. A payer paying CAD 8,000 of spousal support would save CAD 1,640 by deducting it and CAD 2,303.28 with the credit. The choice affects only the payer’s return: the recipient still includes the spousal support. The fifth chart shows the crossover for the incomes entered; provincial credits and rates change it in practice. Knock-on effects: RRSP room and income-tested benefits RRSP room. Earned income for RRSP purposes adds taxable support received and subtracts deductible support paid. In the default case, the recipient’s 2027 RRSP room rises by CAD 3,240 (18% of CAD 18,000) and the payer’s falls by the same amount, both subject to the annual dollar limit and each person’s other earned income. Benefits based on net income. Taxable spousal support raises the recipient’s net income, which is the starting point for the Canada child benefit, the GST/HST credit and many provincial benefits paid from July of the following year. Deductible support lowers the payer’s net income. For a recipient in a benefit phase-out range, the after-tax and after-benefit value of each dollar of spousal support is lower than the tax calculation alone shows. Child support does not count as income for these benefits. Instalments. No tax is withheld from support payments. A recipient whose taxable support is large relative to tax withheld from other income may owe a balance at filing and may be asked to pay instalments. Who deducts support: CRA statistics CRA’s final statistics for the 2024 tax year (data as of 30 November 2025) show 51,360 returns deducting support payments made, for CAD 1.12 billion, about CAD 21,884 each. These are deductible amounts, mostly spousal support under current-rule orders, plus support under older orders that never moved to the new rules; child support paid under current orders does not appear. Counts are rounded to the nearest ten and dollars to the nearest thousand, so the ranges add to 51,390 returns and CAD 1,123,951 thousand rather than the published totals. Deductions are concentrated at high incomes: returns with CAD 250,000 or more deducted 54% of the dollars, an average of about CAD 68,855 each. The table does not show support received, the recipients’ incomes, or how many payers lost a deduction under the priority rule. Checklist and limits of the model Find the date of the order or agreement and any later change: current rules apply from May 1997 or the change. Check that spousal support is stated as a separate amount; an undivided amount is child support. Register the order or agreement with CRA if you will deduct spousal support. Keep records of every payment, date and recipient; both people report the total on line 21999 or 12799. Pay child support for the year and any arrears in full before counting anything as deductible spousal support. Check third-party payment clauses and any lump sum against the Folio before deducting or excluding them. In the year of separation, compare the deduction with the line 30400 credit for the child. Recipients: plan for the tax on spousal support, possible instalments and the effect on next year’s benefits. The model uses 2026 federal brackets and treats net income as taxable income, with the basic personal amount, Canada employment amount and base CPP and EI credits on the employment income entered. It assumes an order made after April 1997, periodic payments the recipient controls, one recipient, and that the CRA registration and living-apart conditions are met. Provincial and territorial tax, other credits, income-tested benefits and Quebec’s separate system are not included, and it does not decide how much support is owed. Use tax software, a family lawyer or a tax professional for an actual case.
documents.keywords: Spousal and child support and tax in 2026: what the payer deducts, what the recipient reports, and why child support is paid first A worked guide to the federal tax treatment of support under a court order or written agreement made after April 1997: why child support is neither deductible nor taxable, when spousal support goes on lines 22000 and 12800, the priority rule that turns a short payment into lost deductions, lump sums and third-party payments, the year-of-separation choice against line 30400, the effect on RRSP room, and CRA statistics on who deducts support. Six charts and an editable model.

documents.description: 付款人按自己的联邦边际税率扣除，受款人按自己的税率缴税，所以净变化取决于两个税级的差距。付款人抚养费前净收入为 110,000 加元、受款人为 35,000 加元时，每一元都在两份报税表之间转移，直至把受款人推上更高税级或把付款人拉低一个税级为止。子女抚养费不会出现在此图中。

documents.keywords: Federal tax saved and paid as deductible spousal support rises The payer deducts at their own marginal federal rate and the recipient pays at theirs, so the net change depends on the gap between the two brackets. With the payer at CAD 110,000 and the recipient at CAD 35,000 of net income before support, each dollar moves between the two returns until it pushes the recipient into a higher bracket or the payer into a lower one. Child support never appears here.

documents.keywords: How short payments are split between child and spousal support Each bar is the CAD 30,000 owed under this order for 2026 including child support arrears. Whatever is paid fills child support first, so a payer who falls short loses the spousal deduction dollar for dollar until child support is caught up, and the unpaid child support is added to next year’s amount owed before spousal support can be deducted again.

documents.keywords: Year of separation: deduction or eligible dependant credit In the year a couple separates, a payer who meets the line 30400 conditions for the child can claim either the line 30400 credit (and lines 30425 and 31800 for that child) or the support deduction, not both. Here the deduction is worth more once spousal support passes about CAD 11,235. The credit uses CAD 16,452 at 14% for a child with no income and is capped by the payer’s federal tax.

documents.title: 2026 年受养人额度（eligible dependant amount）：谁可申报第 30400 行、受养人收入如何削减它，以及照护者补足额
documents.description: 2026 年第 30400 行实例指南：谁符合单身申报人和受养人资格、每户一项申报和共同监护规则、子女抚养费限制、受养人每一元收入如何削减额度、2,740 加元体弱附加额与第 30425 行补足额、收入较低的单亲父母为何可能用不上，以及谁在申报的 CRA 统计。包含六张图表和可编辑模型。
documents.body: For 2026 a claimant with no spouse or common-law partner (or one they neither live with nor support) who supports a qualifying relative in a home they maintain can claim their own basic personal amount, CAD 16,452 for most people, less the dependant’s net income. An infirm dependant adds CAD 2,740 and, at 18 or older, a line 30425 top-up that keeps the total at CAD 8,773 until the dependant’s income passes CAD 20,601. The credit is 14% federally, about CAD 2,303 at most, and only reduces federal tax the claimant actually owes. What the eligible dependant amount is Every filer gets the basic personal amount (line 30000). A couple can claim a second one through the spouse or common-law partner amount (line 30300) when one partner supports the other. The amount for an eligible dependant on line 30400, often called the “equivalent-to-spouse” amount, gives the same second amount to a person without a supporting partner who supports a child, parent or other qualifying relative at home. The amount is worked out on Schedule 5. It starts from the claimant’s own basic personal amount, adds CAD 2,740 if the dependant depends on the claimant because of a mental or physical infirmity, and subtracts the dependant’s net income from line 23600: The 2026 amounts are CRA’s published figures after 2.0% indexation; the CAD 29,374 end point is derived as CAD 8,773 + 20,601, and the same sum for 2025 gives the CAD 28,798 printed on the 2025 form. At 14%, the full CAD 16,452 is worth CAD 2,303.28 of federal tax, and the infirm maximum of CAD 19,192 is worth CAD 2,686.88. Who can claim it Under CRA’s line 30400 rules and Income Tax Act paragraph 118(1)(b), you may be able to claim for one eligible dependant if, at any time in the year, all of these applied: You did not claim the spouse or common-law partner amount on line 30300. You had no spouse or common-law partner or, if you had one, you were not living with them, supporting them or being supported by them. You supported the dependant and lived with them in a home you maintained, alone or with others. A person who was only visiting does not count; a dependant away at school who usually lives with you does. The dependant was related to you by blood, marriage, common-law partnership or adoption and was your parent or grandparent ; your child, grandchild, brother or sister under 18 ; or one of those 18 or older with a mental or physical infirmity . Their net income was less than your basic personal amount (plus CAD 2,740 for an infirm dependant). A parent or grandparent qualifies at any age without an infirmity. An adult child or sibling qualifies only with one. The dependant generally must live in Canada, but your own child need not, provided they lived with you. The “at any time in the year” wording means a person who separated during the year, or whose child was born during it, can still qualify, provided they do not also claim line 30300. Schedule 5 asks for the date of a change in marital status. One claim per home, shared custody and child support Three restrictions decide many family situations: One claim per household. Only one line 30400 claim can be made for a home, even if it has several dependants, and the amount cannot be split. Two siblings sharing an apartment with their mother cannot each claim for her. One claimant per dependant. If two people could claim for the same dependant and cannot agree, neither can claim. Folio S1-F4-C2 (paragraph 2.57) explains that separated parents who share custody of two or more children may each claim for a different child, provided each meets every condition for that child. Child support. You generally cannot claim for a child you had to pay support for (subsection 118(5)). The exceptions: when both parents had to pay support for the child, the one the parents agree on may claim; and in the year of a separation part-way through the year, you can choose between claiming line 30400 (plus lines 30425 and 31800 for that child) or deducting support paid to the spouse on line 22000. A parent who receives support is not barred. The rule turns on who had to pay it under the agreement or order, not on who had the child more often. Where both parents had to pay support for the child, for example under a set-off arrangement, the claim needs both payers’ agreement. How the dependant’s income reduces it The dependant’s net income for the whole year, not just the part they lived with you, comes straight off the claimant’s amount. For a child under 18 without an infirmity and a claimant with CAD 52,000 of income, the first chart shows: No income : CAD 16,452, a credit of CAD 2,303.28. A teenager earning CAD 6,000 from a summer job: CAD 10,452, a credit of CAD 1,463.28. The teenager’s pay costs the household CAD 840 of the parent’s federal credit, even though the teenager probably owes no tax on it. A dependant with CAD 16,452 or more of net income: nothing. Net income is after the dependant’s own deductions. A teenager with RRSP room from a previous year’s earnings could, for example, deduct a contribution and so lower their net income; the trade-off is a locked-up contribution for a 14% credit to the parent, and it only works if the room exists. Child support paid to the parent is not the child’s income, and CCB payments belong to the parent. A parent or grandparent with CPP, OAS and a small pension usually exceeds the threshold. A widowed mother with CAD 15,000 of income leaves only CAD 1,452 to claim (CAD 203.28 of credit), and at CAD 16,452 nothing. If she depends on you because of an infirmity, the picture changes, as the next section shows. Infirm dependants: the CAD 2,740 addition and line 30425 For an infirm dependant, two pieces of the Canada caregiver credit combine with line 30400: CAD 2,740 is added to the basic personal amount before the dependant’s income is subtracted. For an infirm child of yours under 18, the CAD 2,740 is claimed on line 30500 instead, which does not depend on the child’s income. For a dependant 18 or older , line 30425 adds the amount by which the lesser of CAD 8,773 and (CAD 29,374 minus their net income) exceeds what was claimed on line 30400. The effect is that lines 30400 and 30425 together equal the larger of the line 30400 amount and the caregiver amount the dependant would otherwise support. The infirm parent with CAD 18,000 of income works out as follows: Without the infirmity, the same parent gives no claim at all. With it, the claim stays at CAD 8,773 until the parent’s income reaches CAD 20,601 and ends at CAD 29,374. “Infirmity” means dependence because of a mental or physical impairment for a considerable period, not a temporary illness or injury. CRA may ask for a medical practitioner’s statement, but not if it already holds an approved Form T2201 disability tax credit certificate for the period. When the claimant cannot use it The credit is non-refundable . It reduces federal tax left after the claimant’s own credits, and any excess is lost: it cannot be carried forward, refunded or moved to anyone else. That matters for single parents on modest incomes, who are the main group this amount is designed for. In the model, a claimant whose income is all employment income has their own basic personal amount, the CAD 1,501 Canada employment amount and base CPP and EI credits. Against that: at CAD 20,000 , they owe only CAD 126.59 of federal tax before the dependant credit, so CAD 2,176.69 of the CAD 2,303.28 credit is wasted; at CAD 28,000 , CAD 1,172.90 is usable; from about CAD 36,643 , the whole credit is used. The third chart shows this cut-off; the grid shows it for five types of dependant. Other credits not modelled, such as tuition, medical expenses or donations, compete for the same tax. Provincial and territorial versions of the amount (line 58160 of Form 428) have their own values and may still be usable. Lower-income single parents get most of their federal support through refundable programs, the Canada child benefit, the GST/HST credit and the Canada workers benefit, which do not depend on this claim. How it links to other claims Line 31800, disability amount transferred from a dependant : claiming, or being able to claim, line 30400 for a dependant is one route to transfer their unused disability amount. The two claims add up. Line 30450 : someone who cannot claim line 30400 because they have a spouse may still claim the caregiver amount for an infirm dependant 18 or older there. Nobody can claim line 30450 for a dependant already claimed on line 30400. Line 30500 : when a child does not live with both parents, only the parent claiming line 30400 for that child can claim the CAD 2,740 infirm child amount, with exceptions for a parent who claimed line 30300 or line 30400 for someone else. Canada child benefit : CCB is based on adjusted family net income and is neither reduced nor increased by this claim; its primary-caregiver rules are separate from the line 30400 tests. Spouse amount : line 30300 and line 30400 cannot both be claimed. A couple living together claims line 30300, never line 30400, for their child. Who claims it: CRA statistics CRA’s final statistics for the 2024 tax year (data as of 30 November 2025) count 1,002,220 returns claiming the amount for an eligible dependant, for CAD 14.97 billion of amounts, about CAD 14,937 each. That is close to the full amount, which suggests most dependants claimed have little or no income. For comparison, 344,670 returns claimed a Canada caregiver amount (CAD 2.25 billion) and 187,990 the caregiver amount for infirm children under 18. Counts are rounded to the nearest ten, so the ranges add to 1,002,240 rather than the published total. About a quarter of claims (249,420) come from returns with under CAD 20,000 of total income, where a non-refundable federal credit can reduce little tax. The table does not show how much of the credit was used, the dependants’ ages, or the claimants’ family type, so it cannot say how many of those claims were wasted federally or still helped provincially. Checklist and limits of the model Confirm there was no line 30300 claim and no spouse you lived with or supported at the relevant time. Confirm the relationship and age (or infirmity) of the dependant, and that you lived together in a home you maintained. Check that nobody else in the home, and no other parent, is claiming; in shared custody, agree in writing who claims which child. Read the support agreement or order: if you had to pay support for the child, you generally cannot claim them. Use the dependant’s full-year net income from line 23600 of their return, or estimate it if they do not file. For an infirm dependant, add CAD 2,740 and complete line 30425 for those 18 or older; for your infirm child under 18, use line 30500. Keep in mind that the federal credit is worth at most CAD 2,303.28 (CAD 2,686.88 with an infirmity), and only if you owe that much federal tax. The model is federal only and uses 2026 amounts with the structure of the 2025 schedule. It treats net income as taxable income and estimates the claimant’s federal tax after only the basic personal amount, the Canada employment amount and base CPP and EI credits on employment income. It assumes the eligibility conditions are met and does not test support payments, residency, the part-year separation choice or the disability amount transfer. Provincial and territorial amounts, the Quebec system and the refundable family benefits are not included. Use tax software or the CRA schedule for an actual return.
documents.keywords: The 2026 amount for an eligible dependant: who can claim line 30400, how a dependant’s income cuts it, and the caregiver top-up A worked guide to line 30400 for 2026: who qualifies as a single claimant and an eligible dependant, the one-claim-per-home and shared-custody rules, the child-support restriction, how every dollar of a dependant’s income reduces the amount, the CAD 2,740 infirmity addition and the line 30425 top-up, why a low-income single parent may not be able to use it, and CRA statistics on who claims. documents.title: 拿不回来的 15%：RRSP、TFSA 和应税账户中的美国股息预扣税
documents.description: 美国股票在扣除美国预扣税后才派发股息，你能否拿回这笔税，取决于账户以及你持有股票的方式。比较在 RRSP、TFSA 和应税账户中的加拿大上市基金与美国上市 ETF，看看每年小小的拖累如何复利累积，以及货币兑换成本何时会超过它。
documents.body: US withholding of 15% on dividends is recovered in a taxable account through the foreign tax credit, is avoided by an RRSP or RRIF holding US-listed securities directly, and is lost everywhere else: in a TFSA, FHSA or RESP, and inside any Canadian-listed fund. On a 1.5% yield the loss is about 0.23% a year, a real but modest cost that compounds. Converting currency to avoid it costs money too, so the right choice depends on yield, conversion cost, fees and how long you hold, not on the withholding alone. A small line on the statement Someone who holds US stocks, through an index fund, an ETF or a balanced fund with a US equity sleeve, receives dividends that have already been cut. The United States taxes dividends paid to foreign investors at source, and for Canadian residents the Canada–US tax convention caps that tax at 15% of the gross dividend for ordinary portfolio holdings (Article X, paragraph 2(b)). Whether that 15% is a real cost depends on two things this guide separates: the account , whose tax rules decide whether the withholding can be credited, and the structure of the holding, which decides who the US treats as the shareholder. The tool below follows the same US stocks held four ways and measures what the withholding, and the currency conversion some people use to avoid it, costs over time. The amounts are smaller than most fund fees, and that is the first lesson. Withholding tax is worth understanding and arranging sensibly; it is rarely worth taking on extra risk, concentration or complexity to avoid. The rules in four sentences Taxable account. US dividends are foreign income, taxed in full at your marginal rate. The US tax withheld is generally credited against the Canadian tax on that income through the federal foreign tax credit , so the withholding is not an extra cost as long as you owe at least that much Canadian tax on it. A Canadian fund passes the foreign income and the foreign tax it paid to you on the T3 slip (boxes 25 and 34), CRA explains , so the credit works through a fund too. RRSP or RRIF, US-listed securities. Article XXI, paragraph 2 of the treaty exempts dividends and interest received by an arrangement “operated exclusively to administer or provide pension, retirement or employee benefits”. RRSPs and RRIFs are treated as such arrangements, so a US-listed ETF or US share held directly in them normally pays its dividends without withholding. TFSA, FHSA or RESP. These are not retirement trusts for treaty purposes. CRA warns that foreign dividends paid to a TFSA or an FHSA could be subject to foreign withholding tax, and its foreign tax credit folio (¶1.69) says foreign tax on income earned in an RRSP or TFSA does not count for a foreign tax credit. The 15% is simply lost. Any Canadian-listed fund holding US stocks. The fund, a Canadian trust, is the shareholder. It suffers the 15% itself, whatever account you hold its units in. In a taxable account it can pass the credit to you; in an RRSP, TFSA or other registered plan nothing can recover it. A further layer applies when a Canadian-listed fund holds a US-listed ETF that in turn holds stocks outside the US: foreign taxes withheld by those other countries at the bottom level are also lost, and are not shown here. Chart 1: one year of dividends, four ways With the defaults, $100,000 of US stocks yielding 1.5% pays $1,500 of dividends in the first year. The first chart follows that $1,500. In an RRSP holding a US-listed ETF, all of it is reinvested. In an RRSP holding a Canadian-listed fund, or in a TFSA, FHSA or RESP holding either kind, $225 is withheld and never returns, and $1,275 is reinvested. In a taxable account the $225 is also withheld, but it counts toward the $444.75 of Canadian tax due on the dividend at a 29.65% marginal rate; you pay the remaining $219.75, and $1,055.25 is left to reinvest. The taxable account loses the most to tax in that year, but not because of withholding: foreign dividends are fully taxed as income in Canada. The registered accounts shelter the dividend from Canadian tax; only the US share stays behind. Keep the comparison straight: the RRSP figures are before the tax due when money is eventually withdrawn, and a TFSA withdrawal is tax-free. Chart 2: a small yearly drag compounds The withholding takes yield × rate from the holding every year: 1.5% × 15% = 0.225% a year with the defaults. That looks tiny, but money lost early never grows. Against the same stocks with no withholding, which grow to about $482,770 over 25 years at 5% price growth plus 1.5% dividends, a Canadian-listed fund in an RRSP or TFSA ends about $24,862 lower, around 5% of the ending value. A US-listed ETF avoids the withholding only in an RRSP or RRIF, and it needs US dollars. At a conversion cost of 1% each way, converting in and converting back takes about 2% of the money, about $9,607 by year 25 on the larger ending balance. In a TFSA the US-listed ETF pays both the conversion and the withholding, and falls furthest behind, about $33,975. None of these figures includes fees. Many Canadian-listed US index funds and their US-listed equivalents differ in management fee by a few hundredths of a percent a year, which over 25 years can be as large as the effects shown. Compare the whole cost, not one line. Chart 3: when the conversion cost pays for itself In an RRSP the real trade-off is between a fixed cost now (converting dollars twice) and a yearly cost forever (withholding). The heatmap finds the first year in which the US-listed route is worth at least as much, for dividend yields from 0.5% to 4% and one-way conversion costs from 0.1% to 2%. With the defaults the answer is 10 years . At a 1.5% yield and a cheap 0.25% conversion it takes 3 years; at a 0.5% yield and a 2% retail spread it takes 57. High-yield holdings and low conversion costs favour the US-listed route; low-yield growth holdings and expensive conversions favour the Canadian-listed fund. Other differences sit outside this calculation. A US-listed ETF reports in US dollars and needs records of the exchange rate for each purchase and sale in a taxable account; the currency and cost base guide explains why. Large holdings of US-listed securities can also raise US estate tax questions. Simplicity has value too. Chart 4: yield and time decide the size The last heatmap scales the withholding loss in a registered account to $100,000 for yields from 0.5% to 4% and holding periods from 5 to 40 years. At a 0.5% yield the loss is about $464 after 5 years and $10,520 after 30; at 4% it is about $4,188 after 5 years and over $200,000 after 30, because the lost dividends are a much larger share of the return. This explains a common rule of thumb: in an RRSP, consider holding the highest-yielding US holdings directly; in a TFSA, which cannot avoid the withholding either way, keep US dividend payers small or hold growth-oriented equities. The asset location guide covers the wider question of what to hold in which account. Yields change. A US stock index yielding around 1% to 2% is typical of recent decades, but the yield of any fund depends on what it holds and on prices; the figures here are scenarios, not a forecast of income or return. Practical steps Look at the account first. The account’s tax rules, not the fund, decide whether US withholding can be credited, avoided or not. A fund is not more or less tax-exempt because of the account label on it. In a taxable account, keep the slips. Claim the foreign tax shown in box 34 of a T3 (or on your broker’s slip) on Form T2209. The credit is limited to the Canadian tax on that foreign income; if your income is very low, part of it may not be usable. In an RRSP, compare total cost. For a large, long-held US equity position, a US-listed ETF can come out ahead once yield × 15% exceeds the extra yearly fee, and the holding period is long enough to recover the conversion. For small or short holdings the Canadian-listed fund is usually simpler and close in cost. In a TFSA, FHSA or RESP, do not convert to avoid withholding. It cannot be avoided there. A Canadian-listed fund saves the conversion. Keep perspective. Diversification, total fees, your risk capacity and staying invested through market falls matter far more over decades than a fraction of a percent. Returns are uncertain and US stocks can fall sharply in Canadian-dollar terms, through both prices and the exchange rate.
documents.keywords: The 15% that never comes back: US dividend withholding tax in an RRSP, a TFSA and a taxable account US stocks pay dividends after US tax is withheld, and whether you ever get that tax back depends on the account and on how you hold the stocks. Compare a Canadian-listed fund with a US-listed ETF in an RRSP, a TFSA and a taxable account, see how a small yearly drag compounds, and find when currency conversion costs outweigh it.

documents.description: 加拿大按金额而非购买力对资本利得征税，因此利得中仅仅追上通胀的部分会像真实利润一样被征税。看看对于持有数十年的基金，这部分有多大，它如何提高你实际回报所承担的真实税率，2006 年以来 9 月份的 CPI 意味着什么，以及为什么 TFSA 或 RRSP 会改变这个算术。
documents.body: A capital gain on a fund includes a portion that only restores purchasing power, and in a taxable account that portion is taxed too, because the cost base is not adjusted for inflation. With 4% real growth and 2.5% inflation over 20 years, about a quarter of the reported gain is inflation, and tax takes 19.7% of the real gain instead of the 14.8% headline rate. Interest taxed every year fares far worse. Inside a TFSA neither part is taxed. A gain on paper, a gain in tax, and a smaller gain in life Suppose you bought a balanced or equity fund in a non-registered account 20 years ago, and its units are now worth more than three and a half times what you paid. The tax return calls the difference a capital gain. But groceries, rent and wages also rose over those 20 years. Part of the “gain” is just the same purchasing power expressed in more dollars. Canada taxes the dollar gain: the proceeds minus the adjusted cost base, as CRA’s capital gains guide defines it, with no allowance for inflation. Half of that gain is included in income. This guide asks how much of the gain is inflation, how much tax falls on it, and what that does to the tax rate on the part of the return that actually made you better off. The answer is not a reason to avoid investing or to fear inflation. It is a reason to understand why the account you hold a fund in matters, and why a low-return investment held in a taxable account can lose purchasing power even when it shows a profit. Chart 1: splitting the reported gain With the defaults, $10,000 grows 4% a year in real terms while prices rise 2.5% a year, a nominal return of 6.6%. After 20 years the units are worth about $35,904 and the reported gain is about $25,904 . To buy what $10,000 bought at the start, you would need about $16,386 at the end. So $6,386 , about a quarter of the reported gain, is inflation. The other $19,518 is the real gain, measured in the dollars of the sale year. At a 29.65% marginal rate and half inclusion, the tax on the sale is about $3,840 . About $947 of it falls on the inflation part, which bought you nothing. The waterfall shows the four pieces: real gain, inflation, tax on each. The tax rate on what you really gained Measure everything in today’s purchasing power. Without tax, the fund would have turned $10,000 into $21,911 of today’s money, a real gain of $11,911. After the tax at sale it is worth $19,568, a real gain of $9,568. Tax took 19.7% of the real gain, not the 14.8% (half of 29.65%) that the headline rate suggests. The heatmap repeats this for real growth from 1% to 6% and inflation from 0% to 6% over the holding period you enter. With no inflation every cell equals the headline rate. With high inflation and low real growth the effective rate climbs: at 1% real growth and 4% inflation over 20 years, tax takes about half of the real gain. That combination, a cautious investment in a high-inflation period, is exactly when the tax on inflation hurts most. Longer holding helps a little: the deferral of tax until sale lets the untaxed amount compound, and the real part of the gain grows faster than the inflation part when real returns are healthy. Chart 3: what the CPI since 2006 implies The third chart uses Statistics Canada’s all-items CPI ( table 18-10-0004-01 ) for September of each year from 2006 to 2025 and for September 2026 (170.0). It shows how much $10,000 invested in each September had to grow by September 2026 just to keep its purchasing power, and the tax that rise alone would bring if sold in a taxable account at the entered rate. From September 2006 (CPI 109.2) the required rise is about $5,568 , so the units had to be worth $15,568 just to break even in real terms; selling at that price would bring about $825 of tax at 29.65% on a real gain of zero. From September 2021 the required rise is about $1,896 because of the high inflation of 2021 to 2023. These are dated observations; the tax column is a calculation at your entered rate. The same arithmetic means a fund that only kept pace with inflation, sold in a taxable account, leaves you with less purchasing power than you started with. Chart 4: account and income type matter more than the fund The last chart follows the same pre-tax return three ways, in today’s dollars. Inside a TFSA nothing is taxed, so the real value grows at the full 4%. In a taxable account with the gain taxed only at sale, the value trails the TFSA by the tax on both parts of the gain. If the same nominal return were paid as interest and taxed in full every year, as GIC interest and much of a bond fund’s distribution are, the real after-tax return falls to about 2.1% a year and tax takes about 57% of the real gain. This is why the taxable interest guide finds that savings deposits can lose purchasing power after tax, and why balanced funds, which hold bonds, distribute more taxable income each year than equity funds. The income-type guide compares interest, dividends and gains. Note the distinction. A TFSA or RRSP is an account with tax rules; it does not change the fund’s risk, fees or returns. An RRSP defers tax rather than removing it: withdrawals are fully taxed as income, so it removes the inflation-on-gains problem but taxes the whole withdrawal at your rate at that time. What to do with this Use the tax-free and tax-deferred room for long-held growth first. The longer you expect to hold, and the higher inflation might be, the more the TFSA’s freedom from tax on both real and inflation gains is worth. The asset location guide discusses what to put where. Separate new pay from an existing holding. Contributing future savings to a TFSA is simple. Moving an existing non-registered fund into a TFSA is a sale for tax purposes, and the inflation part of its gain is taxed then; the in-kind contribution guide explains. Do not sell early to “reset” the gain. Realizing gains sooner only pays the tax sooner. Deferral is valuable; the gain timing guide shows it. Judge returns in real, after-tax terms. A fund that shows a 50% gain over 15 years may have made far less in purchasing power. Compare plans in today’s dollars, as the inflation and purchasing-power guide does. Keep perspective on risk. Equity and balanced funds can fall sharply and recover slowly; no return here is promised. Tax arithmetic matters, but diversification, fees and staying invested matter more.
documents.keywords: Taxed on inflation: how much of a long-held fund’s capital gain is just higher prices Canada taxes the capital gain in dollars, not in purchasing power, so the part of a gain that merely keeps up with inflation is taxed like real profit. See how big that part is for a fund held for decades, how it raises the true tax rate on your real return, what September CPI since 2006 implies, and why a TFSA or RRSP changes the arithmetic.

documents.title: 为什么 TFSA 额度停在 $7,000，何时会变：以 $500 为台阶的通胀指数化
documents.description: 从法律出发重建 TFSA 金额上限：自 2009 年起每年按 CPI 指数化的 $5,000，取整到最接近的 $500。看看额度为何多年不变后又跳升，18 年的额度按今天的价格值多少，以及在不同通胀率下下一级台阶何时到来。
documents.body: The TFSA dollar limit is $5,000 indexed to inflation since 2009, rounded to the nearest $500. That keeps new room roughly constant in real terms: the $109,000 of limits from 2009 to 2026 is worth about $138,600 in September 2026 prices. A flat limit is not a cut, and a jump is not a gift; both are rounding. Indexing protects the size of the room, not the value of what you hold in it. Three years at $7,000 is not a freeze The TFSA dollar limit was $7,000 in 2024, 2025 and 2026 . Prices rose in each of those years, so it is natural to ask whether the room is quietly shrinking, or whether the government has stopped indexing it. Neither is the case. The limit is still tied to inflation; it simply moves in steps of $500, and inflation of about 2% a year takes several years to add up to a step. This guide rebuilds the limit from the law, year by year, using the same consumer price index the law uses. It then answers four practical questions: why the limit sits still and then jumps, how much the room has really been worth, what the 2027 figure is likely to be, and how quickly future steps come under different inflation rates. The tool below lets you change your age, which sets your first eligible year, the inflation you assume after 2027 and how far ahead to look. One distinction runs through the whole page. The TFSA is an account with tax rules; it is not an investment. The limit decides how much you may put in. What happens to that money depends on what you buy inside the account, which can be a savings deposit, a GIC, a balanced fund or an equity fund, each with its own risk, fees and liquidity. The rule: $5,000, indexed since 2009, rounded to the nearest $500 Section 207.01 of the Income Tax Act defines the “TFSA dollar limit”. For 2009 to 2012 it was $5,000; for 2013 and 2014, $5,500; for 2015, $10,000. For every year after 2015 it is “$5,000 adjusted for each year after 2009” under section 117.1, rounded to the nearest multiple of $500, with an exact tie rounded up. CRA’s indexation page describes the same rule: the limit is fixed at $5,000, indexed for each year after 2009 and rounded to the nearest $500. Section 117.1 sets the yearly factor. It divides the average CPI for the 12 months ending on 30 September before the year by the average for the 12 months before that, subtracts one, and rounds to the nearest 0.1%. The same factors index the federal tax brackets and many credits, which is why the TFSA step and the bracket increase are announced together each autumn. Two features matter. First, the unrounded amount keeps compounding every year, whether or not the published limit moves. Second, the 2013–2014 and 2015 limits were written directly into the law, so they sit above or off the indexed path. Since 2016 every limit has been the rounded indexed amount. Chart 1: a smooth indexed amount, a stepped limit The first chart shows both lines. The dashed line is $5,000 compounded by each year’s factor. The solid line is the limit you actually receive. Recomputing the factors from Statistics Canada CPI gives 0.6% for 2010, 2.8% for 2012, 1.0% for 2021, then 6.3%, 4.7%, 2.7% and 2.0% for 2023 to 2026; the last four are exactly the rates CRA lists, and the rounded results reproduce every published limit from 2016 to 2026. By 2026 the unrounded amount is about $7,184.92 . That is closer to $7,000 than to $7,500, so the limit stayed at $7,000. Unless inflation is very low, a few more years of growth push it past $7,250 and the limit steps up. The large 2023 factor (6.3%) explains the quick move from $6,000 in 2022 to $6,500 in 2023 and $7,000 in 2024: high inflation brought the steps closer together. Change the inflation assumption and the projected steps move. At 2% a year after 2027, the projected limit is $8,000 by 2030, $8,500 by 2033 and $9,500 by 2039. At 1% the next steps arrive years later. These projections only apply the rule; they do not predict prices, and Parliament can change the rule itself, as it did in 2015 and 2016. Chart 2: rounding gives and takes, but never accumulates The second chart shows how far each year’s limit is from the unrounded amount. In 2018 the limit of $5,500 was about $222 below the indexed $5,721.70; in 2019 the limit of $6,000 was about $152 above $5,847.57. In 2026 the limit is about $185 below. Because the law compounds the unrounded amount, not the rounded limit, these gaps do not build up. A year when rounding gives less room is not carried forward as a deficit, and a generous year is not taken back. Over many years the published limits track the indexed amount closely; the bars bounce within $250 either side of zero. For a saver, the lesson is not to read policy into a single year’s figure. A flat limit after a year of inflation means the unrounded amount has not yet crossed the next halfway mark. A $500 jump after a mild year usually means it just did. Chart 3: what each year’s room is worth in today’s prices The third chart converts each year’s limit into September 2026 prices using the all-items CPI ( Statistics Canada table 18-10-0004-01 ), dividing CPI for September 2026 (170.0) by CPI for January of the year the room arrived. The 2009 limit of $5,000 is worth about $7,522 in those prices. The 2026 limit of $7,000 is worth about $7,212, because prices rose between January and September 2026. Most years land between about $7,000 and $7,750 in today’s prices. The outlier is 2015, whose $10,000 limit is worth about $13,677. Indexing has done what it was designed to do: each year’s new room buys roughly the same amount of goods and services. Added up, the $109,000 of limits from 2009 to 2026 is worth about $138,617 in September 2026 prices. If you turned 18 after 2009, enter your age; someone aged 29 at the end of 2026, first eligible in 2015, has $78,000 of limits worth about $94,148. These totals describe room, not wealth. Room only becomes wealth when money is contributed and invested, and they apply only to someone who has been 18 or older and resident in Canada in every year counted. What the September 2026 CPI implies for 2027 Statistics Canada’s CPI for September 2026 completes the averaging window for the 2027 factor. The average CPI for October 2025 to September 2026 is 167.525, against 163.275 for October 2024 to September 2025. The ratio gives a factor of 2.6% after rounding. Applied to the unrounded 2026 amount, it gives about $7,371.72, which rounds to $7,500 . Treat this as a calculation, not an announcement. When this page was checked on 26 October 2026, CRA’s limits page listed TFSA limits only to 2026 and CRA’s indexation page showed factors only to 2026. Section 117.1 also allows the CPI to be “adjusted in such manner as may be prescribed”. The margin here is wide: the unrounded amount would need to fall below $7,250 to keep the limit at $7,000, which would take a factor of 0.9% or less. Even so, contribute based on CRA’s published figure and your own room in My Account, not on this projection. A higher limit adds room on 1 January. It does not change room you already have, does not raise the limit on past years, and does not make any investment inside the account safer or more rewarding. Chart 4: how long the next steps take The heatmap asks how many years after 2026 the limit first reaches $7,500, $8,000, $8,500, $9,000 and $10,000, for constant inflation rates from 0.5% to 4% after 2027. Every row starts from the calculated $7,500 for 2027, so the first column is one year throughout. At 2% a year, the limit reaches $8,000 in four years, $9,000 in ten and $10,000 in sixteen. At 1% a year it takes seven years to reach $8,000 and thirty to reach $10,000. At 3% it reaches $10,000 in eleven. Each $500 step needs the unrounded amount to grow by about $500, which is around 7% of the current limit, so at 2% inflation a step arrives roughly every three to four years. Inflation does not arrive at a constant rate, so the real calendar will be lumpier than any single row. The rows are useful for planning a contribution budget: if you plan to fill your room each year from pay, expect the required amount to rise in occasional $500 jumps rather than every year. Using the limit sensibly inside a long-term plan Know your own room. The yearly limit is only one part. Unused room carries forward; amounts withdrawn are added back on 1 January of the following year; and over-contributions are taxed at 1% a month. The TFSA recontribution calendar follows those rules. Losses inside the account do not restore room; the loss and room guide shows why. Keep the account and the investment separate. Income and gains earned inside a TFSA are generally not taxed and withdrawals are not taxable, but those are account rules. A balanced fund held in a TFSA is still exposed to market falls, fund fees and uncertain returns. The asset location guide compares what to hold where. Distinguish new pay from an existing lump sum. Saving from each paycheque grows with income and the limit rises occasionally; moving an existing non-registered holding into a TFSA is a different decision, because transferring units in kind is a disposition at market value. The in-kind contribution guide covers it. Index your own contributions, not just the room. If your plan is to save a fixed share of income, the inflation-adjusted contribution guide shows why a flat dollar amount loses ground over decades. The RRSP and TFSA comparison covers which account to fill first.
documents.keywords: Why the TFSA limit is stuck at $7,000, and when it moves: inflation indexing in $500 steps Rebuild the TFSA dollar limit from the law: $5,000 indexed to CPI each year since 2009 and rounded to the nearest $500. See why the limit stays flat for years and then jumps, what 18 years of room is worth in today’s prices, and when the next steps arrive under different inflation rates.

documents.title: 在年终分派前买入基金：在非注册账户中的真实成本
documents.description: 在你买入几天后支付的分派，会把你自己的一部分钱作为应税收入还给你。比较同一笔买入在分派前和分派后进行：单位和市值相同，成本基础更高，税款现在缴、之后部分收回。看看成本如何取决于分派规模、税务性质和持有期。
documents.body: Buying a fund in a taxable account just before a distribution does not lose you any investment value, but it pulls tax forward. The cost base rises by the distribution, so part of that tax comes back when you sell. The lasting cost is the growth on the tax cash and, if the distribution is income rather than capital gains, the difference in tax rates. It is usually modest, it is zero in a TFSA or RRSP, and it is rarely worth staying out of the market for long to avoid. A December purchase and a February tax slip Many mutual funds and ETFs pay most of their yearly distribution in December, especially the capital gains the fund realized during the year. Someone who invests a bonus or a year-end lump sum in a non-registered account in mid-December may find, a few days later, that the fund has paid a distribution, the unit price has dropped by about the same amount, and a tax slip is on the way for income they feel they never earned. That feeling is correct in one sense. The distribution is not new profit for the buyer: it is a slice of their own purchase money handed back. But CRA taxes it like any other distribution. This guide puts numbers on the trade-off. The tool compares buying just before the distribution with buying just after, using the same amount of money, and follows both until the units are sold. The question only exists in a non-registered (taxable) account. Inside a TFSA, RRSP, RRIF, RESP or FHSA, distributions are not taxed in the year they are paid, so the date of purchase relative to a distribution makes no tax difference there. Why the distribution is your own money coming back A fund’s unit price is its net asset value per unit. When the fund pays a distribution, that cash leaves the fund, so the unit price falls by the distribution, all else being equal. With the defaults, $20,000 buys units just before a distribution of 8% of the price. The distribution is $1,600 and the units are then worth $18,400. Reinvested at the lower price, the $1,600 buys more units, and the holding is back to $20,000. Someone who waits and buys just after the distribution pays the lower price for the same $20,000 and ends up with exactly the same number of units . The first chart shows the result: equal market value, but a different adjusted cost base and a different tax bill this year. CRA’s guidance on mutual funds explains why. Distributions are taxed while you own the units, and if you reinvest them you must still report them, because you are considered to have received them before reinvesting. Reinvesting buys more units, which raises your average cost per unit. The early buyer’s cost base is $21,600 against the later buyer’s $20,000. That higher cost base is the record of the tax already paid. The character of the distribution sets the first bill A fund distribution can be capital gains, Canadian dividends, foreign income, interest, other income or return of capital, or a mix, and the T3 or T5 slip says which. Each is taxed differently. Capital gains are half included in income. Interest and foreign income are fully taxed. Eligible Canadian dividends get the gross-up and dividend tax credit. Return of capital is not taxed now; it lowers the cost base instead. The tool splits the distribution into a capital-gains part and an “everything else” part, and taxes the second at the full marginal rate. That is conservative for dividends and wrong for return of capital, which would cost nothing now. With 75% capital gains and a 29.65% rate, the $1,600 distribution brings $296.50 of tax: $177.90 on the capital-gains part and $118.60 on the rest. Year-end distributions of equity funds are often mostly capital gains; bond and balanced funds pay more interest through the year. The fund income-type guide compares these characters in detail, and the return-of-capital guide shows how a non-taxable distribution works in the other direction. Chart 2: part of the tax comes back when you sell Because the early buyer’s cost base is $1,600 higher, their capital gain on sale is $1,600 smaller. At half inclusion and 29.65%, that saves $237.20 of tax in the year of sale, whatever the sale price. If the units are sold for less than cost, the same $1,600 enlarges a capital loss instead. So the tax is not doubled; it is moved. The cost is in three places. First, the tax is paid now rather than years later, and the cash used to pay it cannot grow in the meantime. Second, the income part of the distribution was taxed in full, but it is recovered only through a capital gain that is half taxed: in the default, $118.60 paid on income comes back as $59.30 at sale. Third, the early buyer needs cash for the tax this year. The second chart shows the net cost by the year of sale. A sale right after the distribution leaves a net cost of $59.30, the tax-rate difference alone. After 10 years, with the tax cash earning 2.5% after tax, the net cost is about $142 in year-10 dollars, or about $111 in today’s dollars, roughly 0.56% of the $20,000 invested. In today’s dollars about 62% of the first-year tax is won back. Chart 3: where the cost comes from The waterfall breaks the year-10 cost into its parts: $177.90 of tax on the capital-gains part, $118.60 on the income part, $83.05 of growth forgone on that $296.50, less the $237.20 of capital-gains tax saved at the sale. The total is $142.35. Read it as a timing cost, not a loss of investment value. Both buyers own the same units throughout, and the after-tax value of the early buyer’s holding, net of the tax already paid, trails the later buyer’s by only that amount. A large fall in the market a few weeks after either purchase would matter far more than this difference. The cost rises with the size of the distribution, the share taxed as income, your marginal rate and the length of time before you sell. It falls if the distribution is mostly return of capital, if you are in a low bracket this year and expect a higher one later, or if you were going to sell soon anyway. Chart 4: distribution size and holding period The heatmap scales the result to $10,000 invested and varies the distribution from 2% to 16% of the unit price and the year of sale from 1 to 30. With the other defaults, a 2% distribution costs about $8 to $23 in today’s dollars per $10,000; an 8% distribution about $33 to $92; an unusually large 16% distribution about $65 to $183. Large year-end distributions usually come from funds that sold appreciated holdings during the year, for example after a strong market, a manager change or heavy redemptions by other investors. Fund companies often publish estimated year-end distributions in November or early December, with a record date that decides who receives them. Checking the estimate before a large December purchase is cheap; the actual amount and its character are confirmed only on the tax slip. A fund that distributes little and grows mostly through unrealized gains defers tax for its holders in general, which is one reason fund turnover and distribution history matter for non-registered accounts beyond the December question. Should you wait until after the distribution? Inside a registered account, ignore it. In a TFSA, RRSP, RRIF, RESP or FHSA the distribution is not taxed when paid. The account’s rules, not the fund, decide that: a fund is not tax-exempt in itself. In a taxable account, compare a few days with the cost. If the record date is days away and the estimated distribution is large, waiting for it to pass is a reasonable, low-cost habit. Waiting weeks or months to save a cost of this size is market timing, and missing a rise could easily cost more; the waiting-for-a-dip guide shows how cash rules drift. Keep the cost base records. Reinvested distributions raise your adjusted cost base. Many platforms track it, but CRA expects you to calculate it for each fund and series. Missing the reinvested amounts means paying tax twice on the same money when you sell. Keep the cash for the tax. A reinvested distribution produces no cash. The tax cash provision guide shows how to set money aside for it. Do not let tax drive the choice of fund. Diversification, fees, risk and the time until you need the money matter more than one distribution. Returns are uncertain; a fund bought after its distribution can still fall.
documents.keywords: Buying a fund just before its year-end distribution: what it really costs in a non-registered account A distribution paid days after you buy hands part of your own money back as taxable income. Follow the same purchase made just before and just after the distribution: identical units and value, a higher cost base, tax paid now and partly won back later. See how the cost depends on distribution size, its tax character and how long you hold.

documents.keywords: Net cost of buying before, by the year the units are sold Year 0 is a sale immediately after the distribution: the higher cost base creates a capital loss that offsets $237 of tax. The later the sale, the longer the tax cash has been missing and the less a dollar of future tax saving is worth today. Because part of the distribution is taxed as income in full but recovered only as a half-included capital loss or smaller gain, the cost never falls to zero.
