documents.title: 2026 年转移配偶未用的年龄额、养老金额、残疾额和学费额：附表 2 如何运作
documents.description: 2026 年第 32600 行实例指南：配偶或同居伴侣的哪些抵免可以转给另一方，附表 2 如何确定未用部分，它与第 30300 行配偶额的关系，为何 CPP 和 OAS 不会产生养老金额，5,000 加元学费上限，申报人税款太少用不上的情况，以及 CRA 关于谁在申报的统计。六张图表和可编辑模型。
documents.body: For 2026 a spouse can pass the other the part of their age amount (up to CAD 9,208), pension income amount (up to CAD 2,000), disability amount (CAD 10,341) and current-year tuition (up to CAD 5,000) that they do not need to bring their own federal tax to zero. Schedule 2 takes those amounts, subtracts the spouse’s taxable income less their basic personal amount and payroll credits, and the rest goes on line 32600. It is worth 14% federally, and only against tax the claimant actually owes. What Schedule 2 moves Most federal credits are non-refundable : they reduce tax owed, and anything a person cannot use is gone. When one spouse or common-law partner has little taxable income, several of their credits would be wasted. Line 32600 lets the other spouse claim the unused part of five of them, calculated on Schedule 2 : the age amount (line 30100), for a spouse 65 or older at the end of the year; the Canada caregiver amount for infirm children under 18 (line 30500), if the spouse claimed it; the pension income amount (line 31400); the disability amount for the spouse themselves (line 31600); the spouse’s current-year tuition amount , up to CAD 5,000, as designated on their T2202, TL11A or TL11C. The 2026 figures are CRA’s published amounts after 2.0% indexation; the CAD 2,000 and CAD 5,000 caps are fixed dollar amounts. The age amount reaches zero at CAD 46,432 + 9,208 ÷ 15% ≈ CAD 107,819 of net income (derived). At 14%, a full age amount is worth CAD 1,289.12 of federal tax, the pension amount CAD 280 and the disability amount CAD 1,447.74. Who can use it, and what does not count Under the CRA rules for line 32600 you can claim the transfer if you had a spouse or common-law partner at the end of the year, they qualified for at least one of the amounts above, and they did not need all of them to reduce their federal tax to zero. You cannot claim it if you were separated because of a breakdown in the relationship for 90 days or more including 31 December. If the spouse does not file, you use the amounts they would have entered and attach their slips. Three details often trip up households: CPP, QPP and OAS are not pension income for the pension amount. Eligible pension income at 65 or older includes registered pension plan lifetime payments, RRIF and LIF payments, annuity payments and pension income split to you under an election. Under 65, it is mainly a lifetime pension from a registered pension plan, plus certain amounts received because of a spouse’s death. A 66-year-old with CPP and OAS only has no pension amount to transfer; CAD 2,000 a year from a RRIF creates the full one. Only current-year tuition moves . Tuition carried forward from an earlier year stays with the student. The CAD 5,000 cap is reduced by the current-year tuition the student uses themselves, even if some of the year’s amount is still unused. The age amount depends on the spouse’s own net income , not the couple’s. A spouse with CAD 60,000 of income has an age amount of CAD 9,208 − 15% × (60,000 − 46,432) = CAD 7,172.80, but with that income they would need it all. How Schedule 2 works out the unused part The schedule is short. It adds up what the spouse qualifies for, measures how much of that they need, and transfers the difference: Lines 1 to 6: add the spouse’s age amount, caregiver amount for infirm children, pension income amount, disability amount and the tuition designated to you. Line 7: the spouse’s taxable income. If it is above the top of the lowest bracket (CAD 57,375 on the 2025 form), use their federal tax on that income divided by the lowest rate instead, which turns higher-rate tax into an equivalent amount at 14.5% (14% for 2026). Lines 8 to 11: add the spouse’s basic personal amount (line 30000), their line 96 (CPP and EI credits, the Canada employment amount and a few others such as the home buyers’ amount) and the tuition they used themselves (line 32300). Line 12: line 7 minus line 11, not below zero. This is the spouse’s adjusted taxable income , the part of the five amounts they need. Line 13: line 6 minus line 12, not below zero, goes on line 32600 of your return. The model’s default is a retired couple. The lower-income spouse is 67 with CAD 20,000 of income: CAD 16,000 of CPP and OAS and a CAD 4,000 RRIF payment. The claimant is 68 with CAD 85,000, CAD 40,000 of it from a workplace pension. The spouse’s own federal tax is 14% × CAD 20,000 = CAD 2,800. Their basic personal amount and the CAD 3,548 of age and pension amounts they keep give 14% × CAD 20,000 = CAD 2,800 of credits, so they owe nothing federally and the CAD 7,660 they could not use moves across. The claimant has about CAD 10,559 of federal tax left after their own basic, age and pension credits, so they use the CAD 1,072.40 in full. Without the transfer that value would simply be lost. The spouse amount and the transfer are separate claims Line 30300, the spouse or common-law partner amount, is a different credit. It is the claimant’s basic personal amount (CAD 16,452 for 2026 below CAD 181,440 of the claimant’s net income) minus the spouse’s net income, and it applies at any age. The claimant can make both claims in the same year. The first chart moves the spouse’s income with everything else fixed: With no income , the spouse needs none of their amounts. The claimant gets the full CAD 16,452 spouse amount and the full age amount of CAD 9,208 on line 32600 (CAD 3,592.40 together at 14%; the pension amount is zero because there is no pension income). Up to CAD 16,452 , the spouse amount falls dollar for dollar, while the transfer stays complete because the spouse’s basic personal amount alone covers their income. Above CAD 16,452 , the spouse amount is zero and each extra dollar of the spouse’s income keeps one more dollar of age and pension amounts on their own return. In the default, the transfer reaches zero at CAD 16,452 + 9,208 + 2,000 = CAD 27,660 . So the transfer reaches further up the income scale than the spouse amount. For a pensioner couple, the spouse amount often ends with OAS and CPP alone, while line 32600 can still carry several thousand dollars of age amount. What the spouse qualifies for changes the reach The grid compares five kinds of spouse at incomes from zero to CAD 60,000, with all income treated as pension or other non-employment income: Age amount only (CPP and OAS, no RRIF or pension): the full CAD 9,208 moves until the spouse’s income passes CAD 16,452, and nothing is left at CAD 25,660. Age and pension amounts : CAD 11,208 at most, ending at CAD 27,660. Drawing CAD 2,000 a year from a RRIF from 65 is often enough to create the pension amount, which then transfers in part or in full. Age, pension and disability : CAD 21,549 at most, and CAD 8,001 is still left at CAD 30,000 of income; the transfer ends at CAD 38,001. With 2026 rates that combination is worth up to CAD 3,016.86 to the claimant. Disability amount, under 65 : CAD 10,341 until the spouse’s income passes the basic personal amount, ending at CAD 26,793. CAD 8,000 of tuition, under 65 : at most CAD 5,000 moves. A student spouse with CAD 20,000 of income uses CAD 3,548 of the tuition themselves, transfers CAD 1,452 and carries the other CAD 3,000 forward to their own future years. A spouse with employment income also has CPP, EI and Canada employment credits on line 96, which raise line 11 and leave more to transfer. In the model’s tuition example, a student spouse earning CAD 12,000 has CAD 18,569.35 of basic and payroll credits, more than their income, so they transfer the full CAD 5,000. When the claimant cannot use it The transfer helps only if the claimant has federal tax left after their own credits. For a retired claimant those include their own basic personal amount, their own age amount (reduced by their income) and their own pension amount. In the default, the claimant at CAD 85,000 has an age amount of CAD 3,422.80 and about CAD 10,559 of tax left. If both spouses have CAD 20,000 of income, the claimant’s own CAD 16,452 basic, CAD 9,208 age and CAD 2,000 pension amounts already exceed their income, so the CAD 1,072.40 credit from the transfer is entirely wasted. It cannot go back to the spouse, and unused age, pension and disability amounts cannot be carried forward. The claimant-income chart shows the credit becoming usable only once the claimant’s income passes about CAD 27,660, and fully usable a little above CAD 35,000. Schedule 2 only moves amounts the spouse cannot use. If the spouse needs all of them, line 13 is zero whatever the claimant’s income, so the transfer never pushes tax onto the lower-income spouse. How it interacts with pension income splitting Pension income splitting on Form T1032 moves up to half of eligible pension income from one spouse to the other for tax purposes. It changes both sides of Schedule 2: the receiving spouse’s taxable income on line 7 rises, so they need more of their own amounts and less is left to transfer; split pension income counts as eligible pension income for the receiving spouse, so a spouse with only CPP and OAS gains a pension amount of up to CAD 2,000; the transferring spouse’s lower net income can increase their own age amount and reduce OAS recovery tax. The two tools therefore do not add up simply. Tax software usually tests split percentages and then runs Schedule 2 on the result. This model holds incomes as entered and does not optimise a split; the separate pension income splitting guide models the election, including the age amount and OAS recovery. Who claims it: CRA statistics CRA’s final statistics for the 2024 tax year (data as of 30 November 2025) count 1,497,600 returns with line 32600, claiming CAD 10.67 billion of amounts, about CAD 7,122 per return. For scale, 7,268,130 returns claimed an age amount, 6,024,730 a pension income amount and 2,382,380 a spouse amount. Claims are most frequent among claimants with CAD 10,000 to 30,000 of income: about 87 to 89 per 1,000 returns, against about 20 to 22 per 1,000 above CAD 100,000. That pattern is consistent with older couples on modest incomes moving age and pension amounts, but the table does not record ages, the amounts transferred by type or whether the claimant could use them. Counts are rounded to the nearest ten; the grouped amounts add to CAD 10,665,311 thousand against the CAD 10,665,312 thousand total because of rounding. Checklist and limits of the model Complete the spouse’s return, or a notional one, first: Schedule 2 uses their line 30000, line 96, line 32300 and taxable income. Confirm the pension amount comes from eligible pension income; CPP, QPP, OAS and GIS do not count, and a RRIF payment counts from 65. Check the age amount against the spouse’s own net income, and note the year they turn 65 (born 1961 or earlier for 2026). For tuition, the student designates the amount on the back of the T2202; carried-forward tuition stays with them. For a new disability claim, the spouse needs an approved Form T2201. Complete the provincial or territorial Schedule 2 too; provinces use their own amounts, and Quebec is separate. The model covers federal amounts only and treats net income as taxable income. It includes the basic personal amount and the CPP, EI and Canada employment credits from employment income on the spouse’s line 11, but not the home buyers’, home accessibility, adoption or volunteer amounts, nor the caregiver amount for infirm children. The claimant’s room allows for their own basic, age, pension, CPP and EI credits but not medical expenses, donations, dividend tax credits or other claims that would also use their tax. It does not model the infirm-spouse addition to line 30300, pension splitting, OAS recovery tax or provincial credits. Use CRA’s schedules or tax software for an actual return.
documents.keywords: Transferring a spouse’s unused age, pension, disability and tuition amounts in 2026: how Schedule 2 works A worked guide to line 32600 for 2026: which of a spouse’s or common-law partner’s credits can move to the other, how Schedule 2 decides the unused part, how it sits beside the spouse amount on line 30300, why CPP and OAS do not create a pension amount, the CAD 5,000 tuition cap, when the claimant has too little tax to use it, and CRA statistics on who claims. Six charts and an editable model.

documents.keywords: Claimant’s usable credit by the claimant’s own income The claimant must still have federal tax after their own basic, age and pension credits to use the transfer. A low-income claimant gains little; the available credit also falls a little above CAD 181,440, where the claimant’s basic personal amount, and with it any spouse amount, begins to shrink.

documents.title: 2026 年把残疾税收抵免转移给扶养亲属：能转多少，以及照顾者额
documents.description: 一篇实例指南，讲解如何把 2026 年未用完的残疾额从受抚养人转给扶养他们的父母、子女或其他亲属：谁符合资格、决定还剩多少可转移的 CRA 工作表、儿童补充额、加拿大照顾者额、扶养人之间的分摊、扶养人税款太少用不上的情况，以及 CRA 关于谁在申报的统计。六张图表和一个可编辑模型。
documents.body: For 2026 the disability amount is CAD 10,341 (up to CAD 16,373 for a child under 18). A supporting relative can claim only the part the dependant does not need: the lesser of the disability amount and that amount plus the dependant’s basic credits minus their taxable income. An adult dependant with little income may also make the supporter eligible for a Canada caregiver amount of up to CAD 8,773. Both are worth 14% federally, and only against tax the supporter actually owes. What the transfer is The disability tax credit (DTC) is a non-refundable credit for a person with a severe and prolonged impairment whose Form T2201 has been approved by the CRA. It is claimed on line 31600 of that person’s return. Many people who qualify have little or no taxable income, so the credit would be wasted on their own return. The tax system lets the unused part move to someone who supports them: Line 31800 , for a dependant who is your (or your spouse’s) parent, grandparent, child, grandchild, brother, sister, aunt, uncle, niece or nephew, or for whom you claimed or could have claimed the eligible dependant amount. Line 32600 (Schedule 2) , when the person with the disability is your spouse or common-law partner. That route is separate and is not modelled here. The 2026 figures are CRA’s published amounts after 2.0% indexation. The 2026 child maximum (CAD 10,341 + 6,032) and the caregiver end point (CAD 8,773 + 20,601) are derived; the same sums for 2025 match the CAD 16,052 and CAD 28,798 printed on the 2025 forms. At 14%, the base amount is worth CAD 1,447.74 of federal tax and the child maximum CAD 2,292.22. Who can claim it Under the CRA rules for line 31800 you can claim all or part of a dependant’s disability amount if all of these apply: The CRA has approved Form T2201 for the dependant for the year. The dependant was resident in Canada at any time in the year. They depended on you for all or some of the basic necessities of life, such as food, shelter and clothing, on a regular and consistent basis. They do not need all of the amount to reduce their own tax. You claimed, or could have claimed, the eligible dependant amount (line 30400) for them, or the Canada caregiver amount for an infirm dependant 18 or older (line 30450), in the CRA’s “could have if they had no income” sense. For a child under 18, the parent or guardian approved on the T2201 makes the claim. You cannot claim it if the person’s spouse or common-law partner already claims the disability amount or any other non-refundable credit (other than medical expenses) for them, and generally not if you pay support for that child. Several supporters may split the claim, but together they cannot claim more than the dependant’s maximum, and nobody can split it with a person who claimed the eligible dependant amount for that dependant. A separate rule matters for families paying for care: if full-time care in a nursing home, or attendant care beyond the limited amount, is claimed as a medical expense for the person, nobody can claim the disability amount for them that year. The CRA’s Medical Expenses guide allows attendant-care wages of up to CAD 10,000 (CAD 20,000 in the year of death) alongside the disability amount; families with large care bills should compare both routes. How much is left to transfer The CRA’s Federal Worksheet for line 31800 works it out in three steps: Start with the dependant’s disability amount (CAD 10,341, or more for a child under 18). Add the dependant’s line 98 amount: the total of their own basic personal amount, age amount, spouse and dependant amounts, CPP and EI credits, Canada employment amount, pension income amount and the other credits listed before line 31600 on the return. Subtract the dependant’s taxable income. The transfer is the lesser of the disability amount and the result (not below zero). In plain terms: the dependant keeps just enough of the disability amount, together with their other credits, to bring their federal tax to zero, and the rest can move. As long as the dependant’s taxable income is below their own line 98 credits, the whole disability amount transfers. The model’s default is an adult child, 24, with CAD 24,000 of net income, CAD 18,000 of it from a part-time job, supported by a parent with CAD 85,000 of employment income. The dependant’s own federal tax before the disability amount is CAD 3,360 − 14% × CAD 18,964.15 = CAD 705.02, which is exactly 14% of the CAD 5,035.85 they keep, so the worksheet leaves them owing nothing federally. The parent has about CAD 10,458 of federal tax left after their own basic credits, enough to use the CAD 1,495.08 in full. In the model, line 98 includes only the basic personal amount and the credits from employment income; a dependant with other amounts would keep less and transfer more. What happens as the dependant earns more The first chart moves the dependant’s income with everything else fixed. Three ranges matter: Below the dependant’s own line 98 credits (about CAD 18,964 in the default), the whole CAD 10,341 transfers. Above that , each extra dollar of taxable income reduces the transfer by a dollar, because the dependant now needs that much more of the credit. With CAD 18,000 of employment income the transfer reaches zero at about CAD 29,305 . The caregiver amount runs on a separate clock: the full CAD 8,773 until the dependant’s net income passes CAD 20,601, then down a dollar per dollar to zero at CAD 29,374. For a dependant with no income at all, the parent can claim CAD 10,341 + CAD 8,773 = CAD 19,114, worth CAD 2,675.96 federally. At CAD 24,000 the dependant uses part of the disability credit themselves, so the family total is CAD 705.02 + CAD 1,495.08 = CAD 2,200.10: less in the parent’s hands, but the dependant also pays no federal tax on CAD 24,000. A child under 18: the supplement and care expenses For a child under 18 at the end of the year, the disability amount includes a supplement of up to CAD 6,032, reduced by child care and attendant care expenses claimed for the child (by anyone, for example as child care expenses or medical expenses) above CAD 3,533. The total therefore runs from CAD 16,373 down to the CAD 10,341 base once those expenses reach CAD 9,565. No care expenses claimed: CAD 16,373, worth CAD 2,292.22 at 14%. CAD 5,000 of care expenses: CAD 6,032 − (CAD 5,000 − 3,533) = CAD 4,565 supplement; total CAD 14,906, worth CAD 2,086.84. A child with no income needs none of it, so the whole amount transfers to the parent approved on the T2201. The caregiver amount on line 30450 is for dependants 18 or older; for an infirm child under 18, a separate CAD 2,740 amount (line 30500) applies and is not modelled here. When the supporter cannot use it The transfer moves an amount , not cash. It becomes valuable only if the supporter has federal tax to reduce. In the default, a parent with CAD 20,000 of employment income has only CAD 126.59 of federal tax left after the basic personal amount, Canada employment amount and CPP and EI credits. The CAD 1,495.08 credit would be cut to CAD 126.59 and the other CAD 1,368.49 would be lost : it does not go back to the dependant, and it does not carry forward. That is why, when two relatives support the same person, it is usually better for the one with more tax to claim, or to split so that each claim fits within each claimant’s tax. A 50/50 split in the default gives each claimant CAD 5,339.58 of amounts and CAD 747.54 of credit, the same CAD 1,495.08 in total, provided each has that much tax. The model’s share input shows the effect for one claimant. What the official figures show CRA’s statistics for the 2024 tax year (data as of 30 November 2025) show: The line 31800 average is above the 2024 base amount (CAD 9,872) because transfers for children include the supplement and one return can include more than one dependant. Measured against all returns in each total-income range, line 31800 claims rise from about 6 per 1,000 returns under CAD 10,000 to about 24 per 1,000 at CAD 150,000–249,999. That pattern fits transfers going to the relative who has tax to reduce, but the table counts returns, not families, and does not show why people claim or not. Counts are rounded to the nearest ten. A practical checklist Get the T2201 approved first. Nothing transfers until the CRA approves it; approval can cover past years. File the dependant’s return , even with little income, so their taxable income and line 98 credits are on record; the transfer is calculated from them. Check the caregiver amount for an adult dependant whose net income is below CAD 29,374. Choose the claimant with enough federal tax, or split between supporters so each claim can be used. Watch large care bills. Claiming full-time nursing-home or unlimited attendant care as a medical expense rules out the disability amount for that year; compare both routes. Remember the province. Provincial credits have their own amounts and rates and transfer through the provincial forms. Limits of the model The model is federal only and uses 2026 amounts with the structure of the 2025 worksheet. It treats net income as taxable income for both people and includes in the dependant’s line 98 only the basic personal amount, Canada employment amount and base CPP and EI credits on the employment income entered; age, pension, home buyers’ and other amounts are left out. The supporter’s tax is estimated from 2026 brackets after the same basic credits, so other credits that would use up the supporter’s tax first are ignored. It does not model the spouse transfer (Schedule 2), the eligible dependant amount, the line 30500 child amount, medical expenses, the attendant-care choice, provincial credits or the Registered Disability Savings Plan and Canada Disability Benefit, which use DTC eligibility but are separate programs. Use tax software or the CRA worksheets for an actual return.
documents.keywords: Transferring the disability tax credit to a supporting relative in 2026: how much moves, and the caregiver amount A worked guide to moving the unused 2026 disability amount from a dependant to the parent, child or other relative who supports them: who qualifies, the CRA worksheet that decides how much is left to transfer, the child supplement, the Canada caregiver amount, splitting between supporters, when the supporter has too little tax to use it, and CRA statistics on who claims. Six charts and an editable model.

documents.title: 2026 年医疗费用税收抵免：2,890 加元门槛、哪位配偶申报，以及 12 个月期间
documents.description: 2026 年联邦医疗费用税收抵免详解：取 3% 或 2,890 加元中较低者的门槛、为什么通常由收入较低的配偶申报以及这个建议何时失效、如何选择 12 个月期间、成年受抚养人的单独申报、可退还医疗费用补助，以及 CRA 关于申报人群的统计。六张图表和一个可编辑模型。
documents.body: For 2026, eligible medical expenses count only above the lesser of 3% of the claimant’s net income and CAD 2,890; the rest earns a 14% federal credit. A lower-income spouse has a lower threshold, but a non-refundable credit is worth nothing to someone with no federal tax, so check the tax that is left before choosing. Picking a 12-month window that holds two years’ bills applies the threshold once instead of twice. What the credit is and how it is calculated The medical expense tax credit (METC) is a non-refundable federal credit for eligible medical expenses paid by you or your spouse or common-law partner. It reduces federal tax payable; it cannot create a refund on its own. Every province and territory has its own version with its own rate and threshold. For the 2026 tax year the federal calculation is: Add up eligible expenses for you, your spouse and your children born in 2009 or later that were paid in a 12-month period ending in 2026 (line 33099). Subtract the lesser of 3% of the claimant’s net income (line 23600) and CAD 2,890 . Add the allowable amount for each other dependant (line 33199), worked out the same way but with the dependant’s own net income. Multiply the total (line 33200) by 14% , the lowest federal rate for 2026. The 2026 amounts are CRA’s published figures, indexed by 2.0%. The 14% rate follows the cut in the lowest federal rate from 15% (14.5% for 2025 as a whole). The two “at which” rows are derived: CAD 2,890 ÷ 3% and CAD 33,960 + 1,534 ÷ 5%; the 2025 supplement end point matches the CAD 63,374 limit CRA publishes. Eligible expenses include, among others, prescription drugs, dental and vision care, many medical devices, travel for treatment not available locally, and premiums paid to a private health services plan, including the employee share of a group plan. An amount that was or will be reimbursed by an insurer or employer plan is not eligible. CRA’s RC4065 guide and the folio list what qualifies. The threshold is personal, and that is why the claimant matters The threshold is based on the net income of the spouse who claims, not on family income. The CRA page itself notes that it may benefit you if the spouse with the lower net income claims. Either spouse can claim expenses for either of them and for their children, whoever’s name is on the receipt, as long as the same expense is not claimed twice. Below CAD 96,333.33 of net income the threshold is 3% of income; above it, it is the fixed CAD 2,890. Moving the claim from a spouse earning CAD 70,000 (threshold CAD 2,100) to one earning CAD 26,000 (threshold CAD 780) adds CAD 1,320 of allowable expenses and CAD 184.80 of federal credit. The model’s default is that couple. Person A has CAD 70,000 of employment income; Person B has CAD 26,000 of net income, CAD 20,000 of it from employment. They paid CAD 4,500 of eligible family expenses and CAD 1,800 for an adult child with CAD 9,000 of net income. “Federal tax left” is the model’s estimate: tax on net income at the 2026 rates, less 14% of the basic personal amount (CAD 16,452), the Canada employment amount (up to CAD 1,501) and base CPP and EI contributions on the employment income entered. Person B’s CAD 966.59 is enough to absorb CAD 735, so here the usual advice holds. When the lower-income spouse is the wrong claimant A non-refundable credit only reduces tax that would otherwise be payable. If the lower-income spouse owes little or no federal tax, the lower threshold does not help, and the unused medical credit cannot be transferred to the other spouse or carried forward. (Unclaimed expenses can sometimes be claimed in a later year if they fall in a 12-month window ending in that year, but not ones already claimed.) In the first case Person B’s threshold is lower (CAD 360), but B has no federal tax left after the basic personal amount, so B could only collect the refundable supplement. Person A uses the whole CAD 672 credit and also qualifies for a smaller supplement, because the supplement depends on family net income, which is the same whoever claims. In the second case the spouse with no income cannot use any of the credit. The test is simple: compare the federal value, including the supplement, for each spouse. Tax software does this if you try both. Choosing the 12-month period You may claim expenses paid in any 12-month period ending in the tax year , as long as they were not claimed before. For someone who died in the year, the period is 24 months and must include the date of death. The period does not have to be the calendar year. This matters when large bills straddle 31 December. Suppose Person B in the default pays CAD 2,250 for dental work in November 2026 and another CAD 2,250 in April 2027: Calendar years: 2026 claim CAD 2,250 − 780 + 1,530 dependant = CAD 3,000, credit CAD 420; 2027 claim CAD 2,250 − 780 = CAD 1,470, credit CAD 205.80. Total CAD 625.80 . One window, May 2026 to April 2027, claimed on the 2027 return: CAD 4,500 − 780 + 1,530 = CAD 5,250, credit CAD 735 . The difference, CAD 109.20, is one threshold (CAD 780) at 14%. The cost is waiting a year to claim the 2026 bills, and the 2026 bills cannot also be claimed in 2026. When one year’s share is below the threshold, splitting can lose its credit entirely; the window chart shows this across splits. The model keeps both years at 2026 incomes and amounts; in practice the 2027 threshold and rate may differ. Other dependants: a separate threshold for each one Line 33199 is for dependants other than your spouse and minor children: for example an adult child, a grandchild, or a parent, grandparent, brother, sister, aunt, uncle, niece or nephew who depended on you for support (relatives other than children must have lived in Canada at some time in the year). For each one, the expenses are reduced by the lesser of 3% of that dependant’s net income and CAD 2,890, so a dependant with little income has almost no threshold. There is no longer a dollar cap on the amount claimed for a dependant. In the default, the adult child’s CAD 9,000 of income gives a CAD 270 threshold, so CAD 1,530 of the CAD 1,800 counts. Either spouse can include it, and it is added to the claimant’s line 33200, so it also enlarges the base for the supplement. The refundable medical expense supplement The supplement (line 45200) is refundable: it is paid even if no tax is owed. For 2026 it is the lesser of CAD 1,534 and 25% of the allowable expenses on line 33200 (plus 25% of any disability supports deduction), reduced by 5% of family net income above CAD 33,960. The claimant must be at least 18 at the end of the year, resident in Canada all year, and have at least CAD 4,478 of employment and self-employment income. Family net income is the claimant’s plus their spouse’s, so the reduction is the same whichever spouse claims; what changes is the claimant’s allowable amount and whether that claimant meets the working-income minimum. For a single person with CAD 18,000 of net income (CAD 9,000 from work) and CAD 3,000 of expenses, the allowable amount is CAD 2,460, the supplement is CAD 615 and the non-refundable credit is wasted because no federal tax is owed. With no working income, as for many retirees, there would be no supplement either. What the official figures show CRA’s statistics for the 2024 tax year (data as of 30 November 2025) show 5,828,020 returns with an allowable medical expense amount, out of 31,564,160 returns, for a total of CAD 20.33 billion of allowable expenses (after thresholds). That is about 18.5% of returns and an average of about CAD 3,489 per claiming return. The claim rate peaks at about 30% of returns in the CAD 30,000–50,000 ranges and falls at higher incomes, where the fixed threshold (CAD 2,759 for 2024) applies and couples tend to claim on the lower-income spouse’s return. These are counts of returns, not households, and the averages are allowable amounts after the threshold, not total spending. The pattern is descriptive and does not show why people do or do not claim. Finance Canada’s 2026 tax expenditure report puts the federal cost of the credit at about CAD 2.2 billion in 2024 and CAD 2.37 billion in 2026, and the supplement at about CAD 230 million and CAD 245 million. The report labels its columns as estimates and projections; later years are projections. A practical checklist Keep receipts and plan statements. Claim only the part not reimbursed by an insurer or employer plan, and include your own share of private health plan premiums. Try each spouse. Compare the federal value for each, counting the supplement and the tax actually left to absorb the credit; add the provincial credit, which has its own threshold and rate. Pick the window. Look at the last 24 months of receipts and choose the 12-month period ending this year that holds the most unclaimed expenses. Claim dependants separately. An adult child or parent with low income has a small threshold of their own. Remember what does not carry. An unused non-refundable credit is not transferable to the other spouse and does not carry forward, but expenses never claimed can still fall in next year’s window. Limits of the model The model is federal only and uses 2026 amounts. It estimates federal tax with the 2026 brackets, treats net income as taxable income, and allows only the basic personal amount, Canada employment amount and base CPP and EI credits on the employment income entered (self-employment is treated as employment for these credits). Other credits that would use up tax first, such as the age, pension, disability, tuition and donation credits, are not included, so the tax left may be overstated. It assigns all family and dependant expenses to one claimant, assumes every expense is eligible and unreimbursed, and leaves out provincial and territorial credits, the disability supports deduction, the top-up tax credit and the Quebec abatement. Use tax software or the CRA worksheets for your actual return.
documents.keywords: Medical expense tax credit 2026: the CAD 2,890 threshold, which spouse should claim and the 12-month window A worked guide to the 2026 federal medical expense tax credit: the lesser-of-3%-or-CAD-2,890 threshold, why the lower-income spouse usually claims and when that advice fails, choosing the 12-month period, separate claims for adult dependants, the refundable medical expense supplement and CRA statistics on who claims. Six charts and an editable model.

documents.description: 追踪一个每月供款计划经历假设的市场下跌和回升。比较继续供款与把新资金以现金形式等到原高点再投入，看看哪几个月的供款贡献最大，并找出账户何时回到投入资金以上。
documents.body: Contributions made during a fall buy more units, so an account fed from pay can be back above its contributions well before the market regains its old peak. Pausing in cash avoids buying into further losses, but if a recovery comes, it waits for prices to return before buying. Neither choice makes a recovery happen, and money you may need soon should not be in the fund at all. The month the statement turns red Someone who invests a fixed amount from every paycheque into a balanced or equity fund will, sooner or later, open a statement showing that the account is worth less than the money put in. A common reaction is to stop the automatic contribution and keep the money in savings “until things settle down”. It feels like the cautious choice: why buy more of something that is falling? This guide follows the arithmetic of that choice month by month. It is about new money arriving from earned pay , a stream of contributions that would not exist all at once. Deciding how to invest an existing lump sum, such as an inheritance or the proceeds of a sale, is a different question, compared in the lump-sum and phased-investing guide . Deciding whether to sell what is already invested is different again, and is tested in the exit-and-re-entry guide . A hypothetical fall and recovery The default scenario starts with CAD 20,000 already invested at a market peak and adds CAD 500 at each month-end. The market falls 35% over 18 months, so the price at the low is 65% of the old peak. It then takes 42 more months to climb back, regaining the old peak in month 60, and grows 6% a year afterwards. Each phase moves by the same percentage every month, a smooth shape chosen so that each effect can be seen; real markets move in jumps and false starts. The comparison plan stops buying in month 1, holds every contribution in cash earning 2.5% a year, invests all of that cash in one purchase in month 60 when prices are back at the old peak, and then resumes the monthly contribution. Both plans put in exactly the same money: CAD 50,000 by month 60 and CAD 68,000 by month 96. The recovery length is the decisive assumption, and it is the one nobody knows in advance. The Ontario Securities Commission’s investor site notes that markets have historically recovered from declines but that this can take months or several years. Change the inputs to try a faster bounce, a slower climb, or a recovery that does not arrive within the horizon. What the two plans are worth along the way The first chart plots both account values against the money put in. At the low in month 18, the continued plan is worth about CAD 20,400 against CAD 29,000 contributed; the paused plan is worth about CAD 22,159, because the CAD 9,000 held in cash did not fall. This is the stretch that makes pausing feel right. The picture changes on the way back up. In month 60, when the market is exactly at its old peak, the continued plan is worth about CAD 57,500 , while the paused plan is worth about CAD 51,898 after investing its cash at the peak price. By month 96 the values are about CAD 88,104 and CAD 81,432 . The gap of roughly CAD 6,672 comes from the units that the monthly contributions bought below the old peak, less the interest the paused cash earned. Set the cash rate to 0% and the paused plan ends at about CAD 79,172; the interest on the waiting cash is worth roughly CAD 2,260 here, not enough to close the gap. The result reverses if the market keeps falling or stays below the old peak for the whole horizon: then every unit bought during the fall is still at a loss, and holding cash would have been better. The model does not know which world you are in. Back above your contributions before the market is back The second chart compares two ratios: the market price as a share of the old peak, and the account value as a share of the money put in. With contributions continued, the account is back above its contributions in month 46 , 14 months before the market regains its peak. At that point the market price is still about 13% below the peak. The paused plan crosses in month 53, helped by its cash interest and by the partial recovery of its starting balance. The reason is the average price. The 60 contributions made until the peak returned bought their units at an average price of about 80% of the old peak . FINRA describes this as a benefit of regular investing in a decline: a fixed amount buys more units when prices are lower. The same page sets out the limits: holding cash and spreading purchases out often produces lower returns than investing at once, especially over longer periods, and per-transaction fees can erode returns. The heatmap repeats the break-even month for different fall sizes and starting balances, keeping the 60-month round trip. Two patterns stand out. With no starting balance, the account is back above its contributions by month 32 or 33 whatever the depth of the fall, because a deeper fall also means cheaper units. With a starting balance of 240 monthly contributions, CAD 120,000 here, break-even moves out to month 55 or 56: a large existing balance follows the market, and new contributions are too small to pull the average down much. The earlier in a saving life a crash happens, the more the contributions dominate. Which months’ contributions did the work The third chart values each year’s block of purchases at the old peak price in month 60. Contributions made in months 13 to 24, around the low, show a paper gain of about 46.7% . Contributions in the first year of the fall show about 17.2%, and those made in the last year before the peak returned show only about 5.9%. The starting balance, bought at the peak, shows nothing. These are the purchases that a pause skips. They also show why a pause is hard to undo in practice: the months that turned out best were the months when statements looked worst, and an investor waiting for “things to settle down” usually restarts after prices have risen. The waiting-for-a-dip guide tests the opposite habit, holding new money back until prices fall, and finds the same difficulty from the other side. When pausing is the right decision The case for continuing rests on contributions that can stay invested for many years. Pausing, or redirecting, can be the right call when the reason is your own cash flow rather than the market: Your income is at risk. If a layoff or a cut in hours is plausible, building an emergency reserve comes first. The income-interruption guide sets a cash floor before contributions resume. The money has a near deadline. Savings for a home deposit or tuition within a few years should not depend on a recovery date. The short-term goal guide shows how a loss close to a deadline cannot be waited out. High-interest debt is growing. Paying down a credit card charging 20% or more is a known return; a fund’s return is not. The fund was the wrong choice to begin with. If the fall revealed a risk level you cannot live with, change the mix deliberately, for future contributions, rather than stopping and starting with the headlines. The balanced-fund crash guide compares mixes. Costs matter too. Check whether your plan charges a commission or fee on each purchase; if it does, many small purchases can cost more than a few larger ones. The fund’s own ongoing fees apply to every dollar invested either way, and are already inside the market path in this model. The account and the fund are separate decisions Contributions into a TFSA or RRSP use room that is not otherwise used, and growth inside those accounts is not taxed while it stays there; pausing does not normally lose the room, which carries forward, but cash parked outside the account earns taxable interest. In a non-registered account, every month’s purchase adds to the adjusted cost base, and units bought near the low carry larger future gains, which are taxed only when units are sold. The fund itself does not change its tax treatment; the account’s rules decide it. None of this predicts the next crash or its recovery. The OSC cautions that diversification provides reasonable protection in normal markets but can be less effective in extreme conditions, when most investments fall together, and warns against selling in a downturn. The decision that holds up in most scenarios is less about timing the market and more about making sure each contribution is money you will not need before a recovery could plausibly arrive.
documents.keywords: Keep investing from each paycheque during a crash, or pause until the market recovers? Following the units month by month Follow a monthly contribution plan through a hypothetical market fall and recovery. documents.body: Redeeming fund units in a non-registered account is not fully taxed: part of each withdrawal returns your own cost, and only half of the gain is taxable. That makes early withdrawals light on tax. As withdrawals continue and the fund grows, the cost base shrinks and the taxable share rises, while reinvested distributions are taxed every year whether or not any units are sold. A withdrawal is not the same thing as income Many people approaching retirement hold part of their savings in mutual funds in an ordinary, non-registered account, often because their TFSA and RRSP room was already used. When they start drawing cash from it, a common worry is that every dollar taken out will be added to taxable income, as it would be from an RRSP or RRIF. It is not. CRA describes two separate ways a mutual fund in a non-registered account is taxed. While you own the units, the distributions the fund pays are taxable each year, even when they are reinvested in more units. When you sell or redeem units, you are taxed on the gain , if any, usually as a capital gain. A redemption therefore has three parts: your own cost coming back, which is not taxed; half of the gain, which is left out of income; and the other half of the gain, which is taxed at your marginal rate. The fund itself has no special tax status; a fund held in a TFSA or RRSP follows that account’s rules instead. This guide is about the non-registered case. The first year, step by step The default fund is worth CAD 300,000 and has an adjusted cost base (ACB) of CAD 200,000: the total paid for the units, including reinvested distributions. The investor redeems CAD 18,000 at the start of the year. Cost returned: CRA treats units of the same fund series as identical property, so the ACB of the units sold is their share of the average cost. CAD 18,000 is 6% of the fund’s value, so it carries 6% of the ACB, CAD 12,000. Capital gain: CAD 18,000 − CAD 12,000 = CAD 6,000, a third of the withdrawal. Taxable capital gain: half of CAD 6,000, CAD 3,000, is added to income. Tax: at a combined 29.65% marginal rate, CAD 889.50. That is 4.9% of the cash redeemed. The 29.65% default is the 2026 federal rate of 20.5% plus Ontario’s 9.15%, which together apply to taxable income between about CAD 58,523 and CAD 107,785 in 2026 according to CRA’s rate tables. Your rate depends on your income and province, so change the two inputs; Ontario’s surtax, credits and income-tested benefits are not modeled. The fund also pays distributions of 1.5% a year on the remaining CAD 282,000, CAD 4,230, which are reinvested. The model taxes them at the full marginal rate, CAD 1,254.20, which is conservative: distributions of eligible dividends or capital gains would be taxed less, as the fund income-type guide shows. After both amounts, about CAD 15,856 of the CAD 18,000 is left to spend if the tax is paid from it. The same withdrawal from different accounts The first chart compares the tax on the same CAD 18,000 at the same 29.65% rate. A TFSA withdrawal is not taxed. Non-registered units bought recently, with a cost near their value, produce almost no gain. With the entered cost base the tax is CAD 889.50. If the units had no cost base left, the whole CAD 18,000 would be gain and the tax would be CAD 2,668.50. An RRSP or RRIF withdrawal is fully taxable, CAD 5,337 at this rate. Two cautions keep this from being a ranking of accounts. The RRSP contributions were deducted from income when they were made, so taxing the withdrawal completes a deal that began with a refund; the RRSP and TFSA timing guide compares the full cycle. And the RRSP cash flow differs: for a lump-sum withdrawal, CRA says the institution withholds tax at source, 30% outside Quebec on an amount over CAD 15,000, which may be more or less than the final tax, as the withholding guide explains. Non-registered redemptions have no such withholding, so the tax is settled with the return or through instalments. Why the taxable share keeps rising The second and third charts follow the plan for 20 years, with the withdrawal rising 2% a year and units growing 4% a year after fund costs. Each redemption removes cost base in proportion to value, and growth adds value but not cost. Reinvested distributions add to both. Over time the ACB falls behind the market value, so each dollar redeemed carries less cost and more gain. In year 1, a third of the redemption is gain. By year 20 the redemption has grown to about CAD 26,223 and about 58.5% of it is gain; the tax on that year’s redemption is about CAD 2,274, plus about CAD 415 on that year’s distributions. Over the 20 years, CAD 437,353 is redeemed and total tax is about CAD 50,674 : CAD 31,605 on redemption gains and CAD 19,069 on distributions. That is about 11.6% of the cash redeemed, far below the 29.65% that would apply if every dollar were income. The fund still holds about CAD 98,468 at the end, with an ACB of about CAD 40,150. The tax on that unrealized gain, about CAD 8,646 at the same rate, has been deferred, not avoided: gains are taxed when units are sold or are considered to be sold (a deemed disposition). The gain-timing guide values what deferral is worth. Extend the plan to 25 years and the default fund runs out in year 24: lower tax does not make a withdrawal rate sustainable. Cost base and growth matter more than the withdrawal itself The heatmap reruns the 20-year plan for starting cost bases from 100% to 0% of value and unit growth from 0% to 8% a year. A fund bought recently with no growth pays about 3.2% of its withdrawals in tax, all of it on distributions. A fund with no cost base left that grows 8% a year pays about 21.7%. In between, the starting ACB sets the level and growth sets the slope. That has practical consequences. Keeping a careful ACB record matters, because without one an investor may overpay by treating too much of a redemption as gain; the reinvested-distributions guide shows how reinvestments and returns of capital change it. Distributions are taxed every year even when nothing is sold, which is one reason the asset-location guide places the most heavily taxed income in registered accounts where room allows. Planning withdrawals from a non-registered fund Separate the cash from the tax. Only the gain portion is taxed, but the tax still has to be paid. The sale-proceeds guide earmarks it before spending. Know which income-tested amounts are affected. Taxable capital gains and fund distributions are part of net income, which income-tested benefits and credits use. The GIS withdrawal-timing guide shows how the source of a withdrawal changes them. Group redemptions within a year correctly. CRA says multiple redemptions from the same fund in the same year should be grouped together, and each class or series of a fund has its own ACB. Watch for losses as well as gains. A redemption made while units are below cost realizes a capital loss, which can offset gains under CRA’s rules; this model gives such losses no value. The tax-loss selling guide covers them, including the 30-day rule. Keep the market risk in view. A lower tax bill does not make a fund safer. Returns are uncertain, a fall early in withdrawals does lasting damage, and the withdrawal-source guide shows how to sell without drifting away from the planned mix.
documents.keywords: Drawing cash from a fund in a non-registered account: how much of each withdrawal is taxed, and why the share rises over time Split each redemption from a non-registered mutual fund into returned cost, untaxed gain and taxable gain, using CRA’s average-cost rule. Compare the tax on the same withdrawal from a TFSA, an RRSP or RRIF and a fund with little cost base left, and follow the cost base over 20 years of withdrawals.

documents.title: 股票和债券在同一年下跌时：平衡基金如何经历加息和高通胀
documents.description: 把平衡基金的糟糕年份拆分为股票亏损、债券收益、债券价格下跌和购买力损失，然后观察更高的债券收益率此后如何发挥作用，以及实际价值需要多长时间才能恢复。
documents.body: Bonds usually cushion a stock decline, but when inflation forces interest rates up, bond prices can fall at the same time. The same higher yields then raise the bond sleeve’s later income, so the damage is partly repaid over roughly the bond fund’s duration. Purchasing power, not the nominal balance, is the measure that recovers last. The year the cushion did not cushion A balanced fund holds stocks and bonds together so that a bad year for one is softened by the other. Most of the time that works: when stocks fall because the economy weakens, interest rates often fall too, and bond prices rise. The Ontario Securities Commission’s investor site notes the limit of that idea: diversification provides reasonable protection in normal markets but becomes less effective in extreme conditions, when the prices of most investments can drop together. A different kind of bad year arrives when inflation is the problem. Central banks raise rates to slow prices, bond yields rise, and the prices of bonds already held fall at the same time as stocks. For a balanced-fund investor this year can feel worse than a larger stock crash, because the part of the portfolio that was supposed to be safe is also down, and the money that remains buys less. This guide splits such a year into its parts, then follows what happens afterwards. It does not predict when the next one will come. What the official data show for 2022 The first chart plots three dated series for Canada. Consumer price inflation, measured by Statistics Canada as the 12-month change in the all-items CPI, rose from 4.8% in December 2021 to a peak of 8.1% in June 2022 . The Bank of Canada raised its target for the overnight rate from 0.25% in early 2022 to 4.25% by December 2022 and 5% by July 2023. The Government of Canada 10-year benchmark bond yield ended December 2021 at 1.42% and December 2022 at 3.30% , a rise of almost two percentage points in one year. By September 2026 the latest observations were 3.1% inflation, a 2.25% policy rate and a 3.99% 10-year yield. These are dated readings, not a forecast. The chart does not show any fund’s return; the model below uses its own editable assumptions so that each effect can be seen on its own. Splitting the shock year into four pieces The default fund starts at CAD 100,000 with 60% in stocks and 40% in bonds. In the shock year stocks fall 12%. Bond yields start at 1.5% and rise by 2 percentage points, and the bond sleeve has a duration of 7 years. Duration is a measure of interest-rate sensitivity: a bond fund with a duration of 7 loses roughly 7% of its value for each 1-point rise in yields. Inflation is 6.3% in the shock year. Stocks: 12% of CAD 60,000 is a loss of CAD 7,200. Bond income: 1.5% on CAD 40,000 adds CAD 600. Bond prices: 7 × 2 points = 14% of CAD 40,000, a loss of CAD 5,600. The bond sleeve returns about −12.5%, almost the same as stocks. Inflation: the fund ends the year at CAD 87,800, a −12.2% return, but after 6.3% inflation that buys what about CAD 82,596 bought at the start. The real loss is about 17.4% . If yields had not risen, the same stock fall would have left the fund at CAD 93,400, down 6.6%. The rate rise alone cost CAD 5,600 in the shock year. The duration rule is a first-order estimate; for large yield moves the actual loss on a bond is somewhat smaller because of convexity, explained in the bond convexity guide . Higher yields are the part of the damage that pays back The loss on bonds from rising yields has a second side. After the shock, the bond sleeve earns 3.5% a year instead of 1.5%. In the third chart, the fund that went through the rate rise trails the no-rise version by CAD 5,600 after year one, then closes the gap each year and passes it in year 10 . After 15 years it is worth about CAD 173,838 against about CAD 166,148 for the fund whose yields never rose. The catch-up time is close to the bond sleeve’s duration, which is no coincidence: duration is also roughly the holding period over which a yield change’s price effect and its income effect balance out. The bond reinvestment guide shows that mechanism for a single bond. Two caveats matter. The model holds the new yield constant, while real yields keep moving. And it gives every duration the same yield, while longer bonds often, but not always, pay more; a short-duration bond fund is not simply a better version of a long one. Purchasing power is what recovers last The real concern for most savers is not the nominal balance but what it will buy. In the default case the fund is back above CAD 100,000 in nominal terms in year 4, but in start-year dollars it regains CAD 100,000 only in year 9 . After 15 years it is worth about CAD 115,738 in start-year dollars. Inflation in the shock year is a permanent step up in the price level: prices do not fall back when inflation slows, they just rise more slowly, as the inflation and purchasing power guide explains. The heatmap repeats the calculation for stock shares from 20% to 100% and stock falls from 0% to 40%, keeping the entered rate rise and inflation. Two patterns stand out: With no stock fall at all, a 20% stock fund takes until year 13 to regain its real value, while a 100% stock fund takes until year 3. In a pure rate-and-inflation shock, the bond-heavy fund is the one that suffers. With a 40% stock fall, every mix needs 18 or 19 years. The balanced structure still spreads risk, but the usual ranking of “more bonds, less loss” is weaker when both assets fall together. These counts are arithmetic results for one set of constant later returns. Markets have historically recovered from declines, but the OSC cautions that this can take months or several years; no recovery date is guaranteed. Responding to the worry without abandoning the plan Separate the money by when it is needed. Spending planned within a few years belongs in savings or short-term deposits whose value does not depend on bond prices. Money for goals ten or more years away can usually ride out the shock year described here. Look at the bond sleeve’s duration. Fund Facts and the fund’s reports describe the bond holdings. A longer duration means a larger price fall when yields rise, and a larger benefit when they fall. Keep contributions going from your paycheque. New money invested after a rate rise buys bonds at the higher yield and stocks at lower prices; FINRA describes dollar-cost averaging as a way to reduce the impact of a decline on purchases, without protecting money already invested. Moving an existing lump sum into the fund in stages is a different decision, compared in the phased-investing guide . Keep the account rules separate from the fund. A balanced fund in a TFSA or RRSP has no tax on its rebalancing; the same fund in a non-registered account distributes taxable income and gains. The account changes the tax, not the market risk. Check the mix against the loss you can live through. The risk-profile stress test turns a stock share into dollars. Choosing a lower-risk mix once, deliberately, differs from switching to cash after a bad year, which the crash-warning guide tests.
documents.keywords: When stocks and bonds fall in the same year: a balanced fund through rising rates and high inflation Break a balanced fund’s bad year into its stock loss, bond income, bond price fall and lost purchasing power, then follow how a higher bond yield works afterwards and how long the real value takes to come back.

documents.body: Selling a fund at a loss in a non-registered account can turn a paper loss into a tax saving now, but it lowers the cost base of the replacement and raises tax at the final sale. The benefit is mostly timing, it depends on gains to offset and on future tax rates, and it disappears if the same fund is bought back within 30 days. A paper loss can have a tax value, but only if it is realized correctly After a market fall, a fund held in a non-registered account may be worth less than its adjusted cost base (ACB), the total paid for the units including reinvested distributions. That difference is only a paper loss until the units are sold. Selling them realizes a capital loss . Half of it is an allowable capital loss, which CRA says must first be applied against taxable capital gains of the same year; any remainder becomes a net capital loss that can reduce taxable capital gains in any of the three previous years or any future year . Many investors who sell for this reason want to stay invested, so they buy something else at once. That is where the timing rules and the long-run arithmetic come in. This guide is about funds in non-registered accounts only. Losses inside a TFSA or RRSP have no tax value, because gains there are not taxed either; the TFSA loss guide explains what happens to room. The superficial loss rule: 30 days before, 30 days after CRA describes a superficial loss as a loss on a sale where both of these are true: you, or a person affiliated with you, buy or have a right to buy the same or identical property in the period from 30 calendar days before the sale to 30 calendar days after it; and you, or that affiliated person, still own or have a right to buy it 30 calendar days after the sale. CRA lists a spouse or common-law partner, and a corporation controlled by you or your spouse, among affiliated persons. A superficial loss cannot be deducted. If you are the person who acquires the substituted property, you can usually add the denied loss to its ACB, which lowers the gain or raises the loss when that property is sold later. The first chart sorts a CAD 25,000 loss into what happens under four choices. Selling and buying a different fund lets CAD 20,000 offset available gains now, with CAD 5,000 carried forward. Rebuying the same fund within 30 days moves the whole loss into the new units’ cost base, so the benefit is postponed, not lost. Buying the same fund inside your TFSA or RRSP is the trap: the loss is generally denied, and the cost-base addition belongs to the registered plan, where it does you no good. Reinvested distributions inside the window, including automatic reinvestment in the fund being sold, can also count as purchases. When in doubt, have a tax professional review the specific transactions. “Different fund” has to mean different property The rule turns on whether the replacement is identical property. Units of the same ETF or the same mutual fund are identical property. Whether a different series of the same fund, or another provider’s fund tracking the same index, is identical is less clear-cut and calls for professional judgement. Funds with different mandates from different providers are generally treated as different property. This guide does not decide that question; it measures what is at stake once it has been answered. The replacement also needs to fit the plan. If the point is to stay invested in a similar mix, the new fund should hold a comparable asset mix and risk level. A switch that changes the portfolio’s risk is an investment decision, not just a tax step. The fund-switch break-even guide covers the reverse case, a switch that realizes a gain. The saving now is partly repaid at the final sale In the default case, units bought for CAD 100,000 are worth CAD 75,000. Selling realizes a CAD 25,000 loss. CAD 20,000 offsets other gains taxed at a 40% marginal rate, so half of it, CAD 10,000, comes off taxable income and saves CAD 4,000 . The remaining CAD 5,000 is carried forward. The proceeds, less a 0.25% switching cost, plus the CAD 4,000 saving, buy a different fund. Both funds then return 6% a year for 10 years. Kept holding: about CAD 127,451 after tax on the final sale. Sold and switched: about CAD 129,675 , about CAD 2,225 more. Sold and rebought the same fund: about CAD 127,145, slightly less than holding because only the switching cost changed. The waterfall shows where the CAD 2,225 comes from. The CAD 4,000 saving grows to about CAD 7,163 by year 10. The switching cost and its lost growth take about CAD 336. The replacement starts from a cost base about CAD 25,000 lower, so the final sale reports a larger gain and the extra tax is about CAD 4,603 . Harvesting a loss mostly moves tax from now to later. It helps because money saved now compounds, and it helps more if the final sale happens at a lower rate. When it helps, and when it does not The heatmap varies the years until the final sale and the marginal rate at that sale. With a 20% rate at the sale, for example in a low-income retirement year, switching ends about CAD 4,526 ahead after 10 years. With a 50% rate, about CAD 1,074. The pattern is not always smooth: after 5 years with a 50% rate at the sale, switching is about CAD 220 behind, because the held fund is barely above its old cost base while the replacement already has a taxable gain beyond the carried-forward loss. Other inputs can wipe out the benefit: No gains to offset. With no gains in the current or three previous years, nothing is saved now; the switch costs about CAD 306 in the default case, and the carried-forward loss only shelters later gains. A lagging replacement. If the new fund returns half a point a year less, switching ends about CAD 2,990 behind after 10 years. A difference in fees alone can do that. Costs. A 2% cost to sell and buy, from spreads, commissions or a remaining deferred sales charge on an older fund purchase, reduces the advantage to about CAD 82. The model assumes the tax saving is reinvested immediately. In practice it arrives as a refund or a smaller balance owing after the return is filed, which can be more than a year later. It also assumes one combined marginal rate; a large final sale can push income into a higher bracket. A checklist before selling for a loss Confirm the ACB. Include reinvested distributions and subtract any return of capital; the fund cost-base guide shows how. An understated ACB understates the loss. Check the 61-day window. Look 30 days back and plan 30 days ahead for purchases of the same fund by you, your spouse, a corporation you control and your registered plans, including pre-authorized contributions and automatic reinvestment of distributions. Know what the loss will offset. Gains this year and in the three previous years produce a saving now; otherwise the loss waits for future gains. The carryback guide charts which years are eligible and the request form CRA uses. Do not move a losing fund into a TFSA in kind. A transfer in kind is a sale at market value, and a loss on property transferred to a TFSA is denied; the in-kind contribution guide shows the arithmetic. Selling in the non-registered account and contributing cash is the usual alternative. Keep contributions and a lump-sum decision separate. Regular contributions from your paycheque can continue throughout; the decision here concerns only the existing non-registered units. Let the investment plan lead. A tax loss is a by-product of a fall, not a reason to change the portfolio’s risk. Selling in a crash and staying in cash is a market-timing decision with its own costs, tested in the crash-warning guide . This guide explains mechanics using CRA’s published rules. It is not tax advice, and CRA may view a specific set of transactions differently.

documents.keywords: What happens to the $25,000 loss under four choices CRA treats a loss as superficial when you or an affiliated person, such as a spouse, buy the same or identical property in the 30 calendar days before or after the sale and still hold it 30 days after. A superficial loss cannot be deducted. When you are the buyer you can usually add it to the cost base of the new units, which only postpones the benefit. When the substituted property is bought in a registered plan, the loss is generally denied without a cost-base addition you can use. Confirm a specific case with a tax professional.

documents.title: Giving fund units to charity instead of cash: how a gift in kind removes the tax on the gain
documents.description: Compare donating mutual fund units directly with selling them and donating the cash, see what the donation credit is worth in each province, and test the step that resets your cost base if you want to keep holding the fund.
documents.body: When fund units in a non-registered account have risen above their cost, giving the units themselves to a registered charity can qualify for a zero capital-gains inclusion rate, while selling first makes half the gain taxable. The receipt and the donation credit are the same either way. The edge depends on the size of the gain, not on the fund, and disappears for units held in a TFSA or RRSP or bought near today’s price. Two ways to give the same amount Many people who give to charity each year also hold a balanced fund or an equity fund in a non-registered account. If that fund has grown, there are two ways to turn part of it into a gift. One is to sell units, pay any tax on the gain, and give the cash. The other is to ask the fund company or dealer to transfer the units themselves to the charity, which then sells them. The charity ends up with the same money. The difference is on your tax return. CRA’s guide Gifts and Income Tax lists units of a mutual fund trust and shares of a mutual fund corporation among the properties for which a donor may be entitled to an inclusion rate of zero on the capital gain, reported on Form T1170. When the same units are sold first, the gain is an ordinary capital gain, and CRA’s capital gains guide shows half of it being taxable. This guide prices that difference, shows where the credit rate comes from, and covers the related case where you want to give and still keep the fund. The credit is the same either way, and it is large The first chart shows the combined credit rate CRA lists for gifts above the first CAD 200 in the 2025 tax year: a federal rate of 29% plus each province’s rate. The combined rate runs from about 40% in Ontario to about 51% in Newfoundland and Labrador ; British Columbia’s is 45.8%. Donors with income in the top federal bracket can claim 33% federally on the part of the gift covered by that income, and some provinces list a higher top rate too. Quebec’s credit is administered by Revenu Québec. The credit is non-refundable: it reduces tax you would otherwise pay. CRA limits the gifts you can claim in a year to 75% of net income, and unused gifts can be carried forward up to five years. The model assumes the gift fits within that limit and that your first CAD 200 of gifts this year has already been claimed at the lower first-tier rate, so the whole gift earns the entered rate. Rates for 2026 returns may differ slightly, so check the current table before you file. Because the receipt is for the fair market value of what the charity receives, the credit does not depend on whether you give units or cash. What changes is the tax on the gain. Pricing the default case The default gift is fund units worth CAD 20,000 with an adjusted cost base of CAD 12,000, so the units carry an unrealized gain of CAD 8,000. The combined credit rate is 45.8% and the marginal tax rate on capital gains income is 40%. Either route: a receipt for CAD 20,000 and a credit of CAD 9,160. Giving the units: no tax on the gain if the zero inclusion rate applies. Your net cost for a CAD 20,000 gift is CAD 10,840. Selling first: half of the CAD 8,000 gain, CAD 4,000, is added to income and taxed at 40%, which is CAD 1,600. Your net cost for the same gift rises to CAD 12,440 . The second chart stacks those amounts. The heatmap repeats the comparison for cost bases from 0% to 100% of market value and marginal rates from 20% to 50%. Units with a cost base of 20% of their value save CAD 3,200 at a 40% rate; units bought near today’s price save almost nothing. A balanced fund held for many years, with distributions reinvested, often has a mix: the oldest purchases carry the largest gains, and the fund cost-base guide shows how reinvested distributions raise the cost base. For tax purposes, identical units of the same fund share one average cost base, so you cannot choose to give only the oldest, lowest-cost units. Giving the units and buying the fund back A common situation is a donor who planned to give cash from savings but likes the fund and wants to keep it. The third chart compares three routes that all give CAD 20,000 and all leave you holding CAD 20,000 of the same fund: Give your cash and keep the old units. No tax now, but the units keep their CAD 12,000 cost base. Give the units and use your cash to buy the fund again. No tax now, and the new units have a CAD 20,000 cost base. Sell the units, give the proceeds and rebuy with your cash. CAD 1,600 of tax now, and the new units also have a CAD 20,000 cost base. With a 6% fund return, the after-tax value if everything is sold after 10 years is about CAD 32,654 for route 2, CAD 31,054 for route 1 and CAD 29,788 for route 3. Route 2 beats route 1 by the CAD 1,600 of tax that would otherwise be paid on the old gain at some later sale; route 3 is behind by the CAD 1,600 paid now plus the growth it gave up. The edge of route 2 over route 1 is a postponed tax that is never paid, so it matters most when the eventual sale is likely to happen at a similar or higher marginal rate. Buying back the same fund after giving units at a gain does not run into the superficial-loss rule, which denies losses when identical property is bought within 30 days. That rule is explained in the fund tax-loss selling guide . Which account the units are in matters more than which fund The saving comes from the account’s tax rules, not from the fund. The benefit exists only for units held in a non-registered account, where a sale creates a taxable capital gain. TFSA: gains are not taxed, so there is no gain to exempt. Withdrawing cash and giving it produces the same credit with no tax cost, and the withdrawal is added back to your room on 1 January of the next year. RRSP or RRIF: money leaves the plan as a withdrawal, which is taxable income and subject to withholding. The donation credit can offset that tax, but there is no capital gain to exempt, so the in-kind advantage does not apply. Units at a loss: with the value below cost there is no gain to exempt, and the model shows no difference between the routes. A loss on units that are sold is a capital loss you can use against other gains, as covered in the capital-loss carryback guide . This also links the gift to capital-gain timing : units you planned to sell anyway in a high-income year are good candidates to give instead. Practical steps and cautions Ask the charity first. CRA advises checking that an organization is a registered charity or other qualified donee before you give. Not every charity can receive fund units; many use a brokerage account or a donation platform. Gifts to a donor-advised fund at a public foundation are another route, with their own fees and rules. Transfer the units, do not sell them. The zero inclusion rate is for a gift of the property itself. A sale in your account followed by a cash gift is a sale. Leave several weeks before 31 December, because transfers between institutions take time and the gift counts in the year the charity receives it. Check fees and sales charges. Units bought with a deferred sales charge may trigger a redemption fee when the charity sells; that reduces the gift but not your tax saving. Keep the records. You need the official receipt for the fair market value on the date received, Form T1170 with your return, and your cost-base record for the units given. Fit the gift to your budget first. A tax saving makes a planned gift cheaper; it does not make an unplanned gift free. The charitable giving budget guide covers the cash side. Special rules apply to flow-through shares, gifts with an advantage back to the donor, employee stock options and gifts by will. Those are outside this model; confirm a specific case with a tax professional.
