documents.title: Fill your TFSA in January or contribute every payday? It depends on where the money comes from
documents.description: Separate money you already have from money you are still earning. Compare a January TFSA deposit with monthly staging, test which half-year returns favour each, and price the cost of saving paycheques for a once-a-year deposit.
documents.body: New TFSA room arrives on 1 January. If the money is already in your savings, depositing it in January and then deciding how fast to invest it inside the account usually beats keeping it outside, and investing it at once is ahead on average when the fund is expected to earn more than savings, though not in every year. If the money comes from paycheques, there is no lump sum to front-load: investing each payday puts it to work sooner than saving up for a January deposit. One decision that is really two Every January brings new TFSA room, CAD 7,000 for 2024, 2025 and 2026. A common question is whether to put the whole amount in at the start of the year or to contribute a little every payday. The answer depends on a question that is easy to skip: does the money already exist? Money you already have , such as savings, a bonus or a maturing GIC, can be invested on 1 January or staged over the year. That is a choice between a lump sum and dollar-cost averaging. Money you are still earning arrives with each paycheque. There is nothing to front-load. The only choice is whether to invest each instalment when it arrives or to let it build up in savings for a later deposit. Mixing the two leads to the wrong comparison. Someone saving from a paycheque who reads that “lump sums usually beat dollar-cost averaging” may decide to save all year and deposit in January, which is the reverse of what that finding implies. This guide takes each case in turn and keeps a third question separate: whether the money waiting to be invested sits inside or outside the TFSA. How TFSA room arrives The first chart shows CRA’s TFSA dollar limits. The limit was CAD 5,000 from 2009 to 2012, CAD 10,000 in 2015, CAD 6,500 in 2023 and CAD 7,000 from 2024 to 2026; a resident who was 18 or older in 2009 and never contributed would have CAD 109,000 of room in 2026. CRA’s TFSA guide explains that unused room carries forward, that withdrawals are added back at the start of the following year, and that excess contributions are taxed at 1% a month. Two consequences matter here. First, the year’s room is fully available on 1 January, so a single January deposit and twelve monthly deposits use the same room. Second, money deposited in January does not have to be invested in a fund that day. It can sit as cash or a savings product inside the TFSA, where its interest is not taxed, while you move it into the fund on your own schedule. The pace of investing and the account the cash waits in are separate decisions. Money you already have: January versus staging The default case uses CAD 7,000 already in savings, a fund return of 6% a year and a savings rate of 2%. The Bank of Canada’s policy rate was 2.25% on 23 October 2026; savings rates vary by product and change with that rate. The second chart follows the money through one year: Deposited and invested on 1 January: CAD 7,420 by 31 December. Deposited in January, moved into the fund one twelfth a month: CAD 7,290. The waiting cash earns tax-free interest inside the TFSA. Invested one twelfth a month, the rest waiting outside the TFSA with its interest taxed at 30%: CAD 7,271. On these smooth assumptions investing at once is ahead by about CAD 130, because on average half the money spends half the year in cash instead of the fund. FINRA’s page on dollar-cost averaging notes that it often produces lower returns than lump-sum investing, especially over longer periods, in exchange for lower risk of buying just before a decline. The third chart shows the risk side. It keeps the default savings rate and changes the fund’s return in each half of the year. If the fund falls 20% from January to June and rises 20% from July to December, staging ends about CAD 937 ahead , because the later instalments bought at lower prices. If the fund rises 20% and then falls 20%, investing in January ends about CAD 458 ahead. In flat years the higher-yielding choice depends on the savings rate. Which cell a coming year will land in is not known in advance; the phased-investing guide follows the same choice over longer staging periods. Money you are still earning: invest on arrival For most people saving from employment income the money arrives in pieces. The fourth chart compares investing CAD 7,000 a year in twelve monthly instalments as each paycheque arrives with saving the same instalments in a taxable savings account and depositing them in one amount each 1 January. Each instalment in the second path waits 6.5 months on average before it reaches the fund. After one year, the payday path is worth CAD 7,225, while the saved instalments, deposited on the next 1 January, amount to CAD 7,053. Repeated for 20 years, with CAD 140,000 contributed in both cases, the payday path ends at about CAD 265,793 and the January path at about CAD 259,448, a gap of about CAD 6,346. There is no expected-return argument for waiting here: investing a paycheque when it arrives is the lump-sum choice for that paycheque. It also removes the temptation to spend the savings or to start guessing about the market, which the waiting-for-a-dip guide tests. If per-trade fees apply, weekly or very small purchases can cost more than they gain; the batched-purchases guide prices that tradeoff. When the smooth answer is not the right one The money may be needed soon. Savings meant for an emergency fund or a purchase within a few years should not go into a fund at all, whatever the TFSA calendar. The short-term goal guide shows the risk. A crash early in the year would make you stop. Staging a lump sum over several months is a reasonable way to reduce regret if a large fall right after investing would lead you to sell. The expected cost in the default case is about CAD 130 on CAD 7,000; that may be a price worth paying for staying invested. Withdrawals and re-contributions. Money withdrawn from a TFSA cannot be put back in the same year unless unused room remains. The re-contribution calendar explains the timing. RRSP and FHSA questions differ. An RRSP deposit also creates a deduction, and the RRSP deadline falls 60 days after year-end. The RRSP and TFSA comparison covers that wrapper choice. The TFSA shelters income and gains from tax; it does not reduce the fund’s risk. A balanced fund in a TFSA can still fall, and a loss inside a TFSA does not give back room, as the TFSA loss guide shows.

documents.title: 靠平衡基金生活而崩盘先来时：反向定额投资，以及现金储备能做到和做不到的事
documents.description: 当你每月固定提款时，市场早期下跌会迫使你以低价卖出更多基金单位。了解为什么回报相同但顺序不同会留下不同金额，通胀如何提高你需要的提款额，以及持有一两年现金的成本和好处。
documents.body: Saving from each paycheque buys more fund units when prices fall. Withdrawing a fixed amount each month does the reverse: it sells more units when prices fall, and those units are not there when the fund recovers. With the same yearly returns in a different order, a crash in the first year of withdrawals can leave noticeably less money decades later than the same crash near the end, even though without withdrawals the two would end level. A cash reserve can avoid selling during a fall, but idle cash usually earns less than the fund, so a reserve is insurance with a cost, not free protection. The mirror image of saving from each paycheque While you are working, a fixed amount invested from each paycheque buys more units of a fund when the price is low and fewer when it is high. That is the familiar argument for dollar-cost averaging , and it is why a fall in the market while you are still contributing is less damaging than it looks: the paycheque contributions made through a crash buy cheap units. Once you start living off the money, the arithmetic turns around. A fixed withdrawal of, say, CAD 1,875 a month has to be raised by selling units. When the price is low, more units must be sold for the same cash. Those units are gone before the recovery, so the fund recovers on a smaller base. This guide follows that effect through a single balanced fund, asks how much the timing of a crash matters, and tests the common remedy of keeping a year or two of withdrawals in cash. First, the withdrawal itself has to keep rising A withdrawal plan is usually set in today’s dollars, but the bills it pays rise with prices. The first chart uses Statistics Canada’s Consumer Price Index for September of each year. The all-items CPI rose from 109.2 in September 2006 to 170.0 in September 2026 (2002=100), an increase of about 55.7%. To keep the purchasing power of CAD 1,875 a month from 2006, a household needed about CAD 2,919 a month by September 2026. Left unchanged at CAD 1,875, the same withdrawal bought only what about CAD 1,204 bought in 2006. The increase was not steady: the September index rose 0.5% from 2019 to 2020 and 6.9% from 2021 to 2022. The Bank of Canada aims to keep inflation at the 2% midpoint of a 1% to 3% target range, which is why the calculator starts with a 2% yearly increase in the withdrawal. That is an assumption, not a promise; you can change it. A withdrawal that rises each year makes the order of returns matter more, because the amounts being sold keep growing. Selling units in a falling market The calculator starts with CAD 500,000 in a balanced fund at CAD 10 a unit, or 50,000 units. It withdraws 4.5% in the first year, CAD 22,500 paid as CAD 1,875 at the start of each month, and raises that by 2% a year. In ordinary years the fund earns a hypothetical 5% after fees. In the crash scenario the fund falls 25% over the first year. To keep the comparison fair, the next year earns whatever brings the two years back to exactly two ordinary years of growth: (1.05)² ÷ 0.75 − 1 = 47% . Every scenario therefore has the same set of yearly returns; only the order changes. Real markets do not promise a recovery of that size or speed. The second chart shows units sold each month. Without a crash the first withdrawal sells 187.5 units and the twelfth about 179.3, because the price has risen. With the crash, the twelfth withdrawal needs about 244.1 units at a price near CAD 7.68, and the first withdrawal of year two, now CAD 1,912.50, needs 255. Over the first two years the crash path sells about 818 more units for exactly the same cash paid out. The price is back above CAD 10 by month 22, but the fund has fewer units to benefit from it. Same returns, different order, different result The third chart follows three paths over 30 years with no cash reserve: no crash, a crash in year 1, and the same crash in year 29 with its recovery in year 30. If nothing were withdrawn, all three would end at exactly the same value, because they share the same growth factors. With withdrawals: No crash: about CAD 227,420 left after 30 years, after paying out about CAD 912,800 in rising withdrawals. Crash in year 1: about CAD 192,052 , roughly CAD 35,368 less. Two years in, the gap is only about CAD 9,000 (CAD 494,401 against CAD 503,423); it compounds from there because the lost units never earn the later returns. Crash in year 29: about CAD 211,712 , roughly CAD 15,708 less than no crash. The late crash still costs something, because withdrawals are taken during it, but the balance it hits is much smaller and there are few years left for the damage to compound. The effect becomes severe when the withdrawal rate is high or the fall is deep. At a 5% first-year rate and a 40% fall, the no-crash path still has about CAD 12,580 after 30 years, while the early-crash path runs out in month 345, during year 29. At a 6% rate and a 25% fall, the early-crash path runs out in month 268 and even the no-crash path runs out in month 277, during year 24. At 4% and a 25% fall, both last comfortably and the early crash leaves about CAD 31,000 less. Change the inputs to see where your own plan sits; none of these figures is a forecast. A cash reserve: what it buys and what it costs A common answer is to keep one or more years of withdrawals in cash or a short-term deposit and draw on it while the fund is below its earlier high, so no units are sold during the fall. The fourth chart tests that rule. The reserve comes out of the same CAD 500,000, earns a hypothetical 3%, and is not refilled. Crash in year 1: a one-year reserve lifts the 30-year value from about CAD 192,052 to about CAD 210,900 . It pays the withdrawals through the fall and early recovery, so far fewer cheap units are sold. No crash: the same reserve lowers the 30-year value from about CAD 227,420 to about CAD 184,789 , because CAD 22,500 sat in cash at 3% for 30 years instead of in the fund at 5%. Bigger is not always better. With a crash in year 1, a two-year reserve ends near CAD 208,057 and a three-year reserve near CAD 165,427, below having no reserve, because the part not needed during the fall stays idle. So a reserve is insurance. It pays off when a fall comes early and the reserve is spent while the fund is down; it costs money in the many years when it is not used. Refilling the reserve from the fund after a recovery, or treating it as the short-term part of the portfolio’s fixed income, changes these numbers, which is why the rule here is deliberately simple. The withdrawal-source guide looks at selling whichever asset is above its target instead, and the spending guardrails guide looks at the other lever: taking a little less after a bad year. Balanced funds, fees, accounts and what this does not show Why a balanced fund. A fund that holds both bonds and stocks usually falls less than an all-equity fund in a crash, which reduces the units sold at low prices. It can still fall a lot, and bonds and stocks have fallen together, as the 2022 example shows. The 25% fall here is an input, not a description of any fund. Fees. The 5% return is after fees. A management expense ratio comes out of the fund every year, in good and bad years alike, so a higher fee works like a permanently higher withdrawal rate. The account changes the tax, not the market risk. CRA says amounts paid out of a RRIF are taxable on receipt, so a gross withdrawal must cover the tax as well as the spending. CRA says TFSA withdrawals are tax-free, and the amount withdrawn is added back to contribution room on January 1 of the following year. In a non-registered account each redemption can realize a capital gain or loss measured against the average cost of the units; the non-registered withdrawal guide follows that split. Selling units in a crash in any of these accounts has the same effect on the units left. An existing lump sum is not a paycheque. This guide is about money already invested being drawn down. Earnings saved from each pay are invested as they arrive; they are a different question from whether to stage a lump sum, covered in the phased-investing guide . Limits. One crash, smooth returns in ordinary years, no taxes inside the model, no changes in spending and no other income such as CPP, OAS or a pension. Real crashes can be deeper, can come more than once and can take years to recover, or may not recover in real terms within your horizon.
documents.keywords: Living off a balanced fund when the crash comes first: reverse dollar-cost averaging and what a cash reserve can and cannot do When you withdraw a fixed amount each month, a market fall early on forces you to sell more fund units at low prices. See why the same returns in a different order leave different amounts, how inflation raises the withdrawal you need, and what holding a year or two in cash costs and buys.

documents.body: Dollar-cost averaging invests the same amount from every paycheque. Value averaging invests whatever it takes to keep the fund on a target path, so after a fall it asks for more money exactly when prices are low. That sounds like a better version of the same idea, but the extra money has to wait somewhere in cash beforehand, the rebound itself does much of the catching up, and the rule may ask for more than you have. With the same savings, the two can end within a few hundred dollars of each other, in either order. Value averaging is a way to plan for crash-time buying, not a way to remove market risk. Two rules for the same paycheque Suppose you set aside CAD 500 from each month’s pay for a balanced fund. The simplest rule is to invest the CAD 500 every month, whatever the market is doing. That is dollar-cost averaging : a fixed amount buys more units when the price is low and fewer when it is high. Value averaging is a more demanding rule. Instead of fixing the amount you invest, you fix the value you want the fund to have each month, and invest whatever closes the gap. If the fund has fallen, the gap is large and you invest more than CAD 500. If it has risen faster than planned, the gap is small, and under the strict version of the rule you sell units. People who worry about a crash are often drawn to it because it turns a fall into a planned buying opportunity. This guide asks what it actually does to the same savings, where the extra money comes from, and what the waiting money earns. How the target path works The calculator uses the most common form of the target. Each month the target grows by a chosen rate and then rises by the month’s saving. With CAD 500 a month and a 5% yearly growth in the target, the target is CAD 500 after the first purchase, about CAD 6,136 after a year, about CAD 12,579 after two years and about CAD 77,182 after ten. That path is simply what the fund would be worth if your monthly savings earned exactly 5% a year. Each month value averaging compares the fund’s value with the target. Both investors here save the same CAD 500 and start with the same CAD 3,000 already saved. Dollar-cost averaging invests the CAD 500 and leaves the CAD 3,000 in cash. Value averaging puts the CAD 500 into a cash pot beside the fund and pays for each month’s purchase from that pot. Money from any sale goes back into the pot. When the pot is empty, value averaging buys what it can and falls behind its target; the calculator counts those months instead of assuming you can find more money. One consequence follows straight away. If the fund earns exactly the target rate every year, both rules invest exactly CAD 500 a month and end at the same value, CAD 81,336 after ten years with the defaults. The rules differ only when returns differ from the target, which is to say almost always. What a crash does to each rule In the default scenario the fund earns 5% in ordinary years, falls 25% through year 2 and recovers in year 3, so that years 2 and 3 together grow exactly as two ordinary years would. The second chart shows what each rule asks you to invest: During the fall , value averaging asks for more each month as the fund slides further below the target, up to about CAD 834 in month 24, the bottom. Over year 2 it invests about CAD 8,849 against CAD 6,000 for dollar-cost averaging, at an average price of about CAD 9.10 a unit. The pot nearly runs dry. By the end of year 2 only about CAD 270 is left, and in month 25 the pot cannot pay the full purchase; it is about CAD 79 short. During the rebound , the fund’s own recovery lifts it back to its target within months, so value averaging invests only about CAD 1,406 in year 3, when prices are still low, and even sells a little near the end of the year. Dollar-cost averaging keeps buying CAD 500 a month through the cheap rebound. The result. After ten years dollar-cost averaging has about CAD 84,686 and value averaging about CAD 84,072 , including the cash left in the pot. Value averaging’s average purchase price is about CAD 12.11 a unit against CAD 12.09. So the rule that buys more at the bottom did not come out ahead. It did buy cheaply in the fall, but it skipped the rebound, and the savings it did not need to invest during the rebound, about CAD 6,576 by year 10, stayed in cash earning 2.5% instead of 5%. Change the crash year and the order can flip. With the crash in year 9 value averaging ends about CAD 176 ahead, but it would have needed up to CAD 2,168 in a single month and its pot was short in 19 months, once by about CAD 15,798, because a fall in a much larger fund needs far more money to fill. The fourth chart puts these totals side by side. The money that waits: what short-term cash has earned since 2006 Value averaging only works if there is cash ready to spend when prices fall. That cash has a cost, and the first chart puts a dated number on it. Statistics Canada publishes the 3-month Government of Canada treasury bill yield each month. Rolling CAD 10,000 over in 3-month bills from September 2006, earning one twelfth of each month’s yield, would have grown to about CAD 13,935 by September 2026. Over the same years the all-items CPI rose from 109.2 to 170.0, about 55.7%, so that balance bought only what about CAD 8,951 bought in 2006. Yields ranged from 0.06% in early 2021 to 5.08% in 2023, and were 2.39% in September 2026. This is an approximation before tax, not the rate of any savings account. It shows why the size of the pot matters. In the calculator, setting the target growth lower than the fund’s return makes the fund run ahead of its target, so value averaging keeps selling and saving: at 3% the pot grows to about CAD 13,361 and the total falls to about CAD 83,369. Setting it higher keeps the pot empty: at 7% the pot runs out in 12 months and the total is about CAD 84,808, slightly above dollar-cost averaging. A target that is too generous makes the rule demand money you may not have; one that is too modest turns it into a slow way of holding cash, a version of the problem in the guide to waiting for a crash . Accounts and tax: keep the pot inside the same account The account sets the tax; the fund and the rule do not. A balanced fund held in a TFSA, an RRSP or a taxable account carries the same market risk, but the extra trades value averaging makes are treated differently: TFSA. Buying and selling inside the account is not a withdrawal. Moving sale proceeds out to a bank account and back again is. CRA says an amount withdrawn is added back to contribution room only on January 1 of the next calendar year, and advises against re-contributing in the same year without room; an over-contribution is taxed at 1% a month while it remains. Keeping the cash pot as a cash or savings holding inside the TFSA avoids that trap. RRSP. CRA says income earned in an RRSP is usually exempt from tax while the funds remain in the plan, and payments from the plan are generally taxed. The pot can also sit inside the plan; taking it out to wait in a bank account would be a taxable withdrawal. Non-registered account. CRA says selling or redeeming mutual fund units can produce a capital gain or loss, with the cost of the units sold based on the average cost of all units held. Dollar-cost averaging never sells; strict value averaging does, so it can realize taxable gains in good years. Interest earned on a pot held in cash is generally taxable each year, as the after-tax interest guide shows. Setting the calculator to never sell avoids the sales but leaves more cash waiting after rallies. A fund is not tax-exempt in itself: the same fund units are taxed differently depending on the account they sit in. Practical choices This is a rule for earnings, not for a lump sum. Value averaging, like dollar-cost averaging, is usually applied to money saved from pay as it arrives. If you already have a large sum and are deciding how fast to invest it, that is a different question, about staging money that could be invested today; the phased-investing guide covers it. Decide where the crash money comes from before the crash. The starting cash and the pot are the only sources in the calculator. With no starting cash the pot runs short in 19 months in the default crash; with CAD 10,000 it never does. Emergency savings should not double as the buying fund, as the income-interruption guide explains. A crash is when the rule is hardest to follow. Value averaging asks for the largest purchases when the news is worst and, often, when jobs are least secure. A rule you abandon halfway through the fall is worse than a simpler one you keep. The guide to pausing contributions in a crash shows what stopping costs. Judge the result by total money, not average price. A lower average cost per unit can coexist with less money overall, because the comparison leaves out the cash that never got invested. The return-measure guide explains why timing contributions changes the money-weighted return but not the fund’s own return. New contributions can rebalance without sales. In a balanced portfolio, sending new money to the part that has fallen is another way to buy what is cheap without selling in a taxable account; see rebalancing with new contributions . What the calculator leaves out One crash, spread evenly through a single year, with smooth returns otherwise. Real markets can fall further, fall more than once, fall within weeks or take many years to recover; a recovery by any particular date is not assured. The fund return is after fees. Fees are charged every year whatever rule you use; frequent trading can add costs, and some funds charge short-term trading fees. No tax is calculated, savings do not rise with pay or prices, and the target is not reset after a missed month. Many investors cap the purchase or raise the target with inflation, which changes the results. The calculator ignores what else the cash in the pot could have done, such as paying down debt. None of this predicts the returns of any fund. Both rules leave you fully exposed to the market once the money is invested.
documents.keywords: Value averaging or plain dollar-cost averaging: the rule that buys more after a crash, and the cash it has to keep waiting Value averaging tops a fund up to a target path each month, so it asks for much more money after prices fall and less, or even a sale, after they rise. See what that does to the same monthly savings through a crash, why a lower purchase price is not guaranteed, what the waiting cash earned in treasury bills since 2006 and how the account changes the tax.

Those extra purchases have to come from somewhere: cash saved earlier, or money you no longer have for other uses.

documents.description: 现金池是价值平均法放在基金旁边的现金。当回报超过 5% 的目标时，现金池会累积，但只赚 2.5%；下跌之后，它会被用来买入便宜的单位。如果现金池用光，投资者若不找外来资金，就无法遵守规则。10 年后，有崩盘时现金池有 $6,576，没有崩盘时有 $3,840，有崩盘但从不卖出单位时有 $6,579。余额按每月交易之后计算。

documents.keywords: Cash waiting in the value-averaging pot The pot is the cash value averaging keeps beside the fund. When returns beat the 5% target the pot builds up, earning only 2.5%; after a fall it is drained to buy cheap units. If it runs dry the investor cannot keep to the rule without finding outside money. After 10 years the pot holds $6,576 with the crash, $3,840 without one and $6,579 with the crash if units are never sold. Balances are taken after each month's trade.

documents.keywords: Total after 10 years, fund plus cash, for each crash timing Both columns count the same savings and the same starting cash. With the crash in year 2, value averaging ends $614 behind. Here value averaging did not pay less per unit on average ($12.11 against $12.09 for dollar-cost averaging): it bought more while prices fell, but then bought much less in the rebound year, when prices were still low, because the rebound itself lifted the fund back to its target. The savings it did not need to invest stayed in the cash pot. Value averaging can end with less in total when its pot sits in cash for long stretches, when it sells into a rising market, or when a crash comes late and the pot is too small to buy the dip. The rule changes the timing of money going in; it does not change the fund's returns.

documents.title: Your RRSP refund, every payday: reducing tax at source instead of waiting for spring
documents.description: If you contribute to an RRSP from each paycheque, the tax saving usually comes back months later as a refund. Compare that with having less tax withheld each payday so the saving is invested at once, and see why spending the refund matters even more.
documents.body: An RRSP contribution saves tax at your marginal rate, but with ordinary payroll withholding that saving reaches you only as a refund after you file. Contributing through payroll, or getting a CRA letter of authority with Form T1213, moves the saving into each pay so the same monthly effort buys a larger contribution straight away. The timing gain is modest; the much bigger risk is that the spring refund is spent rather than invested. Where the RRSP tax saving goes while you wait Many people invest in an RRSP a little at a time: a fixed amount from each paycheque into a balanced fund or an index fund. That is dollar-cost averaging from earnings, and it works the same way inside an RRSP as anywhere else. What is different is the tax. Each dollar contributed can be deducted from income, which saves tax at your marginal rate. Under ordinary payroll withholding, though, your employer keeps deducting tax as if you had made no contribution. The saving builds up with CRA during the year and comes back as a refund after you file the following spring. So a monthly saver is, in effect, making a once-a-year lump-sum investment of the tax saving, roughly a year late. This guide asks what that delay costs, how the rules let you remove it, and what happens to the plan if the refund never makes it back into the RRSP. How much a deduction saves depends on your bracket The first chart shows the 2026 statutory rates CRA lists for federal tax and for British Columbia, combined band by band. The federal rate starts at 14% on taxable income up to CAD 58,523 and rises to 33% above CAD 258,482; BC’s rates run from 5.6% to 20.5%. Combined, they run from 19.6% in the lowest band to 53.5% in the highest. An RRSP deduction comes off the top of your taxable income, so it saves the rate of the band you are in. For taxable income between CAD 58,523 and CAD 100,728 in BC, that is 28.2% , the default in the calculator. Two cautions. These are bracket rates before the basic personal amount and other credits; at low incomes the credits can mean the deduction saves less than the chart shows. And a large deduction can cross into a lower band, so the last dollars save a lower rate. The marginal and average tax guide shows the slices. RRSP room limits the deduction too: 18% of the previous year’s earned income, up to CRA’s dollar limit of CAD 33,810 for 2026 and CAD 35,390 for 2027, plus any unused room. Three ways to save the same monthly amount The calculator holds your monthly effort fixed: the default is CAD 500 a month after tax . It then follows three routes for 25 years with a hypothetical 6% fund return: Tax reduced at source. Less tax is withheld from each pay, so the same CAD 500 of take-home pay funds a contribution of CAD 500 ÷ (1 − 28.2%) = about CAD 696 a month, about CAD 8,357 a year. There is no RRSP refund, because the saving was already received. Spring refund invested. CAD 500 a month goes in, and each refund is invested in May of the following year. The first refund is 28.2% of CAD 6,000, or CAD 1,692. Each refund is also an RRSP contribution, so it produces a smaller refund of its own the year after. Refund spent. CAD 500 a month goes in, and the refunds go to other spending. The second chart shows the first two years. By the end of year 1 the reduced-at-source RRSP holds about CAD 8,626 against CAD 6,193 in the other two; the spring-refund route closes part of the gap in May of year 2 and keeps chasing it. The third chart shows the long run. After 25 years the reduced-at-source route is worth about CAD 473,246 and the spring-refund route about CAD 463,970 , a gap of about CAD 9,276. The refund-spent route ends near CAD 339,790 , about CAD 124,000 behind the spring-refund route. To keep the comparison fair, the spring-refund value at each year-end counts the refund still owed for that year, plus the refunds it would generate in turn. With a 0% return the first two routes then end exactly level: the difference is only timing. When the timing gap is worth acting on The heatmap repeats the comparison for marginal rates of 20% to 50% and fund returns of 0% to 9%. The gap grows with both: a higher rate means a larger refund waiting with CRA, and a higher return means the months of waiting cost more. At a 20% rate and a 3% return it is about CAD 1,781 over 25 years; at a 50% rate and a 9% return it is about CAD 75,275. A higher expected return also comes with more risk: the money moved forward is invested sooner, so in a year when the fund falls early it can buy at higher prices than the refund later would. Over many years, though, investing earnings as they arrive is the same logic the TFSA payday guide applies to paycheque money: there is no lump sum to stage, so waiting has no expected-return benefit. The larger lesson is the refund-spent line. A refund feels like a windfall, but in this plan it is part of the contribution. A refund used for spending turns a pre-tax RRSP contribution of about CAD 696 a month into an after-tax one of CAD 500, which the RRSP-versus-TFSA comparison in the account guide shows is the step that removes most of an RRSP’s advantage. How to have less tax withheld Group RRSP or payroll contributions. CRA’s payroll guidance says that an RRSP contribution an employer withholds from pay and makes on the employee’s behalf automatically reduces the pay on which tax is deducted. No form is needed; the saving appears on each pay stub. Your own RRSP at a bank, dealer or fund company. Your employer needs a letter of authority from CRA before it can deduct less tax. You ask for it with Form T1213, Request to Reduce Tax Deductions at Source , with documents showing the contributions you will make, such as a pre-authorized contribution schedule. CRA usually issues the letter for one tax year and generally will not issue one if you have a balance owing or unfiled returns, so it has to be renewed each year. Quebec residents also deal with Revenu Québec for provincial tax. Keep the promise. The reduced withholding assumes the contributions are made. If they stop, you will owe the tax when you file. Keep the pre-authorized contributions running even in a bad market; the crash contribution guide shows what pausing does. Leave room for the timing of the request. A request filed late in the year leaves fewer pays to spread the reduction over. CRA aims to issue refunds for online returns within about two weeks, so the refund route’s delay comes mostly from waiting for the year to end and the filing season, not from processing. What this does not change Reducing tax at source changes when the tax saving arrives, not its size. The deduction is still limited by RRSP room, and over-contributing more than CAD 2,000 above your limit is taxed at 1% a month. RRSP withdrawals are taxable income later, so the comparison is between RRSP balances before that tax, which applies to every route in the same way; the RRSP withdrawal guide covers it. If you expect a much lower income soon, for example a parental leave or a year of study, the deduction timing guide tests whether to contribute now and deduct later, in which case reducing withholding this year would be the wrong step. Finally, the fund inside the RRSP is unchanged. A balanced fund in an RRSP can still fall in value; the account defers tax, and the payroll route only changes how fast money reaches the fund.

documents.title: T-series payouts or a systematic withdrawal plan? Drawing cash from a non-registered balanced fund
documents.description: Compare monthly T-series distributions made mostly of return of capital with selling units through a systematic withdrawal plan, follow the cost base down to zero, and see when the tax deferral helps and when it only moves the bill.
documents.body: Return of capital is not taxed when you receive it, but it lowers your cost base, so the tax arrives later: as a larger gain when you sell, or each year once the cost base reaches zero. With the same tax rate throughout, a T-series and a systematic withdrawal plan from the same fund pay about the same total capital-gains tax; the T-series pays it later. The deferral helps most when the final sale falls in a lower-income year, and the payout rate is not a measure of what the fund earns. Two ways to turn a fund into a monthly cheque Someone who has built up a balanced fund in a non-registered account, often near or in retirement, eventually wants it to pay a regular amount. Fund companies offer two common routes. A systematic withdrawal plan (SWP) sells enough units each month to pay a chosen amount. Each sale is a disposition, so it can realize a capital gain or loss. A T-series (sold as Series T, T5, T8 or similar) is a series of the same fund that pays a target percentage each year in monthly distributions. RBC Global Asset Management’s description of its Series T, for example, sets the monthly amount as the previous 31 December value per unit times 5% (or 8%) divided by 12, and says return of capital is used to top up the interest, dividends and capital gains the fund earns to reach that rate. The portfolio and its risk are the same in both routes. What differs is how the cash is labelled for tax, and that changes when tax is paid. This guide follows both routes from the same fund, with the same cash in hand each year. What CRA does with return of capital CRA’s page on the tax treatment of mutual funds sets out the rules the model uses: A return of capital is not income when received; it reduces the adjusted cost base (ACB) of your units. For a mutual fund trust it is reported in box 42 of the T3 slip. For a mutual fund corporation it is not reported on the T5 slip, so you have to track it yourself. If returns of capital would take the ACB below zero during a year, the negative amount is deemed to be a capital gain in that year and the ACB is reset to zero. When units are sold, the gain is the proceeds minus the ACB, and identical units of the same fund series share one average cost. CRA’s capital gains guide shows half of a capital gain being taxable. The part of a T-series payout that is the fund’s own interest, dividends or realized gains is taxed in the year received, just as it would be in any other series. The calculator treats that income, 2% of the fund’s value by default, as identical in both routes and leaves its tax out of the comparison. The fund income guide covers how each type is taxed. Following the cost base The default case starts with units worth CAD 300,000 and an ACB of CAD 180,000, so CAD 120,000 of the value is unrealized gain. Both routes pay 5% of the previous year-end value, CAD 15,000 in year 1 . The fund earns a hypothetical 5% a year, so the value and the payout stay level. The first chart shows the cost base. Of each CAD 15,000, CAD 6,000 is the fund’s income and CAD 9,000 is the rest. In the T-series the full CAD 9,000 is return of capital, so the ACB falls by CAD 9,000 a year and reaches zero in year 20 . In the withdrawal plan, each CAD 9,000 sale removes only the cost share of the units sold, so the ACB falls more slowly and is still about CAD 85,969 after 25 years. The second chart shows the capital-gains tax paid each year at a 30% marginal rate. The withdrawal plan pays some from the start, about CAD 6,591 over the first ten years. The T-series pays none until its ACB is used up; from year 21 CRA deems each year’s CAD 9,000 of return of capital a capital gain, and its annual tax of CAD 1,350 is then higher than the withdrawal plan’s. Deferral, not exemption The third chart adds the tax due when the remaining units are sold after 25 years. With the same 30% rate throughout, the totals are the same: about CAD 51,750 for each route. That is not a coincidence. Both routes take the same cash out of the same fund and end with the same units, so the total gain is the same; return of capital only changes when it is counted. The deferral still has value in three situations: A lower rate at the final sale. With the final sale taxed at 20% instead of 30%, the T-series total falls to about CAD 36,750 against CAD 41,048 for the withdrawal plan, because more of its gain waits for the lower rate. Units still held at death are deemed sold at fair market value, so the final rate may be the estate’s final-return rate, not a low one. Income-tested benefits. Return of capital is not income, so lower taxable income in the early years can reduce the OAS recovery tax or keep income below other thresholds. The OAS recovery tax guide shows how those thresholds work. The time value of tax paid later. Money not paid in tax this year can stay invested. That benefit is modest at ordinary returns and is reversed once the ACB reaches zero. A withdrawal plan from a fund bought recently, near today’s price, also realizes very little gain at first, so the T-series edge is largest for units with a low cost base relative to their value. A payout rate is not a return, and inflation keeps working The heatmap shows how many years the T-series cost base lasts for payout rates of 4% to 8% and fund returns of 0% to 8%, keeping the default value, cost base and income. Higher payouts use up the cost base faster: at an 8% payout and a 4% return it lasts about 13 years. A cell showing 60 means the cost base lasts at least 60 years, which happens when low returns shrink the fund and the payout with it. The more important point is what happens to the fund. A distribution that is mostly return of capital is, by definition, partly your own money coming back. If the payout is higher than the fund’s return, the fund shrinks, and because the T-series payout is reset each year on the previous year-end value, the cheque shrinks too. RBC’s description notes that the distribution may be adjusted downward after a year in which the fund falls, which is what happens after a crash. Even when the fund and the payout hold level in dollars, as in the default case, inflation lowers what they buy. The Bank of Canada aims to keep inflation at 2%; at that rate a payout fixed at CAD 15,000 for 25 years buys about 39% less by the end. The balanced fund crash and inflation guide tests withdrawal rates against both risks. Choosing between them Only for non-registered money. In an RRSP, RRIF or TFSA there is no capital gain to defer, so a T-series offers no tax advantage there; every withdrawal from an RRSP or RRIF is taxable and every TFSA withdrawal is tax-free whatever the series. Compare the same fund. T-series and other series of the same fund usually carry the same management fee, but check the Fund Facts; a difference in fees or in advice charges can outweigh a tax deferral. Keep cost-base records. Track the ACB each year from the T3 slips, or yourself for a fund corporation, so the final sale and any deemed gains are reported correctly. The fund cost-base guide shows a ledger. Match the payout to a spending plan, not the other way round. A withdrawal plan lets you choose the amount and pause it; a T-series sets it from the fund’s value. Either can be combined with a cash reserve for the years after a large fall, as the withdrawal sources guide explains. This guide is a model, not tax advice. Distributions, special year-end capital gains and the mix of return of capital vary by fund and by year; check a specific fund’s documents and confirm a personal case with a tax professional.

documents.title: 2026–27 年度安大略省 Trillium 福利：租金、年龄和收入如何决定各部分金额，以及是否应等待 6 月一次性付款
documents.description: 按 CRA 的 2026 年计算表逐一了解安大略省 Trillium 福利中的三项抵免，看看为何租金只计入 20%、为何 64 岁很重要，并比较每月付款与 2027 年 6 月一次性付款。
documents.body: The Ontario trillium benefit is three credits paid together: the energy and property tax credit, the sales tax credit and, in the north, the Northern Ontario energy credit. For July 2026 to June 2027 they are based on 2025 rent or property tax, age on 31 December 2025 and 2025 family income. Rent counts at only 20%, people 64 or older get a much higher property tax component, and the sales tax credit fades fastest as income rises. Waiting for a single June payment pays the same total and gives up only a little interest; it is a budgeting choice. One deposit, three credits Many Ontario households see a deposit labelled “Ontario trillium benefit” around the 10th of each month and treat it as one payment. CRA’s Province of Ontario page describes it as the combined payment of three separate credits, each with its own rules: Ontario energy and property tax credit (OEPTC) , for people who paid rent or property tax on their main home in Ontario, or who lived in a public or non-profit long-term care home, on a reserve or in a designated student residence. Ontario sales tax credit (OSTC) , which needs no housing cost at all, and is paid for each adult and each child in the family. Northern Ontario energy credit (NOEC) , only for people who lived in Northern Ontario on 31 December and paid rent, property tax or a similar housing cost there. The payments from July 2026 to June 2027 are based on the 2025 return, filed in spring 2026, and on Form ON-BEN for the energy and property tax credit and the northern credit. That one-year lag matters for planning: a pay rise in 2026 does not change these payments, but it will change the ones starting in July 2027. This guide follows each credit through CRA’s 2026 calculation sheets and then looks at the one real choice the benefit offers, how it is paid. Energy and property tax credit: why only part of your rent counts CRA’s 2026 OEPTC sheets start from an occupancy cost : 20% of rent paid for 2025, plus property tax paid for 2025. Rent counts at one fifth, so CAD 10,000 of rent counts the same as CAD 2,000 of property tax. The credit then has two parts. The energy component is the occupancy cost up to CAD 290. The property tax component is a base amount plus 10% of the occupancy cost, with that 10% capped, and never more than the occupancy cost itself: Under 64 on 31 December 2025: CAD 73 plus 10% of occupancy cost, with the 10% capped at CAD 944. The highest total, CAD 1,307, needs an occupancy cost of CAD 9,440, which is rent of about CAD 47,200 a year. 64 or older (for a couple, if either spouse was): CAD 617 plus 10%, with the 10% capped at CAD 581. The highest total, CAD 1,488, is reached at an occupancy cost of CAD 5,810, or rent of about CAD 29,050. The third chart draws both lines. At CAD 12,000 of rent a year, the credit before any income reduction is CAD 603 under 64 and CAD 1,147 at 64 or older; the senior sheets are worth nearly twice as much on the same rent. The credit is then reduced by 2% of adjusted family net income above CAD 29,047 for a single person under 64 with no children, CAD 36,309 for a family under 64 or a single senior, and CAD 43,571 for a senior family. A “family” on these sheets means a spouse or common-law partner, or a single parent with the sole care of a child; parents who share care use separate sheets that split the amounts. Sales tax credit and the northern credit The OSTC pays up to CAD 378 for each adult and each child in the family for July 2026 to June 2027, up from CAD 371 a year earlier. It falls by 4% of adjusted family net income above CAD 29,047 for a single person with no children, or above CAD 36,309 for a single parent or a couple. A single person’s OSTC therefore ends at about CAD 38,500 of income, while a couple with two children keeps some credit until about CAD 74,100. The OSTC is the only part that does not depend on housing costs, so someone living with parents who pays no rent can still receive it. The NOEC is CAD 189 for a single person with no children and CAD 290 for a family, for residents of districts including Algoma, Cochrane, Kenora, Manitoulin, Nipissing, Parry Sound, Rainy River, Sudbury, Thunder Bay and Timiskaming. CRA’s 2026 NOEC sheets reduce it by only 1% of income above CAD 50,833 (single) or CAD 65,356 (family), so it is often the last part of the benefit left as income rises. The second chart shows all three for the inputs you enter, across income. Where the OEPTC and OSTC are both falling, each extra CAD 1,000 of 2025 income costs CAD 60 of benefit the following year, before income tax. The benefit phase-out guide shows how such reductions stack with tax on a pay rise, and the federal Groceries and Essentials Benefit guide covers the federal credit that phases out over a similar income range. Three worked households All three use CRA’s 2026 sheets as summarised above, before any rounding CRA applies. Single renter in Toronto, age 35 (the default). Rent CAD 24,000 for 2025, income CAD 35,000. Occupancy cost CAD 4,800; energy component CAD 290; property tax component CAD 73 + CAD 480 = CAD 553. Income is CAD 5,953 above the CAD 29,047 threshold, so the OEPTC falls by CAD 119.06 to CAD 723.94 , and the OSTC falls by CAD 238.12 to CAD 139.88. Total CAD 863.82 , about CAD 71.99 a month. Senior couple who own a home in Sudbury. Property tax CAD 4,200, income CAD 48,000, both 64 or older. Energy component CAD 290; property tax component CAD 617 + CAD 420 = CAD 1,037. The OEPTC is reduced by 2% of CAD 4,429 to CAD 1,238.42. The OSTC on two adults (CAD 756) falls by 4% of CAD 11,691 to CAD 288.36. Income is below the CAD 65,356 family NOEC threshold, so the full CAD 290 applies. Total CAD 1,816.78 . Family of four in Thunder Bay with income of CAD 80,000. Rent CAD 24,000. The OEPTC ends at about CAD 78,460 of income and the OSTC at about CAD 74,110, so both are zero. The NOEC is CAD 290 minus 1% of CAD 14,644, or CAD 143.56 , paid in one July payment because the year’s total is CAD 500 or less. A senior homeowner may also qualify for the Ontario senior homeowners’ property tax grant, up to CAD 500, which the senior sheets subtract in part from the OEPTC. That step is not in the calculator. Monthly or one June payment CRA pays the year’s entitlement in twelve monthly payments on the 10th, starting 10 July 2026, moved earlier to the last working day when the 10th falls on a weekend or holiday. Three rules change that, according to CRA and Ontario pages for the 2026 benefit year: If the annual total is CAD 500 or less , it is paid in one payment in the first month, usually July. If the annual total is more than CAD 2 but no more than CAD 10, CAD 10 is paid; CAD 2 or less is not paid. If the total is over CAD 500 and you chose on the 2025 return to wait, it is paid in one payment on 10 June 2027 . Ontario notes the total is the same either way. The fourth chart shows what waiting costs. In the default case, CAD 71.99 a month saved at 2.5% until June would be worth CAD 873.67, so the single payment gives up about CAD 9.85 of interest. For the senior couple above, it is about CAD 20.72. Waiting does not raise the benefit; it only changes when the cash arrives. That makes the June option a budgeting tool. Someone who pays a large annual bill in late spring, such as property tax instalments or home insurance, may prefer one payment they will not spend. Someone with a tight monthly budget is usually better off with the monthly amount and a separate savings plan; the annual bills sinking-fund guide shows how to set money aside each month for once-a-year costs, and the child benefit calendar lays out other monthly deposits. What to check before relying on the estimate You must file, and apply. The OSTC is assessed from your return; the OEPTC and NOEC also need Form ON-BEN completed with your 2025 rent or property tax. Missing the form means no OEPTC even with high rent. CRA’s OTB questions and answers cover who in a couple applies and how shared accommodation is reported. Status is fixed at 31 December 2025. Marital status, age 64 and northern residence are taken at that date for the whole benefit year. A move out of Ontario, a death, or a change in the care of a child can change or stop later monthly payments. Income is “adjusted family net income”. That is net income for both spouses, with some adjustments CRA makes, not take-home pay. RRSP deductions lower it; RRSP and RRIF withdrawals raise it. The GIS withdrawal-timing guide shows the same one-year lag for seniors. Amounts are set each year. The 2027 benefit year will use new figures. Check CRA’s child and family benefits calculator or your notice for your actual amount.
documents.keywords: Ontario trillium benefit 2026–27: how rent, age and income set each part, and whether to wait for one June payment Work through the three credits inside the Ontario trillium benefit with CRA’s 2026 calculation sheets, see why only 20% of rent counts and why age 64 matters, and price the choice between monthly payments and one payment in June 2027.

documents.title: RRSP 终身学习计划：还款何时开始、每年须还多少，以及漏还一期的真正代价
documents.description: 按照 CRA 的终身学习计划规则，了解为全日制学习可从 RRSP 提取多少、还款从哪一年开始、每年金额如何决定，以及差额在税款和 RRSP 增长损失上的代价。
documents.body: The Lifelong Learning Plan lets you take up to CAD 10,000 a year and CAD 20,000 in total from your RRSP, tax-free, to pay for full-time study by you or your spouse. It is a loan from your own RRSP: repayments start once the student stops studying (at the latest in the fifth year after the first withdrawal) and run for 10 years, at one tenth of the balance a year. A missed repayment is not a penalty, but it is added to income and the money never returns to the RRSP. Even when every dollar is repaid, the growth the withdrawn money would have earned is gone. A tax-free loan from your own RRSP An adult going back to school often has more in an RRSP than in a savings account. A normal RRSP withdrawal is taxable income, and the issuer withholds tax up front, so using retirement savings for tuition can be expensive. The Lifelong Learning Plan (LLP) is the exception. CRA describes it as a way to withdraw from your RRSPs to finance training or education for yourself or your spouse or common-law partner; the amounts are not included in income and the issuer does not withhold tax. The price is a repayment schedule. You owe the money back to your RRSP over, generally, 10 years, and any amount not repaid when due is added to your income for that year. So the real questions are: how much can you take, when do repayments start, how large is each one, and what happens if you cannot make one? The calculator follows CRA’s rules for each. Who can use it, and how much CRA’s pages on participating in and withdrawing from the LLP (dated 16 and 17 September 2026) set these conditions: Limits: up to CAD 10,000 in a calendar year and CAD 20,000 in total each time you participate. There is no cap on the number of withdrawals, but each needs its own Form RC96. Tax is withheld on any part above the CAD 10,000 annual limit, which is then a normal taxable withdrawal. The student must be you or your spouse or common-law partner, never a child. You must keep the same student until the year after your LLP balance is back to zero. The program must be a qualifying educational program at a designated institution: post-secondary level (or occupational skills at a certified institution), lasting three consecutive months or more , and requiring at least 10 hours a week of courses or work, not counting study time. Full-time enrolment is required, unless the student meets a disability condition, in which case part-time works. Timing: a student who has not yet enrolled needs a written offer, even a conditional one, before March of the year after the withdrawal. Withdrawals can continue until the repayment period starts, or January of the fourth year after the first withdrawal, whichever is earlier. You must be a Canadian resident, and you cannot participate after the year you turn 71. The first chart puts the CAD 10,000 annual limit next to Statistics Canada’s preliminary 2026/2027 tuition averages. The national weighted average for a full-time Canadian undergraduate is CAD 8,021; only Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Saskatchewan average more than CAD 10,000. For many undergraduate programs, then, one year’s LLP withdrawal covers tuition but not fees, books or living costs, and a two-year program can use the whole CAD 20,000. Which year repayments start CRA checks each year whether the student was a qualifying student, which in practice means enrolled full time in a qualifying program, for at least three months . Repayment starts in the second of two consecutive years in which the student fails that test, and no later than the fifth year after the first withdrawal . For a first withdrawal in 2026: CRA’s own examples follow the same pattern: Joseph withdraws in 2024, finishes in 2025, is not a student in 2026 or 2027, and starts repaying in 2027; Sarah withdraws from 2022 and is still a student in 2027, so the cap applies and she starts in 2027. One gap year does not trigger repayment, but two in a row do. The repayment period starts sooner for programs that never reach three consecutive months in a year; CRA treats those separately. How each year’s repayment is set The required amount is the LLP balance at the start of the year divided by the years left in the 10-year period. With nothing unusual, that is one tenth of the total withdrawn each year: CAD 2,000 on CAD 20,000, or CAD 1,000 on CAD 10,000. Paying it: contributions to any of your own RRSPs, PRPPs or SPPs made during the repayment year or in the first 60 days of the next year count, once you designate them on Schedule 7 of your return. A repayment is not a contribution, so it is never deductible, and it does not need RRSP room. What does not count: contributions to a spouse’s RRSP, direct transfers from other registered plans, contributions already deducted for the previous year, and amounts designated as Home Buyers’ Plan repayments for the same year. Paying less: the shortfall is added to income on line 12900 . In CRA’s example, Josée owes CAD 1,000, designates CAD 700, and includes CAD 300 in income. Her next requirement is still CAD 1,000, because the balance falls by the full required amount. Paying more: an early or extra repayment lowers later amounts. CRA’s Alexander has CAD 8,500 at the start of 2021, repays CAD 850 for three years and then CAD 4,000 in 2024; the 2025 requirement drops to CAD 325, which is CAD 1,950 divided by six years left. The second chart draws the balance and required amount for your inputs. CRA sends an LLP Statement of Account with each notice of assessment, showing the balance and the amount due next year; it is the figure to follow, not this estimate. Three worked cases All three assume the RRSP would otherwise earn 5% a year, withdrawals at the start of their year, and repayments at the end of each repayment year. Two-year program, full repayment (the default). CAD 10,000 withdrawn in 2026 and again in 2027; the student studies in 2026 and 2027. Repayments of CAD 2,000 are due for 2029 through 2038. No tax is ever paid on the CAD 20,000. But by the end of 2038, the two withdrawals would have grown to about CAD 36,815 in the RRSP, while the ten repayments are worth about CAD 25,156: roughly CAD 11,659 of retirement savings given up, even though every dollar was repaid. The same program, repaying 70%. If cash is tight and only CAD 1,400 of each CAD 2,000 is designated, CAD 600 a year, CAD 6,000 in all, is added to income. At a 30% marginal rate that is CAD 1,800 of tax spread over ten years. The RRSP ends about CAD 19,206 short of the no-withdrawal path: CAD 6,000 of principal that never came back and CAD 13,206 of lost growth. One-year certificate. CAD 10,000 withdrawn in 2026; the student finishes that year. Repayments of CAD 1,000 start for 2028 and end for 2037. With full repayment, the growth given up by 2037 is about CAD 5,381. The third chart shows how the income added and the tax change as you repay less of each requirement. Skipping every repayment on CAD 20,000 adds CAD 2,000 a year to income, CAD 6,000 of tax in total at 30%. The fourth chart shows the growth gap year by year. Is it a good deal? The LLP has no interest charge and no tax if you repay on time, so it compares well with a student line of credit charging prime plus a margin. Its cost is the tax-sheltered growth the money would have earned. In the default case, about CAD 11,659 at 5% a year; at 0% the cost would be nothing. Unlike a loan, a missed repayment is never sent to collections: it becomes taxable income, and the RRSP is permanently smaller. Three points matter in practice: Compare with an ordinary withdrawal. Taking the same CAD 20,000 as a normal RRSP withdrawal would put it all into income in the withdrawal years, with tax withheld up front, and the RRSP room would not come back; the RRSP withholding guide shows that gap. The LLP spreads any shortfall over ten years, often at a lower rate once the student is working again. Repayments compete with new saving. They use cash but give no deduction. During the repayment years, an employer RRSP match or an FHSA may deserve the money first; a shortfall is a deliberate, priced choice rather than a disaster. The education is the return. The calculator prices only the RRSP side. The career retraining payback guide sets the cost of a program against the income it may add. Situations the calculator does not cover Leaving the program or never enrolling. CRA allows a withdrawal to be cancelled, by repaying it to an RRSP of your own, if the student did not enrol in time, or left before April of the year after the withdrawal with at least 75% of tuition refundable. Residents generally must repay by 31 December of the year after the withdrawal; anything not repaid is added to income for the withdrawal year. New contributions just before withdrawing. A contribution must stay in the RRSP for 90 days before an LLP withdrawal to be fully deductible; part of a contribution made in the 89 days before may not be deductible if the plan’s value after the withdrawal is less than the contribution. Turning 71, death and emigration. No repayments are allowed after the year you turn 71, so the remaining balance is added to income in yearly slices. At death the balance is included in income unless a resident surviving spouse elects to take over the repayments with Form RC98. Becoming a non-resident generally makes the balance repayable within 60 days, or taxable. One plan at a time. You can participate again only from the year after your balance reaches zero, and a Home Buyers’ Plan repayment cannot also count as an LLP repayment. The Home Buyers’ Plan guide covers that program’s different schedule.
documents.keywords: RRSP Lifelong Learning Plan: when repayments start, what each year requires, and what a missed repayment really costs Use CRA’s Lifelong Learning Plan rules to see how much you can take from an RRSP for full-time study, which year repayments begin, how the yearly amount is set, and what a shortfall costs in tax and lost RRSP growth.

documents.keywords: LLP balance and required repayment by year, 2029 to 2038 Each year CRA divides the balance at the start of the year by the years left in the 10-year period. With full repayments, that is $2,000.00 every year. A shortfall is added to income on line 12900, and the balance falls by the full required amount anyway, so the next year’s requirement does not rise. Paying more than required lowers every later amount, because the smaller balance is divided by the years left.

documents.keywords: Income added and extra tax over 10 years, by the share of each required repayment you make Skipping every repayment adds the whole $20,000 to income, one tenth a year, costing $6,000 of tax at a 30% rate. The tax is the visible cost; the larger one is that the money never returns to the RRSP and loses tax-sheltered growth for good. A shortfall is not a penalty, but it is permanent: the RRSP room used by the original contributions does not come back.

documents.title: 加拿大培训抵免：每年 250 加元如何累积、课程费用能拿回多少，以及推迟是否划算
documents.description: 用 CRA 的加拿大培训抵免规则，看清额度如何增长、为何在额度内退回课程费用的一半、它如何减少您的学费额，以及推迟读书实际能多拿多少。
documents.body: Adults aged 26 to 65 who work and file a return build up CAD 250 a year of Canada training credit limit, to a lifetime maximum of CAD 5,000. When you pay eligible fees to a Canadian institution, the credit refunds the smaller of your limit and half the fees, even if you owe no tax. The fees it covers no longer count for the 14% federal tuition credit, so each dollar of training credit is really worth 86 cents more than you would get otherwise. By 2026 nobody can have more than CAD 1,750, and most claims are far smaller: CRA counted 643,900 claims averaging about CAD 387 for 2024. A refundable credit most adults never use Paying for a course as a working adult usually brings one federal tax break: the tuition tax credit , worth 14% of eligible fees in 2026, but only against tax you owe. The Canada training credit (CTC) , available since the 2020 tax year, adds a second one that is refundable : CRA pays it even if you owe no tax at all. The CTC has its own running balance, the Canada training credit limit (CTCL) , which grows by CAD 250 in each year you qualify and is printed on your notice of assessment. The questions a household faces are: how large is my limit, how much of a course will it cover, how does it interact with the tuition credit, and is it worth waiting for the limit to grow before enrolling? The calculator follows the rules for each. How the limit builds up Under section 122.91 of the Income Tax Act , your limit for a year is nil unless you are at least 26 and under 66 at the end of that year. Otherwise, it is last year’s limit, plus CAD 250 if you qualified last year, minus any CTC you claimed last year, and never more than CAD 5,000 minus all the CTC you have ever claimed . You qualify for the CAD 250 in a year when you: filed a tax return and were resident in Canada all year; had working income (employment and self-employment earnings, plus EI maternity or parental benefits and similar Quebec parental benefits) at or above an indexed threshold; and had net income no higher than the top of the 26% federal bracket. CRA publishes the thresholds each January. Its indexation page, dated 12 March 2026, lists them as follows. The year shown is the year whose limit receives the CAD 250; the income tested is the year before. For the 2027 limit, 2026 net income will be compared with CAD 181,440, the top of the 2026 26% bracket on CRA’s rate page; the 2027 working income threshold is not yet published. Because the first CAD 250 was added for 2020, the most anyone can have for 2026 is CAD 1,750 (seven years), and the CAD 5,000 lifetime cap cannot bind before 2039. The CAD 250 and the CAD 5,000 are not indexed. How much comes back, and what it does to the tuition credit CRA’s Canada training credit page and Schedule 11 set the claim. On Schedule 11, line 1 is eligible fees paid to Canadian institutions for the year (more than CAD 100 per institution). The credit is the lesser of your limit and 50% of line 1 , entered on line 45350 . Then, on line 6, the amount you claim is subtracted from your fees before the tuition amount is worked out. That subtraction matters. A dollar of fees covered by the CTC no longer earns the 14% tuition credit, so the CTC is worth 86 cents more per dollar than the tuition credit alone, not a full extra dollar. Up to fees of twice your limit, the two credits together return 57% of what you paid federally: 50% from the CTC and 14% of the other half. Past that point, each extra dollar of fees earns only 14%, and only if you owe federal tax, as the tuition credit guide shows. Other conditions are the tuition credit’s. CRA’s eligible tuition fees page includes admission, lab, exam and certificate fees for post-secondary courses, or occupational-skills courses at a certified institution if you are 16 or older, and some occupational, trade or professional examination fees. It excludes fees paid or reimbursed by an employer, or by a government job training program, when that amount is not included in your income. Fees paid to foreign universities go on a separate line and do not count for the CTC. Four worked cases Each starts in 2026 with the maximum CAD 1,750 limit and no earlier claims, and assumes the income test is met every year. Two years of evening courses (the default). CAD 3,000 of fees in 2026 and again in 2027. In 2026 the credit is the lesser of CAD 1,750 and CAD 1,500: CAD 1,500 . The 2027 limit is CAD 1,750 + CAD 250 − CAD 1,500 = CAD 500, so the 2027 credit is CAD 500 . The tuition credit applies to the other CAD 4,000: CAD 560. Federal relief totals CAD 2,560 on CAD 6,000 of fees, against CAD 840 from the tuition credit alone. CAD 250 of limit is left for 2028. One short certificate. CAD 1,200 of fees in 2026. The CTC is CAD 600 and the tuition credit CAD 84: CAD 684, or 57%. The 2027 limit is CAD 1,400, because only what you claim is used. The same two years, started in 2030. By 2030 the limit has grown to CAD 2,750, enough to cover half of both years: CTC CAD 3,000 , tuition credit CAD 420, total CAD 3,420. Waiting four years gains CAD 860, which is 86 cents on each of the extra CAD 1,000 of CTC. If fees rose 3% a year in the meantime, the 2030–2031 fees would total about CAD 6,855 and the relief about CAD 3,540. Studying in the year you turn 66. Someone aged 65 at the end of 2026 can claim CAD 1,500 for 2026, but the limit is nil for 2027, so the second year of the same course earns only the tuition credit. Unused limit is simply lost at that point. The second chart traces the limit and claims for your inputs. The third shows the kink at fees of twice the limit. The fourth repeats the course with later start years. Who claims it CRA’s 2024 tax-year statistics (data as of 30 November 2025) count 643,900 returns with a CTC claim, totalling about CAD 249.4 million . That is roughly 2% of the 31.6 million returns filed. Earlier editions show 646,610 claims and CAD 219.8 million for 2022, and 681,680 claims and CAD 245.3 million for 2023. The average claim is small compared with the CAD 1,250 maximum limit for 2024, which suggests most claims are capped by half of modest fees rather than by the limit. The first chart shows claims are spread across incomes: the average is between about CAD 374 and CAD 407 in each group. These are counts of returns, not of people who were eligible, and income is total income on the return. Practical choices Claim the full amount when you study. Schedule 11 lets you claim less than the maximum, but holding limit back does not make it grow: a dollar of limit refunds the same dollar now or later, later claims are still capped at half of later fees, and any limit left lapses in the year you turn 66. Waiting adds at most CAD 250 a year. The fourth chart shows the gain from delay stops once the limit covers half of each year’s fees. A course that raises income a year earlier, as in the retraining payback guide , is usually worth more than the extra credit. Keep the income test in mind in a gap year. A year with working income under the threshold, such as a full year of study without a job, adds nothing for the next year. EI maternity and parental benefits count as working income for this test. The tuition credit can still go elsewhere. The part of the fees not covered by the CTC can be carried forward or transferred, up to CAD 5,000 of the current-year amount, to a spouse, parent or grandparent; the CTC itself is the student’s own and is not transferable. Using RRSP money for full-time study? The Lifelong Learning Plan guide covers that separate program; the CTC can be claimed on the same fees. What the calculator leaves out Provincial and territorial credits. Some provinces and territories have their own tuition amounts, and some no longer do; Quebec administers its own system. Only federal amounts are shown. Ability to use the tuition credit. The 14% credit is shown at full value; it is only worth that once you owe federal tax, and otherwise it carries forward. Your actual limit. Missed returns, a year as a non-resident or income outside the thresholds change the limit. The figure on your latest notice of assessment, or in CRA My Account, is the one to use; the calculator only checks that your entry is possible by 2026. Special cases. Bankruptcy and death have their own rules under section 122.91. Fees are claimed for the year in which the courses are taken.
documents.keywords: Canada training credit: how the CAD 250 a year builds up, how much of a course comes back, and whether waiting pays Use CRA’s Canada training credit rules to see how your limit grows, why the credit refunds half of course fees up to that limit, how it reduces your tuition amount, and what delaying a course really adds.

documents.keywords: Returns claiming the Canada training credit, 2024 tax year, by total income Data as of 30 November 2025; counts rounded to the nearest ten and grouped here from CRA’s 19 total-income ranges. documents.keywords: Federal relief for the same course started in different years Each year of waiting adds CAD 250 to the limit, until the limit covers half of every year’s fees.
