documents.title: Every 20-year stretch since 1914: how much a dollar lost, and how wide the range has been
documents.description: A single inflation assumption hides how differently decades have turned out. Using Statistics Canada’s CPI back to 1914, see what a dollar kept over every overlapping 10, 20 or 30-year window, how often prices rose faster than a planning assumption, and how often a steady return after fees and tax kept up.
documents.body: Across the 92 overlapping 20-year windows from 1914–1934 to 2005–2025, Canadian prices rose by a median of 2.82% a year, but the range ran from prices falling 1.75% a year (1920–1940) to rising 7.13% a year (1971–1991), when a dollar kept only about a quarter of its buying power. A goal costing CAD 50,000 today needs about CAD 81,900 in 20 years at 2.5% inflation, and about CAD 198,200 if prices rose as they did over 1971–1991. A steady 4% a year after fees and tax kept purchasing power in 75% of the 20-year windows and 62% of the 30-year windows. History shows the spread a plan should allow for; it does not say which part of it comes next. One number for inflation, many possible decades A long-term plan usually needs one inflation figure: 2% or 2.5% a year is common, and the Bank of Canada aims to keep inflation at the 2% midpoint of a 1% to 3% target range. That target is a policy aim, and the Bank says it was adopted with the Government of Canada only in 1991. A saver who is 35 today is planning across 30 years or more, and over a span that long the average result has varied far more than the year-to-year noise suggests. This guide uses Statistics Canada’s Consumer Price Index from January 1914 to look at every overlapping stretch of years: 1914 to 1934, 1915 to 1935, and so on up to 2005 to 2025. For each one it asks how much a dollar could still buy at the end. The inflation basics guide explains how a constant rate compounds; this one shows how far real decades have strayed from any constant rate. A century of yearly inflation, and why the averages need care The first chart compares each calendar year’s average CPI with the year before. Prices rose 17.96% in 1917 and fell 12.11% in 1921; they fell in ten years in all, the last in 1953. Every year from 1973 to 1982 was above 7%. More recently, inflation was 6.80% in 2022 and 2.07% in 2025, and the index for September 2026 was 3.09% above September 2025. These are dated observations, with two cautions. The basket and the methods behind the CPI have changed many times since 1914, so the early figures describe a different set of purchases from today’s. And an annual average smooths the months: a year-over-year change in a single month, the figure usually quoted in the news, can differ from the change in the annual average. The CPI measurement guide covers those differences. What a dollar kept over every 20-year window The second chart divides the average index in the first year of each window by the average in its last year. With 20-year windows, the median result was inflation of 2.82% a year, close to many planning assumptions. But the worst window, 1971 to 1991, averaged 7.13% a year: CAD 1 at the start could buy only what CAD 0.25 had bought. In the best, 1920 to 1940, prices fell 1.75% a year and a dollar bought more at the end than at the start. Seven of the 92 windows ended with prices lower than they began, and all of them started between 1917 and 1923. Change the window length to see how the spread narrows and widens. Over 10 years the median is 2.35% a year, but the worst window, 1972 to 1982, averaged 9.60%. Over 30 years the median is 3.07% and the worst, 1963 to 1993, averaged 5.72%, enough to cut a dollar to about 19 cents. Longer windows average out good and bad years, yet the total difference between them still grows, because it compounds for longer. The windows overlap, so neighbouring points share most of their years; there are only a handful of truly separate 20 or 30-year periods in the record. How often history ran hotter than your assumption The third chart counts the windows by their average inflation. With the default 2.5% assumption, 55% of the 20-year windows ran above it. That does not mean a 55% chance of the next 20 years doing so: the record includes two world wars, the Depression and the oil shocks, and the inflation-targeting era since the 1990s has been calmer. Set the first year to 1991 and the windows reflect only that era, which leaves far fewer of them to judge by. The practical use is a stress test. A goal costing CAD 50,000 in today’s dollars needs about CAD 81,900 in 20 years at 2.5% a year, about CAD 87,200 at the 2.82% median and about CAD 198,200 if prices rose as they did from 1971 to 1991. A plan does not have to be built on the worst window, but it helps to know what a higher path would require: more saving, a later date, a smaller goal or a mix with more growth potential and more risk. The price-level guide shows why prices do not fall back after a burst of inflation slows. What return kept up, before and after fees and tax The heatmap takes a steady yearly return, removes the fee you enter, taxes what is left at the rate you enter, and counts the share of past windows in which it at least matched the rise in prices. A steady 4% with no fee or tax kept purchasing power in 75% of the 20-year windows and 62% of the 30-year windows; 6% kept up in every 30 and 40-year window. A 1.5% fee turns that 4% into 2.5%, which kept up over 20 years in fewer than half of the windows. Tax matters in the same way. Interest earned outside a registered account is taxed every year on its full nominal amount, including the part that only replaces lost buying power; at a 40% rate, 4% interest leaves 2.4%. CRA says that interest, dividends and capital gains earned in a TFSA are generally tax-free, even when withdrawn, so the account can matter as much as the investment. The tax treatment comes from the account, not from the fund itself: the same balanced fund is taxed differently in a TFSA, an RRSP and a non-registered account, as the guide to tax on inflation gains shows. Why a balanced fund is not the steady line in the grid The grid uses constant returns because they make the comparison exact, not because any investment delivers one. A balanced fund holds stocks and bonds, and its return varies widely from year to year, with losses in some years. High-inflation periods were often hard on both parts at once: rising interest rates push bond prices down, and the guide to years when stocks and bonds fall together uses 2022 as an example. Equities have historically offered more growth potential over long periods than cash, but with larger declines, and no return or recovery by a particular date is assured. What the history does support is that money expected to be spent decades from now has to be judged in real terms. Cash and short-term deposits protect the nominal amount, which matters for money needed soon, but over long windows they have often lost purchasing power after tax. Holding a growth-oriented share of a long-term plan is one response to that, with risk that has to suit the person and the time available; the balanced-fund crash and inflation guide sets those risks side by side. Saving from pay through a high-inflation decade For someone saving from each paycheque, inflation acts on both sides of the plan. A fixed monthly contribution shrinks in real terms if it is never raised, while pay has, over long periods, tended to rise with prices, though not in every year or for every worker. Raising contributions once a year by the CPI keeps the real amount saved roughly level; the indexed contributions guide shows the difference over a career. That is a different situation from a lump sum already saved, where the question is how the existing balance is invested and in which account, not how much new money to add. What this history can and cannot tell you Windows overlap, so the counts are not independent observations; the record holds only a few separate 30-year periods. The CPI is an average basket. Your own costs, such as rent, food or care, can rise faster or slower; the personal inflation guide shows how to weigh them. Annual averages are used throughout. A window measured from one month to another gives slightly different results. The returns in the grid are constant by construction, with the fee and tax applied every year. Real returns vary, taxes depend on the account and the type of income, and fees change. None of this forecasts inflation, interest rates or investment returns, and none of it is a recommendation to buy or sell any investment.

documents.title: Investing through a lower-earning spouse: why a plain gift changes nothing, and when a prescribed-rate loan pays
documents.description: Moving money to a spouse with a lower tax rate does not shift the tax on a fund held outside a TFSA: the income and gains are attributed back. See how a gift into the spouse’s TFSA and a loan at CRA’s prescribed rate change that, what the 30 January interest rule requires, and how the answer depends on the rate gap, the rate locked in and the fund’s payouts.
documents.body: If you give money to a spouse or common-law partner who invests it in a non-registered fund, the Income Tax Act attributes the income and capital gains back to you, so the household pays tax at your rate as before. Money your spouse puts in their own TFSA is excepted. A loan at the prescribed rate, 3% for loans made in the fourth quarter of 2026, also avoids attribution if the interest for each year is paid by 30 January of the next year. With CAD 100,000, a 6% return of which 2.5% is paid out yearly, and tax rates of 48% and 25%, the loan leaves the household about CAD 8,200 ahead after tax over 15 years, and using CAD 30,000 of TFSA room first adds about CAD 14,300 more. With no yearly payouts, or a much smaller rate gap, the interest can cost more than it saves. The same fund, two tax rates in one household When one partner pays tax at a much higher rate than the other, investment income looks cheaper in the lower earner’s hands. A balanced fund held outside a registered account pays out interest, dividends and capital gains each year, and every dollar of that taxed at 25% instead of 48% leaves more to compound. The question is how to get the money there legally. This guide compares three routes for savings beyond each partner’s own RRSP and TFSA: investing in your own name, giving the money to your spouse, and lending it at the prescribed rate. It assumes both partners have already used the room in their own accounts; the account decides the tax, and the fund inside it is the same. Why a plain gift moves the money but not the tax Section 74.1 of the Income Tax Act says that when an individual transfers or lends property to a spouse or common-law partner, income or loss from that property, or from property substituted for it, is deemed to be the individual’s and not the spouse’s, for as long as both are resident in Canada and remain a couple; section 74.2 does the same for capital gains and losses. So a gift that your spouse invests in a non-registered fund is still taxed at your rate. In the calculator, the first bar therefore stands for both investing in your own name and gifting the money for a taxable account. There are exceptions. Section 74.5(12) says the attribution rules do not apply to property your spouse holds in their own TFSA or FHSA, as long as the contribution does not create an excess amount in that account, and a premium you pay to a spousal RRSP and deduct is also excluded. Giving your spouse money to fill their unused TFSA room is therefore usually the first and simplest step: CRA says income and gains earned in a TFSA are generally tax-free, even when withdrawn. The over-contribution tax still applies, so check their room first; the TFSA excess guide explains it. How a prescribed-rate loan avoids attribution Section 74.5(2) switches the attribution rules off for income and gains from lent property in a year if three conditions hold: interest is charged at no less than the lesser of the prescribed rate in effect when the loan was made and an arm’s-length rate; the interest for that year is paid no later than 30 days after the year ends; and the interest for every earlier year was paid on time too. In practice that means paying each year’s interest by 30 January. Missing one payment means attribution applies for that year and every later year of the loan. The rate is fixed when the loan is made and is not reset as CRA’s rate changes. The Income Tax Regulations set each quarter’s rate as the average 3-month treasury bill yield at the auctions held in the first month of the previous quarter, rounded up to the next whole percent. The first chart shows the result: 1% in late 2021 and the first half of 2022, a peak of 6% in the first half of 2024, and 3% since July 2025, including October to December 2026. A loan made at 1% in 2021 still costs 1% today; one made in early 2024 still costs 6%. What the interest costs the household, and what it saves On a CAD 100,000 loan at 3%, your spouse pays you CAD 3,000 a year. You report it as income and, at 48%, pay CAD 1,440 of tax on it. Your spouse borrowed to earn investment income, and CRA lists most interest paid on money borrowed to earn interest and dividends as a carrying charge on line 22100, so at 25% the deduction saves them CAD 750. The household’s net cost is the gap, about CAD 690 a year. CRA notes that if an investment can produce only capital gains, the interest cannot be deducted. Against that, the fund’s yearly payouts and its eventual gain are taxed at 25% instead of 48%. With a 6% return of which 2.5% is paid out each year, the loan leaves the household about CAD 8,173 ahead after tax at year 15, counting the after-tax interest you reinvest in your own name. The break-even prescribed rate is about 4.41%. The third chart shows how much the locked-in rate matters: at 1%, about CAD 19,800 ahead after 15 years; at 5%, about CAD 3,500 behind; at 6%, about CAD 9,300 behind. The loan works on income paid out each year more than on deferred growth The saving comes mainly from yearly taxable payouts, which is why the type of fund matters. If the fund paid out nothing and all of the 6% were deferred growth, the household would be about CAD 1,300 behind with the loan after 15 years at 3%: the interest costs money every year, while the tax saving on a deferred gain arrives only when it is sold and is halved by the 50% inclusion rate. With 4% paid out each year, the loan is about CAD 12,600 ahead and breaks even at a prescribed rate of about 5.2%. The calculator taxes payouts as ordinary income, which suits interest-paying bond funds and overstates the tax on funds that pay eligible dividends or capital gains distributions; the fund income guide compares those types. CRA treats reinvested distributions as taxable in the year paid and adds them to the cost base. Lower returns also weaken the case: at 3% a year the default loan is about CAD 1,000 behind. None of these returns is assured, and a balanced fund can lose value in a year when the interest is still due. The rate gap and the prescribed rate decide most of it The heatmap varies your spouse’s marginal rate and the prescribed rate while keeping you at 48%. A spouse with no income tax and a 1% loan gives the largest benefit; with a spouse at 40% the 3% loan is about CAD 2,700 ahead and at 5% it is behind. Where the two rates are close, a loan adds paperwork and a yearly deadline for little or no gain. Combining TFSA gifts first with a loan for the rest gave the highest after-tax value in the default case, about CAD 206,300 after 15 years against CAD 183,900 in your own name. Making the loan stand up The statutory conditions are only part of it. Tax practitioners commonly recommend a written loan agreement with the amount, rate and date, the loan going to an account in your spouse’s name, and interest paid each January from your spouse’s own money with a record such as a bank transfer, so the arrangement can be shown to be what it says it is. If interest is paid by selling fund units, the sale can realize gains, as the calculator assumes. Separate rules apply to loans to minors, to trusts and to other related adults, including section 56(4.1) on low-interest loans, which this guide does not cover. Because missing a 30 January payment cannot be fixed afterwards, a tax professional can help set it up. This is a decision about who owns an existing lump sum. Saving from each paycheque is a separate question: a lower earner can usually invest their own pay in their own name, and new contributions can be directed to the lower earner’s TFSA. If the higher earner pays more of the household bills so the lower earner can invest their own earnings, that is a different arrangement from a gift or loan of capital. What the calculator leaves out All payouts are taxed as ordinary income at one marginal rate that never changes; half of each realized gain is taxed at that rate. Actual rates depend on province, income and the type of payout. Any income on income already attributed, and any provincial differences, are ignored, and no capital loss is credited. Interest and tax are paid by selling units of the fund each year, and the after-tax interest you receive is invested in the same fund in your name. Separation, death, a change of residence or a change in the prescribed-rate rules would change the result; the calculator assumes none. None of this is tax or legal advice for a particular household, and none of it is a recommendation to buy or sell any investment.

documents.body: TFSA room is limited, so a large lump sum often cannot be sheltered at once. One common plan is to fill today’s room, invest the rest in the same fund in a non-registered account, and move units into the TFSA each January as new room arrives. Under the default assumptions, CAD 120,000 with CAD 45,000 of room is fully inside the TFSA by year 16 and is worth about CAD 21,600 more after tax at year 20 than if only today’s room were used. Moving units in counts as selling them, so gains are taxed as you go, but that tax is on gains that already exist and is paid only once. The benefit depends on returns, on how much of the return is taxable each year, and on keeping room free for the lump sum. When the money arrives before the room Money you already have, such as an inheritance, the proceeds of a property sale or savings that built up in a bank account, can be much larger than the TFSA room available to you. You can invest the lump sum all at once or in stages; that is a market-timing question, covered in the lump-sum and phased-investing guide . This guide is about a different question that remains either way: which account the money sits in while TFSA room catches up. The plan tested here is simple. Put as much as today’s room allows into the TFSA, invest the rest in the same fund in a non-registered account, and each January move units worth the new year’s room from the non-registered account into the TFSA. The calculator follows the two accounts year by year, counts the tax on the part still outside, and compares the result with using only today’s room. How much room you may already have The Canada Revenue Agency adds the year’s TFSA dollar limit to your room each January, carries forward unused room, and adds back withdrawals on 1 January of the following year. The limits were CAD 5,000 a year from 2009 to 2012, CAD 5,500 in 2013 and 2014, CAD 10,000 in 2015, CAD 5,500 from 2016 to 2018, CAD 6,000 from 2019 to 2022, CAD 6,500 in 2023 and CAD 7,000 in each of 2024, 2025 and 2026. CRA had not published a 2027 limit when this was reviewed. The first chart adds those limits from each starting year. Someone who was 18 or older and resident in Canada in 2009 and has never contributed has CAD 109,000 of room in 2026; someone who turned 18 in 2020 has CAD 45,500. Room starts in the year you turn 18 or, for a newcomer, the year you become resident. Your own room also reflects every past contribution and withdrawal, so read it from CRA My Account and your own records rather than from the chart; contributing more than your room is taxed at 1% a month on the excess, as the over-contribution guide explains. Moving units in each January, and the tax that comes with it You can move investments into a TFSA in two ways: sell them and contribute the cash, or contribute the units themselves “in kind” if the TFSA can hold them. CRA says an in-kind contribution is treated as a disposition at fair market value: a gain must be reported, a loss cannot be claimed, and the contribution counts at the units’ market value. So moving units realizes the gain on them either way. The calculator assumes that tax is paid by selling a few more units from the non-registered account, which is why the January sale is slightly larger than the room filled. Under the defaults, CAD 120,000 arrives, CAD 45,000 goes into the TFSA and CAD 75,000 into the non-registered account. The new CAD 7,000 of room each January is more than the 5% a year the waiting part earns, so the non-registered balance shrinks: the second chart shows the last of it moving in during year 16 . The gains realized by the moves are taxed at about CAD 3,657 in total over those years, because only half of a capital gain is included in income, the moved units carry only a few years of gain, and much of the gain each year is a reinvested distribution already added to the cost base. If the room arriving each January is smaller than what the waiting balance earns, that balance never shrinks. With a CAD 300,000 lump sum and the same CAD 45,000 of room, for example, the non-registered part is still growing after 20 years. Enter your own figures to see which case applies. What the waiting part costs each year Outside a TFSA, a fund’s distributions are taxable in the year they are paid, even when reinvested; CRA says to report the amounts on your T3 or T5 slips and to add reinvested distributions to your cost base. The calculator treats a set share of the return, 2% of the value a year by default, as distributed and taxed at 30%, a simple stand-in for a mix of interest, dividends and capital gains distributions; the fund income-type guide shows how different that tax can be. The third chart stacks the two kinds of tax year by year. Moving the lump sum in each January keeps distribution tax to about CAD 3,872 over 20 years, falling to nothing once the non-registered account is empty. Using only today’s room, distribution tax totals about CAD 14,682 and the gain on the CAD 75,000 that never moves is still taxed when it is finally sold. A balanced fund with a large bond share usually distributes more of its return as fully taxed interest, so the waiting cost is higher for it; a fund that distributes little delays most tax until units are sold. Comparing the plans after tax After 20 years at 5% a year, the plan that moves units in each January is worth about CAD 304,320 after the tax that selling the remaining non-registered units would trigger. Using only today’s room leaves about CAD 282,677 on the same basis, about CAD 21,643 less. As a reference only, the whole CAD 120,000 growing tax-free from the first day would reach about CAD 318,396; that is not available here, because the room is not. The heatmap shows how the advantage depends on time and on the share of return that is taxed every year. Over five years it is under CAD 1,100 in every row; over 30 years it ranges from about CAD 32,000 with nothing distributed to about CAD 75,600 with 4% distributed. With nothing distributed the advantage is smaller but still positive here: tax paid now on a gain that is then sheltered costs less than tax deferred on a gain that keeps growing taxably, as long as returns are positive. None of these figures is a forecast; a year of losses changes the order of the comparison, as the next section explains. Saving from pay competes for the same room Each January’s room can shelter one dollar of new saving from your pay or one dollar of the lump sum, not both. If you already contribute from each paycheque, enter that yearly amount in “Room used each year by saving from pay.” At CAD 7,000 a year nothing is left for the lump sum, and the plan becomes the same as using only today’s room. For the household the total sheltered is the same either way; what changes is which money waits outside. The guide to January versus every-payday contributions covers the timing of contributions from pay. Keep the two decisions separate. How much to save from each paycheque depends on your budget and goals. How to place an existing lump sum depends on the room, the tax rates and the investment. An RRSP is a different wrapper with different rules: contributions are deductible and withdrawals are taxed, as the RRSP and TFSA timing guide compares. A fund held in any of these accounts is not tax-free in itself; the account’s rules decide the tax. When the waiting units are worth less than they cost After a market fall, the units in the non-registered account may be worth less than their cost base. CRA says that if you contribute such units in kind, you cannot claim the capital loss. Selling them first and contributing cash realizes the loss on your return instead; CRA’s capital losses page explains that an allowable capital loss is applied against taxable capital gains and that a net capital loss can be carried back three years or forward indefinitely, but not against other income. Buying the same fund back soon afterwards needs care. CRA treats a loss as superficial when you or an affiliated person, such as a spouse, acquire the same or identical property in the 30 days before or after the sale and still hold it 30 days later; a superficial loss cannot be claimed. Whether a purchase inside your own TFSA counts in a particular case is worth confirming with a tax professional before acting. The tax-loss selling guide works through the switch. The calculator does not credit losses, so with a fund return below its distributions it understates the case for selling first. Practical checks before moving money Confirm the room. Use CRA My Account and your own contribution and withdrawal records. Contributions made earlier in the year count against the year’s room, and a withdrawal does not add room back until the following January. Move in January, not before. New room appears on 1 January. Make sure the contribution is dated on or after that day; contributing before the room exists creates an excess. Check that the TFSA can hold the units. CRA says in-kind contributions must be qualified investments; mutual funds and securities listed on a designated exchange can be. Ask the dealer whether the fund can be moved in kind; if it cannot, the move becomes a sale and a cash contribution. Keep the cost records. Each move realizes a gain on the units moved. Average-cost records, including reinvested distributions, make the gain on each move straightforward to report. Hold the same investment mix. Moving units changes the account, not the risk. Choosing a different fund for the TFSA is a separate decision; the asset-location guide covers which fund to shelter first. What the calculator leaves out Returns are the same every year and positive by default. Real funds rise and fall, sometimes sharply, and are not assured to recover by any date; distributions vary. Tax is simplified: one marginal rate with half of each capital gain included, and one rate for distributions. Real distributions mix types with different tax treatment, and rates change with income and province. New TFSA room after 2026 is the amount you enter. Actual limits are indexed to inflation in CAD 500 steps and are announced each year. Fees, sales charges, account fees and transfer fees are left out, as are withdrawals and any income-tested benefits that taxable income can affect. Nothing here is a recommendation of any fund, account or transfer; it is a way to see the trade-offs with numbers you can change.
documents.keywords: A lump sum bigger than your TFSA room: invest it now, move it in each January, and price the tax while part of it waits An inheritance or sale proceeds can be larger than the TFSA room you have. See how much room you may already have, how long moving the rest in each January takes, what the part still in a taxable account costs in tax each year, and why the tax on moving units in is not a penalty.

documents.keywords: Tax paid each year on the part still outside the TFSA Over 20 years the moves realize gains taxed at $3,657 and distributions cost $3,872 in tax. Using only today’s room, distribution tax would total $14,682 and the deferred gain would be taxed when the account is finally sold. The tax on moving units is not an extra cost of the TFSA: it is tax on a gain that already exists, paid earlier than it otherwise would be, and afterwards that money grows without tax.

documents.keywords: After-tax gain from moving the lump sum in each January rather than using only today’s room Each cell repeats the calculation with the other inputs unchanged. The advantage grows with time and with the share of the return paid out as taxable distributions, because those are taxed every year outside the TFSA. With little paid out it is smaller but still positive here: gains taxed now and then sheltered beat gains deferred and taxed at the end, as long as the fund keeps a positive return.

documents.category: Market timing, crash fear and tax
documents.title: 为避开股灾而出售应税基金：税是确定的，市场要跌多少才值得？
documents.description: 在非注册账户中出售基金单位以等待预期中的股灾，会一次过实现收益和税款，而在外面等待的现金也要课税。看看买回前需要多大的跌幅才划算、为什么答案取决于你原本会持有多久，以及为什么在 TFSA 内做同样的事不用缴税。
documents.body: A sale to avoid a crash has one certain cost and one uncertain benefit. The cost is the tax on the gain already in the units, plus tax on the interest the cash earns while you wait. The benefit appears only if the fund is low enough when you buy back. With CAD 100,000 of units bought for CAD 60,000 and a 40% marginal rate, the sale costs CAD 8,000 in tax, and the fund must be at least 6.7% lower a year later just to buy back the same units. If you would have sold anyway within ten years, the tax is mostly a matter of timing and a smaller fall, about 1.3%, is enough after tax. In a TFSA there is no tax on the sale, so the question is only about the market, which nobody can call reliably. A certain cost against an uncertain benefit When markets feel fragile, selling a fund and waiting in cash can feel like the prudent choice. Other guides on this site test the timing itself: the crash-warning guide asks how often a warning must be right, and the exit and re-entry guide shows that getting back in is a second decision. This guide adds the piece that applies only to taxable accounts: selling realizes the gain already in the units , and the tax is due whether or not the crash arrives. The calculator sells a holding, pays the tax, holds the cash for a set number of months, then buys back at a fund value you choose relative to the sale. It compares that with simply holding the units, after tax, and finds how far the fund must fall for the sale to have paid off. What the sale costs on the day CRA calculates a capital gain as the proceeds of the sale less the adjusted cost base and selling costs, and in its worked example 50% of the gain is taxable. Selling CAD 100,000 of fund units with a cost base of CAD 60,000 realizes a CAD 40,000 gain; half of it, CAD 20,000, is added to income, and at a 40% marginal rate the tax is CAD 8,000 , or 8% of the holding. For a mutual fund, the cost base includes reinvested distributions, which CRA says to add each time you reinvest, so check your records rather than the amount you first put in. The cash then earns interest, which is taxed as ordinary income outside registered accounts. At 2.4% a year, close to the 3-month treasury bill yield of 2.39% in September 2026, a year in cash adds about CAD 1,325 after tax. The waterfall shows the steps: CAD 100,000 of units become about CAD 93,325 of cash available to buy back. To own the same number of units again, the fund must be at least 6.7% lower on the day you buy. What waiting in cash has earned after tax and inflation The first chart shows why waiting is not free even before any tax on the sale. From 2006 to 2025, the yearly average 3-month treasury bill yield ranged from 0.12% in 2021 to 4.76% in 2023. Taxed at 40% and adjusted for inflation measured from annual-average CPI, it lost purchasing power in 17 of those 20 years. In 2022 the real return after tax was about −5.1%, and in 2025 about −0.5%, when the yield averaged 2.55% and inflation was 2.07%. Those are dated observations. Interest rates and inflation change, and a high-interest savings account or a GIC may pay more or less than treasury bills. The point is that cash held outside a TFSA or RRSP is taxed on its full nominal interest, so it rarely grows in real terms after tax; the taxable interest guide shows the arithmetic in more detail. Why the answer depends on how long you would have held Not all of the tax on a sale is extra. If you buy back, the new units have a higher cost base, so less gain is left to tax when you eventually sell. The calculator therefore also compares both choices after the tax that selling everything at a later date would trigger . If you would have sold within ten years anyway, the default sale pays off with a fall of only about 1.3% before buying back. If the fund is 20% lower when you buy back, the sale leaves you about CAD 23,202 ahead after tax by year 10. If it is level, you are about CAD 1,619 behind; if it is 10% higher, about CAD 14,030 behind. The heatmap sets this out across gains and holding periods. When you would sell within two years anyway, the tax is due regardless and even a slightly higher buy-back price breaks even. The longer you would otherwise have held, the more the deferred tax is worth, and the answer approaches the last column, the fall needed simply to buy back the same units. With 80% of the value as gain, that is about 14.8% ; with 40%, the default, 6.7%. A higher income makes it larger: with a 50% marginal rate and a cost base of CAD 20,000 on CAD 100,000, the tax is CAD 20,000 and the same units need a fall of about 19.0%. There is no tax-free “never sell” in practice: CRA says that when a person dies they are considered to have sold all their property just before death, so deferred gains are eventually taxed, unless the property passes to a surviving spouse or common-law partner or another exception applies. The longest horizons here describe the value of deferral, not an escape from tax. Inside a TFSA the sale costs no tax, but the timing bet remains CRA says interest, dividends and capital gains earned in a TFSA are generally tax-free, even when withdrawn. Selling a fund inside a TFSA, holding cash there and buying back later therefore costs no tax. In the calculator, the dashed line shows that case: with 2.4% interest for a year, buying back up to about 2.4% higher still breaks even. The gap between the two lines is the tax effect alone. That does not make the TFSA a better place to try market timing. The difficulty of the timing decision is the same in every account. In an RRSP, selling and buying back inside the plan also triggers no immediate tax; withdrawals from it are taxed as income. Taking money out of a TFSA or an RRSP to wait in a bank account is a different step with its own rules, covered in the TFSA and RRSP guides on this site. Will the fall come, and will you buy back? The calculator asks for the fund value at buy-back as an input because nobody can know it in advance. A sale only pays off if three things happen: the fund falls, it falls further than the break-even, and you actually buy back near the low rather than waiting for things to feel safe. The best and worst months guide shows that sharp rebounds have often come close to the worst periods, which makes buying back at the bottom harder than it sounds. If worry about a crash is the reason to sell, it can help to ask what the worry is about. If the fund is too risky for your goals or the time you have, changing the mix to one you can hold through a fall is a lasting decision, not a timing bet; making it gradually in a taxable account can also spread the gains over several tax years. If you need cash soon, setting that amount aside is a planning step with a clear purpose. Saving from each paycheque is a separate question: new contributions can continue into the same fund or into cash without selling anything, as the guide to pausing contributions compares. When the units are below their cost If the fund has already fallen below your cost base, selling realizes a capital loss rather than a gain, and the calculator credits nothing for it. CRA explains that an allowable capital loss is applied against taxable capital gains and that a net capital loss can be carried back three years or forward indefinitely, but not against other income. Buying the same fund back within 30 days, or having an affiliated person such as a spouse do so, can make the loss superficial so that it cannot be claimed. The tax-loss selling guide covers that case. What the calculator leaves out The fund moves straight to the buy-back level and then grows smoothly. Real paths are uneven, and a recovery by any date is not assured. Tax is simplified: half of each gain is taxed at one marginal rate, which stays the same; interest is taxed in full at that rate. Actual rates depend on province and income, and a large gain can push income into a higher bracket in the year of the sale or affect income-tested benefits. Distributions while staying are part of the fund value at buy-back; sales charges, switch fees and trading costs are left out. The comparison is between two positions in the same fund. It does not assess whether that fund suits you. None of this predicts a crash, a recovery or interest rates, and none of it is a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any investment.
documents.keywords: Selling a taxable fund to sidestep a crash: the tax is certain, so how far must the market fall to pay for it? Selling fund units in a non-registered account to wait out a feared crash realizes the gain and the tax at once, and the cash waiting outside is taxed too. See how large a fall is needed before buying back pays off, why the answer depends on how long you would otherwise have held, and why the same move inside a TFSA costs no tax.

documents.description: 高于零表示出售再买回到第 10 年税后留下更多；低于零表示继续持有更好。非注册账户的线在买回时基金比出售价低 1.3% 处穿过零，TFSA 的线则在比出售价高 2.4% 处穿过零。如果买回时基金较高，出售在两方面都吃亏：单位较少，而且税提早缴了。两条线之间的差距就是税的影响本身。

documents.keywords: Selling minus staying, after tax by year 10, by where the fund is at buy-back Above zero, selling and buying back left you with more after tax by year 10; below zero, staying did. The non-registered line crosses zero when the fund is 1.3% below the sale at buy-back, the TFSA line when it is 2.4% above the sale. If the fund is higher when you buy back, the exit loses on both counts: fewer units and tax paid early. The gap between the lines is the tax effect alone.

documents.description: 每个格子保持其他输入不变，只改变价值中属于收益的比例，以及两个持仓都会被出售的年份。如果你很快就会出售，税大多无论如何都要缴，所以几乎不需要下跌。你原本会持有越久，答案就越接近最后一栏：仅仅为了买回同样数量单位所需的跌幅。负数格子表示买回价稍高仍可打平，因为现金利息弥补了差额。

documents.keywords: Fall needed before buying back for the sale to pay off, by gain and by how long you would otherwise have held Each cell keeps the other inputs and changes the share of the value that is gain and the year when both positions would be sold. If you would sell soon anyway, the tax is mostly due regardless, so little or no fall is needed. The longer you would otherwise have held, the closer the answer comes to the last column: the fall needed simply to buy back the same units. Negative cells mean a slightly higher buy-back price still breaks even, because cash interest covers the difference.

documents.title: 2% 的费用占 6% 回报的三分之一，却占跑赢通胀部分的一半以上：用实际回报衡量基金费用
documents.description: 基金费用是相对于全部回报来报价的，但建立购买力的是通胀后剩下的回报。看看同样的费用如何占去这部分实际回报中大得多的比例、它对以今日币值计的每月储蓄计划有何影响，以及加拿大自 1996 年以来的实际通胀如何变化。
documents.body: A fee is a percentage of everything you hold, charged every year whether the fund rises, falls or merely keeps up with prices. Measured against the return before inflation it can look modest. Measured against the part of the return that actually increases what your money can buy, it is often the largest single cost in the plan. With a 6% return before fees and 2.5% inflation, a 2% fee takes about 35% of the return but about 61% of the real return; a 0.5% fee takes about 15% of it. The fee is known in advance while returns and inflation are not, so it is worth comparing in the same real terms as the goal it is meant to fund. Two ways to describe the same fee Suppose a balanced fund earns 6% a year before its fee and charges 2% of assets. Taken in the usual way, the fee is about a third of the return: the fund reports roughly 3.9% instead of 6%. That framing understates what the fee costs a long-term saver, because 6% is not what your money gains in buying power. If prices rise 2.5% a year, most of the return only keeps your savings where they were. This guide measures the fee against the real return , the growth left after inflation. That is the part that pays for a larger retirement, a home or an education, and it is where the fee takes its largest bite. The calculator lets you set the return, inflation and two fees to compare, and follows a saving plan in today’s dollars. Where the return goes The fee is a percentage of the balance, taken from the grown fund each year. So a 6% return with a 2% fee grows the fund by 1.06 × 0.98, or 3.88% a year; the fee takes 2.12 percentage points, slightly more than 2 because it is charged on the year’s growth too. Inflation then divides that by 1.025, leaving a real return of about 1.35% . The second chart shows these three steps as a waterfall: 6% before fees, minus 2.12 points of fee, minus about 2.53 points of lost purchasing power, leaves 1.35%. The inflation step is a little above 2.5 points because inflation erodes the fund’s growth as well as its starting value. Without any fee, the same 6% would have been a real return of about 3.41% . The fee therefore removes about 61% of the real return, against about 35% of the return before inflation. With a 0.5% fee the real return is about 2.90% , and the fee takes about 15% of the real return instead of about 9% of the nominal one. The difference between the two descriptions grows as inflation rises: the fee stays a fixed percentage of assets, while the real return it is taken from shrinks. How much inflation has Canada actually had? The first chart uses Statistics Canada’s all-items CPI. Measured from one year’s average prices to the next, inflation was between 0.3% (2009) and 6.8% (2022) from 1996 to 2025, and averaged about 2.64% a year over the ten years to 2025 and about 2.17% over the twenty years to 2025. In September 2026 the index stood at 170.0, 3.1% above September 2025. The Bank of Canada aims to keep inflation at the 2% midpoint of a 1% to 3% target range. Those are dated observations, not a forecast. The ten-year average line shows how a few years can move a long average: it rose after 2021 because of the surge in 2022 and 2023. For planning, test a range. The guide to inflation expectations shows what households and businesses expect, and the personal inflation guide explains why your own costs may rise faster or slower than the CPI. What the difference does to a saving plan The third chart follows a plan that starts with CAD 10,000 already invested and adds CAD 500 from each month’s pay, raised with inflation each year so the effort stays the same in real terms. After 25 years, the contributions are worth about CAD 158,011 in today’s dollars. With no fee at all, a reference line rather than an available product, the plan would be worth about CAD 254,712 of today’s money, a real gain of about CAD 96,700. With a 0.5% fee it is worth about CAD 236,225 , keeping about four-fifths of that gain. With a 2% fee it is worth about CAD 189,635 , keeping about a third. The fees themselves, deducted month by month and converted to today’s dollars, come to about CAD 13,745 at 0.5% and CAD 47,840 at 2%. The gap between the two plans, about CAD 46,589, is larger than the difference in fees because every dollar deducted would otherwise have kept growing. The same arithmetic applies to money you already have. A CAD 100,000 lump sum invested for 25 years with the same assumptions would be worth about CAD 204,234 in today’s dollars at 0.5% and about CAD 139,702 at 2%. Whether to invest a lump sum at once or in stages is a separate decision about market timing, covered in the phased-investing guide ; the fee applies either way once the money is in the fund. When inflation is high, the same fee can erase the real return The heatmap keeps the 6% return before fees and changes inflation and the fee. With 1% inflation, a 2% fee still leaves a real return of about 2.85%. With 4% inflation the same fee leaves about −0.12%, and with 5% about −1.07%: the fund still reports a positive return of 3.88%, but it loses purchasing power after its fee. A 0.5% fee at 4% inflation leaves about 1.41%. This matters most for the parts of a plan with low expected returns. A balanced fund’s bond holdings, or a conservative fund, may expect a return before fees not far above inflation, so a fee of 1.5% to 2% can absorb most or all of the real return of that portion. The guide to stocks and bonds falling together shows how inflation can also hurt both parts of a balanced fund at once. None of this says a higher fee is never worth paying. It says the fee should be judged against the service it buys and the real return you can reasonably expect, not against the headline return. Fees, tax and the account: three separate layers The fee is paid inside the fund in every account. Tax depends on the account, not on the fund: TFSA. CRA says interest, dividends and capital gains earned in a TFSA are generally tax-free, even when withdrawn. A fee still reduces the return, and with no tax to share the cost, its whole effect falls on you. RRSP. CRA says income earned in the plan is usually exempt from tax while it remains there, and payments from it are generally taxed. The fee reduces the balance that is later taxed on withdrawal. Non-registered account. A fund’s management expense ratio (MER) is paid out of the fund’s assets, so it reduces the income and gains the fund distributes or accumulates; it is not a separate deduction on your return. CRA allows certain fees for managing or advising on non-registered investments to be claimed as carrying charges on line 22100, but not fees for registered plans such as RRSPs and TFSAs. Tax is charged on nominal gains and income, not real ones, so after tax the real return is lower still; the guide to tax on inflation gains shows how much. A fund is not tax-free in itself. The same fund units held in a TFSA, an RRSP or a taxable account are taxed differently, and the fee comes off the return in all three. Practical checks Read the MER in the Fund Facts and translate it. The Ontario Securities Commission’s investor site says MERs run from under 1% to over 3%, that they are charged whether or not the fund does well, and that reported returns are already after them. Divide the fee by the real return you expect, not by the headline return. Know what a trailing commission pays for. In advice-sold series the MER includes a trailing commission to the dealer; the series comparison guide sets the advice-included and fee-based routes side by side. Compare like with like. A cheaper fund with a different mix of stocks and bonds has different risk. Changing the fee is not the same as changing the investment, as the long-term fee guide explains. Raise contributions with prices. With the monthly saving left flat, the default plan with the 2% fee ends at about CAD 148,935 in today’s dollars against contributions worth CAD 121,807. The guide to indexing contributions shows the difference indexing makes. Keep the comparison in real terms throughout. Set your goal in today’s dollars, use a real return after fees and tax, and the plan is consistent. Mixing a nominal return with a goal in today’s prices overstates what the plan will buy; see the inflation and purchasing power guide . What the calculator leaves out Returns and inflation are constant every year. Real funds rise and fall, sometimes sharply, and the order of good and bad years matters for a saving plan; a recovery from any fall by a particular date is not assured. The fee is a single percentage of assets. Real costs can include trading costs inside the fund, sales charges, account fees and separate advice fees with sales tax, which may not appear in the MER. No tax is calculated. Savings and fees are converted to today’s dollars using one inflation rate, which may differ from your own costs. The return before fees is an assumption, not an estimate for any fund. A higher-fee fund might earn more or less before fees than a lower-fee one; only the fee is known in advance. None of this predicts future returns or inflation, and none of it is a recommendation of any fund or account.
documents.keywords: A 2% fee is a third of a 6% return, but more than half of what beats inflation: measure fund fees against the real return A fund fee is quoted against the whole return, but what builds purchasing power is the return left after inflation. See how the same fee takes a much larger share of that real return, what it does to a monthly saving plan in today’s dollars, and how Canadian inflation has actually varied since 1996.

documents.keywords: Canadian inflation each year, 1996 to 2025, and the ten-year average Yearly inflation compares the average of each year’s twelve monthly all-items CPI values with the year before. It ranged from 0.3% in 2009 to 6.8% in 2022. Prices rose 2.64% a year on average over the ten years to 2025 and 2.17% a year over the twenty years to 2025; in September 2026 the CPI was 3.1% above a year earlier. These are dated observations; future inflation is not known, which is why the calculator lets you choose it.

documents.keywords: Where a 6% return goes with a 2% fee and 2.5% inflation The three steps add up exactly. The fee takes 2.12% of return a year, inflation 2.53%, leaving a real return of 1.35%. With the 0.5% fee the fee step is 0.53% and the real return left is 2.90%. A fee is charged on the whole balance whatever inflation does, so the lower the real return, the larger the share of it the fee takes.

documents.keywords: Real return a year after fees, with a 6% return before fees Each cell keeps the 6% return before fees and changes only inflation and the fee. Moving one column right costs about the same in every row, but the rows with higher inflation start with less real return to lose, so the same fee takes a larger share of it. Negative cells mean the fund lost purchasing power after fees, even though its reported return stayed positive.

documents.title: TFSA 超额供款：每月 1% 的税如何计算、为何过早存回会触发它，以及取出超额能解决什么
documents.description: 按月追踪《所得税法》下的超额 TFSA 金额：为何提款要到 1 月 1 日才释放额度、最高超额 1% 的税如何累积、取出超额的成本和节省，以及 CRA 2024 年统计显示哪些人面临风险。
documents.body: A TFSA withdrawal gives its room back only on 1 January of the next year. Put the money back before then without other room and the amount over is an excess TFSA amount, taxed at 1% of the highest excess in every month it exists, including the month you take it out. There is no CAD 2,000 cushion as with an RRSP. Withdrawing the excess stops the tax and loses no room, because that withdrawal also comes back on 1 January. Waiting for January can cost less when the excess is small and the year is nearly over, but each month adds 1% of the excess. In 2024, 5.69 million of 19.32 million TFSA holders made a withdrawal. The usual way people over-contribute Few people set out to put too much into a tax-free savings account (TFSA). The common path is ordinary: you fill your room in January, take some money out in spring for a car repair or a trip that is then cancelled, and put it back in summer. If you had no other room, that second deposit is an over-contribution , and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) charges 1% a month on it until it is gone. The questions are practical: how is the tax counted, when does it stop, is it better to withdraw the excess now or wait for 1 January, and does taking it out cost any room? The calculator follows the rules in the Income Tax Act month by month for 2026 and 2027. What counts as an excess, in the Act’s own terms Section 207.01(1) of the Income Tax Act defines your excess TFSA amount at any moment in a year as A − B − C − D − E, if positive: B + C + D is the room on 1 January that CRA shows you. The key is E. The qualifying portion of a withdrawal is the lesser of the withdrawal and the excess just before it . A withdrawal made while you have no excess has a qualifying portion of nil, so it does nothing to offset a deposit later in the same year. Its room only comes back through C, next year. CRA’s contribution room page puts it the same way: withdrawals are regained as room on 1 January of the following year. Section 207.02 then sets the tax: if you have an excess at any time in a calendar month, you pay 1% of the highest such amount in that month . Three consequences follow: There is no grace amount. The RRSP’s CAD 2,000 cushion, explained in the RRSP room ledger guide , has no TFSA counterpart; the tax applies from the first dollar. Part months count in full. An excess created on the 30th, or removed on the 2nd, still makes that month taxable at 1% of the highest amount reached. The tax is not prorated or compounded. It is simply 1% of each month’s peak, added up. Four worked cases The first three use the calculator’s default: CAD 7,000 of room on 1 January 2026, a CAD 7,000 deposit in January, a CAD 5,000 withdrawal in March and CAD 5,000 put back in July. The 2027 dollar limit is assumed to be CAD 7,000. Taken out in October (the default). The July deposit makes A = CAD 12,000 against room of CAD 7,000; the March withdrawal had no excess to reduce, so E is nil and the excess is CAD 5,000 . July, August, September and October are taxed: 4 × CAD 50 = CAD 200 . Withdrawing CAD 5,000 in October is a qualifying portion and ends the excess, but October still counts. Taken out in July, as soon as it is noticed. One month: CAD 50 . Left in until January. July to December: 6 × CAD 50 = CAD 300 . On 1 January 2027 the room is CAD 7,000 − CAD 12,000 + CAD 5,000 of 2026 withdrawals + CAD 7,000 = CAD 7,000, which is positive, so the excess is gone and nothing is owed for 2027. A misread room figure, with no withdrawal. Someone with CAD 7,000 of room deposits CAD 17,000 in January. The excess is CAD 10,000: CAD 100 a month, CAD 1,200 for 2026 if left in. On 1 January 2027 the room is CAD 7,000 − CAD 17,000 + CAD 7,000 = −CAD 3,000, so CAD 3,000 is still over for all of 2027: another CAD 360 . Withdrawing the CAD 10,000 in March instead would have cost CAD 300. The second chart tracks your inputs month by month. The third repeats them with every possible removal month. The fourth shows what is in the account and what room is left on 1 January 2027 under four choices. Taking the excess out loses no room A common worry is that withdrawing the excess wastes room. It does not. A withdrawal of the excess is counted twice in your favour: its qualifying portion cancels the excess this year (element E), and the whole withdrawal is added back as room next January (element C). In the default case, the net amount in the TFSA plus the room on 1 January 2027 is CAD 14,000 in every version: CAD 2,000 in the account and CAD 12,000 of room if you remove the excess or wait to re-deposit, or CAD 7,000 and CAD 7,000 if you leave it in. The fourth chart shows this for your own inputs. The only real difference is the tax, plus any tax on income earned on the excess. The one thing a withdrawal cannot do is offset a later deposit in the same year if it was made while there was no excess. CRA’s cancelled RC4466 guide, still online, gives exactly this case: someone over by CAD 2,000 withdraws CAD 3,700; only CAD 2,000 is a qualifying portion, and a CAD 1,000 deposit two months later creates a new CAD 1,000 excess even though more was taken out than was needed. The extra CAD 1,700 comes back as room the next January. Withdraw now, or wait for 1 January? The cost of waiting is simple: 1% of the excess for each extra month , which the third chart shows as a straight staircase. Against it, leaving the money in keeps it invested tax-free and saves a withdrawal and re-deposit. A 1% monthly charge is about 12% a year, far more than most investments can be expected to earn over a few months, so removing the excess promptly is usually the cheaper path. The exception is an excess found in December: that month is taxed either way, and the room returning on 1 January may absorb it with no further tax. Two cautions. First, 1 January only clears the excess if the room returning (last year’s withdrawals plus the new dollar limit) is larger; a large over-deposit like case 4 continues into the new year. Second, the 2027 dollar limit had not been announced when this guide was reviewed. Under section 207.01(1) it is CAD 5,000 indexed to inflation and rounded to the nearest CAD 500; the dollar-limit indexation guide explains the rounding. Enter the announced figure once CRA publishes it. Who is exposed CRA’s TFSA statistics for the 2024 tax year (page dated 30 April 2026) count 19,322,830 TFSA holders. Of them, 10,979,910 contributed, 5,685,240 made at least one withdrawal and 1,711,020 maximized their contributions, in CRA’s wording. Holders made 31.9 million withdrawals totalling about CAD 69.9 billion, and 174.6 million contributions totalling about CAD 123.5 billion. Younger holders withdraw more often, while older holders more often fill their room; both groups can trip the same-year rule. CRA does not publish the number of people with an excess or the tax collected in these tables, so the chart shows the population exposed, not the number taxed. Counts are individuals, rounded by CRA, and the age is at the end of the tax year. If you have already over-contributed Withdraw the excess. CRA’s over-contribution page asks you to withdraw it as soon as possible; your financial institution reports the withdrawal to CRA, so you do not need to call. File Form RC243. When any TFSA tax applies, the TFSA return (RC243) and its Schedule A , which lists your highest excess for each month, are due with payment by 30 June of the following year: 30 June 2027 for 2026. CRA may otherwise assess from issuers’ records and send a notice in summer. Ask for relief if it was a genuine mistake. CRA can waive or cancel all or part of the tax if it considers it fair, looking at whether the excess arose from a reasonable error and how promptly it was withdrawn. Remove the excess before you ask. Check your room with your own records. CRA’s room figure is updated only after issuers report, by the end of February for the previous year; deposits and withdrawals made since are not reflected. What the calculator leaves out Growth and income. Amounts are deposits and withdrawals, not market values. Income or gains on an excess can be taxed under the separate advantage rules, especially if an over-contribution is deliberate. Several deposits and withdrawals. The model allows one deposit in January, one withdrawal, one re-deposit and one removal of the full excess. Real accounts may need a full ledger; the same A − B − C − D − E rule applies to each transaction. Transfers, survivors and non-residents. Direct transfers between your own TFSAs are not contributions or withdrawals; exempt survivor contributions and non-resident contributions have their own rules and a separate tax. Late-filing penalties and interest. Not included.

documents.title: RRSP 超额供款：2,000 加元缓冲涵盖什么、每月月底 1% 的税如何累计，以及为何存款日期很重要
documents.description: 按月跟随《所得税法》中的累计超额：2,000 加元缓冲放在哪里、为何在月底前取出可避开当月的税、1 月的新额度如何吸收超额、无法证明月份时 CRA 会如何假设，以及供款中位数与缓冲相比如何。
documents.body: You can have up to CAD 2,000 of contributions above your RRSP deduction limit without tax, if you turned 18 before the year. Above that, the cumulative excess is taxed at 1% at the end of every month it remains. Because the test is the month-end, withdrawing the excess before the end of the month it appears avoids the tax entirely, unlike a TFSA. New room each January absorbs an excess, but payroll contributions can create it again. Keep statements with transaction dates: without them, CRA may place deposits in January or March and withdrawals in December, which can multiply the tax. In 2023 the median RRSP contribution was CAD 4,000. How people end up over their RRSP limit Most registered retirement savings plan (RRSP) over-contributions are not deliberate. A payroll plan keeps deducting every month after a bonus has gone in as a lump sum; the deduction limit on last year’s notice of assessment was read before a pension adjustment was counted; or contributions made in the first 60 days of the year were meant for last year’s return but last year’s room was already full. The Income Tax Act allows a small margin for this, then charges 1% a month on the rest. The calculator follows that rule month by month for 2026 and 2027, with a monthly contribution, one lump sum, one withdrawal and the new room that arrives in January 2027. It answers four questions: when does the tax start, how much does the timing of a withdrawal change it, does new room fix the problem, and what happens if you cannot prove the months. The cumulative excess, in the Act’s terms Section 204.2(1.1) of the Income Tax Act defines the cumulative excess amount at any time in a year as your undeducted RRSP premiums minus A + B + R + C + D + E, if positive. For most people, the pieces reduce to three: D (a group plan amount) and E (a transitional amount for people who were 18 before 1995) apply in narrower cases and are taken as nil here. Section 204.1(2.1) then imposes a tax for each month equal to 1% of the cumulative excess at the end of the month . That last phrase is the important difference from a TFSA, where the tax is 1% of the highest excess at any time in the month: see the TFSA over-contribution guide . CRA’s excess contributions page says the same in plain terms: you may not owe the tax on amounts withdrawn before the end of the month in which the excess contribution was made. The cushion is a fixed dollar amount. CAD 2,000 is written into the Act and is not indexed, while the RRSP dollar limit rises each year: CAD 33,810 for 2026 and CAD 35,390 for 2027, according to CRA’s limits table. The cushion is not extra room. Contributions inside it are not deductible until new room arrives; they are simply not taxed while they wait. The tax is not prorated or compounded. Each month-end’s excess is charged 1%, and the months are added up. Four worked cases All four use the calculator’s default: a CAD 15,000 deduction limit for 2026 and nothing carried in; CAD 1,000 a month by payroll through 2026; a CAD 10,000 lump sum in March; CAD 9,000 of new room for 2027; and CAD 500 a month in 2027. With the cushion, contributions can reach CAD 17,000 in 2026 before tax applies. They reach CAD 18,000 by the end of August. Nothing withdrawn. The month-end excess is CAD 1,000 in August, then CAD 2,000, 3,000, 4,000 and 5,000 to December: 1% of the total CAD 15,000 is CAD 150 for 2026. On 1 January 2027 the new room of CAD 9,000 absorbs the overage, but CAD 500 a month rebuilds it, and the cumulative excess returns in September 2027: CAD 500 to CAD 2,000 for four months, another CAD 50 . Total CAD 200. CAD 5,000 withdrawn in October (the default). August and September are taxed at CAD 10 and CAD 20: CAD 30 . After the withdrawal, contributions stay within room plus cushion through 2027. CAD 5,000 withdrawn in August, before that month-end. No month-end ever shows an excess: nil . Under the TFSA rule, the same timing would still cost a month. Case 2 when CRA has no dates. If the October withdrawal is placed in December and the payroll contributions from March on are placed in March, the excess is CAD 5,000 at every month-end from March to November: 9 × CAD 50 = CAD 450 , fifteen times the CAD 30 from the real dates. The second chart follows your inputs month by month. The third repeats them with the withdrawal moved to every possible month. The fourth compares your months with CRA’s default placement. Withdrawing the excess: timing and the income tax side Because only month-ends count, the cheapest moment to withdraw is before the end of the month in which the excess first appears . Every later month-end adds 1% of what is still over. Two practical points make the withdrawal less simple than it sounds: The withdrawal is income. An RRSP withdrawal is included in income, even when it returns contributions that were never deducted. CRA’s RRSP guide (T4040) explains that you may be able to deduct an equal amount on line 23200, calculated on Form T746, if you withdraw the unused contributions in the year they were made, the following year, or the year a notice of assessment or reassessment for the contribution year is issued or the year after. Outside those windows the same dollars can be taxed on the way out without ever having been deducted. Tax is withheld unless you ask first. To have the issuer pay out unused contributions without withholding, Form T3012A has to be approved by CRA before the withdrawal; that takes time, so the month-end tax may keep running while you wait. The withholding guide shows how withheld tax is settled on the return. Waiting for new room is the alternative. In January each year the new room (18% of last year’s earned income up to the dollar limit, less any pension adjustment) absorbs an excess first. That only ends the tax if contributions in the new year do not rebuild it, which case 1 shows payroll deductions can do. Why the dates of each deposit matter RRSP receipts and T4RSP slips do not show the month of a contribution or a withdrawal, and CRA says it will not accept them as proof of those months. Its T1-OVP instructions say that without documents it may place contributions from the first 60 days of the year in January, the rest of the year’s contributions in March, and withdrawals in December. Every one of those moves pushes deposits earlier or withdrawals later, so the default placement can only increase the tax. The fourth chart shows the gap for your inputs. A monthly statement or transaction history from the issuer showing each date is the evidence to keep with Form T1-OVP. How the CAD 2,000 compares with ordinary contributions Statistics Canada’s Table 11-10-0044-01 (released 1 April 2025, latest year 2023) counts tax filers with RRSP contributions. The cushion has not moved while typical contributions have grown. In 2023 about 21% of tax filers contributed, and total contributions were about CAD 55.7 billion. The median is the middle contributor, so half contributed more than CAD 4,000 in the year; for many of them a single extra payroll month or a misread room figure is more than the cushion. Statistics Canada and CRA do not publish counts of people with an excess or the Part X.1 tax collected in these tables, so the first chart is context, not a count of people taxed. If you are already over Stop or reduce automatic contributions until new room arrives, or the excess keeps growing. Withdraw the amount over room plus CAD 2,000 , ideally before a month-end, after weighing the withholding and the line 23200 deduction above. File Form T1-OVP and pay within 90 days after the end of the year with the excess: by 31 March 2027 for 2026. The guide lists a late-filing penalty of 5% of the balance owing plus 1% a month for up to 12 months, and interest. Ask for a waiver if it was a reasonable error. Section 204.1(4) lets the Minister waive the tax if the excess arose from reasonable error and reasonable steps are being taken to eliminate it. The request is made on Form RC2503 ; withdraw or otherwise fix the excess first. What the calculator leaves out Pension adjustments and reversals. Enter your deduction limit and new room after them; the calculator does not compute them. Group plans and pre-1995 transitional amounts (elements D and E) are taken as nil. Several withdrawals, transfers and special withdrawals. Home Buyers’ Plan and Lifelong Learning Plan withdrawals may not remove the excess for this tax, CRA notes, and transfers from pensions or retiring allowances have their own rules. Growth, penalties and interest. Amounts are contributions, not market values, and late-filing penalties and interest are not included. Age 18. The cushion applies only if you turned 18 in an earlier year; someone who turns 18 during 2026 has no cushion until 2027, which the single yes/no input does not separate.
documents.keywords: RRSP over-contribution: what the CAD 2,000 cushion covers, how the 1% month-end tax adds up, and why the dates of your deposits matter Follow the Income Tax Act’s cumulative excess amount month by month: where the CAD 2,000 cushion fits, why a withdrawal before the month-end avoids that month’s tax, how new room in January absorbs an excess, what CRA assumes when you cannot show the months, and how median contributions compare with the cushion.

documents.title: 首次置业人士新屋 GST 回扣：最多退还 50,000 加元、100 万至 150 万加元之间的 15% 边际税，以及升级的真正成本

documents.body: A first-time buyer who signs an agreement with a builder after 19 March 2025 and before 2031 gets back all of the GST, or the federal part of the HST, on a new home priced up to CAD 1 million, to a maximum of CAD 50,000. Between CAD 1 million and 1.5 million the rebate falls in a straight line to nil, so each extra dollar of price adds 5 cents of tax and removes 10 cents of rebate: a 15% marginal rate. A CAD 50,000 upgrade on a CAD 1.1 million home therefore costs CAD 57,500. First-time status is tested on the day ownership is transferred, with a look-back over that calendar year and the four before it. The PBO projects about 12,900 rebates for homes completed in 2026. Why the price of a new home matters twice A newly built home is taxable: the builder charges GST, or HST in the participating provinces, on the price. For decades the main relief has been the GST/HST new housing rebate, which returns at most CAD 6,300 and disappears at a price of CAD 450,000. Since 2025 there is a much larger rebate for first-time buyers: up to CAD 50,000, enough to cancel all of the federal tax on a home priced up to CAD 1 million. The size of that rebate depends on the price. Above CAD 1 million it shrinks, which changes the arithmetic of every decision that moves the price: a bigger unit, a parking spot, an upgrade package, a price escalation clause. The calculator answers three questions for a home bought from a builder: how much GST or federal HST is still payable after the rebates, what an addition to the price costs once the rebate shrinks, and what that does to the mortgage payment. The rule in the Excise Tax Act and CRA’s worksheet The rebate is in subsection 254(2.1) of the Excise Tax Act . For a home bought from a builder, CRA’s Form RC7190-WS works it out in three lines: line 12 is the GST, or the federal part of the HST, paid; line 13 is the price before tax; line 14 is the rebate. Up to CAD 1 million the Act sets the first-time buyers’ rebate at the lesser of CAD 50,000 and the tax paid, less the new housing rebate, and pays it in addition to that rebate, so together they return the lesser of the two. The calculator shows the two parts separately. At 5% GST, CAD 50,000 is exactly the tax on CAD 1 million, so the cap and the start of the phase-out meet. The HST is handled by converting to the federal part: CRA’s worksheet multiplies the HST by 5/13, 5/14 or 5/15. In Ontario, HST of CAD 143,000 on a CAD 1.1 million home contains CAD 55,000 of federal tax. This rebate applies only to that CAD 55,000. Any provincial rebate is a separate claim; RC4028 notes, for example, that the Ontario new housing rebate (at most CAD 24,000) can be available above the federal thresholds. Who is a first-time buyer, and when it is tested According to CRA’s guide RC4028 , the buyer generally must be at least 18, a Canadian citizen or permanent resident, and must not have lived, as their primary place of residence, in a home that they or their spouse or common-law partner owned, in the current calendar year or the four before it , anywhere in the world. The other conditions for a home bought from a builder are: the agreement of purchase and sale was entered into after 19 March 2025 and before 2031; construction begins before 2031 and is substantially completed before 2036, and ownership is transferred before 2036; the home is bought as the buyer’s primary place of residence, and the buyer is the first individual to occupy it after completion; the buyer has never received the rebate before. It is once per lifetime. The first-time test applies at the moment ownership is transferred , not when the agreement is signed. For a pre-construction condominium that can be years later, often after a period of interim occupancy. A buyer who signs in 2026, then buys and moves into a resale home while waiting, has lived in an owned home in the look-back window by the time the condominium is transferred. A partner’s ownership counts too: moving into a spouse’s owned home is enough. Only one person can claim per home. When two people buy together, at least one must be a first-time buyer who will live there; that person is the claimant. A corporation or partnership cannot claim. RC4028 also excludes an agreement made before 20 March 2025 that is later varied, amended or assigned, and a cancelled-and-replaced agreement where obtaining the rebate was the main reason. The 15% band: what the next dollar of price costs Between CAD 1 million and 1.5 million the GST still payable by a first-time buyer is 5% of the price less a rebate that falls by CAD 50,000 over CAD 500,000, or 10 cents per dollar. The GST payable therefore rises by 15 cents for every extra dollar of price , from nil at CAD 1 million to CAD 75,000 at CAD 1.5 million. Above CAD 1.5 million the rate falls back to the statutory 5%. Other buyers face their own, smaller notch: the new housing rebate makes their rate 3.2% below CAD 350,000 and 11.3% between CAD 350,000 and 450,000, where CAD 6,300 of rebate is lost over CAD 100,000. Five worked cases The calculator’s default is a first-time buyer, never an owner, buying a CAD 1.1 million home from a builder with a CAD 220,000 down payment and a 30-year mortgage at 4.5% compounded half-yearly, and considering CAD 50,000 of upgrades. The base price. GST is CAD 55,000. The rebate is CAD 50,000 × (1,500,000 − 1,100,000) ÷ 500,000 = CAD 40,000 , leaving CAD 15,000 payable. If that is financed, the mortgage is CAD 895,000 and the monthly payment about CAD 4,513. Adding CAD 50,000 of upgrades. At CAD 1.15 million the GST is CAD 57,500 and the rebate CAD 35,000, so the GST payable rises by CAD 7,500 , three times the CAD 2,500 that 5% would suggest. The upgrade costs CAD 57,500 in all and adds about CAD 290 a month to the payment. The same CAD 50,000 at other prices. From CAD 900,000 or CAD 950,000 it adds no GST, because the total stays within CAD 1 million. From CAD 1 million, or from CAD 1.45 million up to exactly CAD 1.5 million, it adds CAD 7,500. From CAD 1.5 million it adds CAD 2,500. Not a first-time buyer. Someone who lived in a home they owned three years ago gets no first-time rebate, and no new housing rebate at this price: the full CAD 55,000 is payable, CAD 40,000 more than the first-time buyer. A CAD 450,000 condominium. GST is CAD 22,500 and the first-time buyer gets all of it back. Any other buyer gets nothing, because the new housing rebate ends at CAD 450,000. An independent 40-digit decimal check reproduces every figure above, and the tests check that the rebate never exceeds CAD 50,000, never exceeds the GST, and that the GST payable never falls as the price rises. What the Parliamentary Budget Officer projects No count of rebates claimed has been published yet. The Parliamentary Budget Officer’s June 2025 costing (RP-2526-001-S) built its estimate from projected housing completions and narrowed them step by step. The figures are projections, not observations: The PBO projected 71,711 rebates averaging CAD 26,832, a cost of about CAD 1.9 billion over six years, covering 4.8% of projected completions. Its first-time share, about 20% of qualifying sales, came from Statistics Canada’s Canadian Housing Statistics Program data for three provinces. It assumed agreements after 26 May 2025, the date in the bill at the time; the law as enacted reaches back to 20 March 2025, so the 2025 figure is likely understated. Before you sign, and before closing Check the look-back for both partners against the expected transfer year, not the signing year. A resale purchase while waiting for a new build can end eligibility. Inside the CAD 1 million to 1.5 million band, every dollar added to the price costs CAD 1.15. Upgrades, parking, a storage locker and escalation clauses bought from the builder raise the price; in the calculator, add them to the price to see the GST that follows. An assignment price paid to a previous buyer is also part of the price on line 13. Ask whether the builder will pay or credit the rebate. RC4028 allows the builder to credit the new housing rebate and the first-time buyers’ rebate against the amount due at closing (Form GST190 , Type 1A, sent by the builder). If the builder does not, apply to CRA yourself (Type 2); for a home bought from a builder this is generally within two years after ownership is transferred. Keep the cash plan separate. A rebate credited at closing reduces the amount owing; one claimed later is cash that arrives after the down payment, land transfer tax and closing costs have been paid. What the calculator leaves out Provincial tax. Only the federal 5% is modelled. In the HST provinces the provincial part, and any provincial rebate, are not shown. Other ways to buy. Owner-built homes, co-op shares, and homes on leased land (Types 1B, 3 and 5 on the worksheet) use different price thresholds and are not modelled. Eligibility dates. The calculator checks age, status and the look-back only. It does not check the agreement date, construction dates or whether you will be the first occupant. Closing costs and insurance. Land transfer tax, legal fees and adjustments are left out. A down payment under 20% needs mortgage default insurance, whose premium and price limits are not applied; amortization is entered, not checked against lender rules. Mortgage terms. The payment uses a fixed rate for the whole amortization, compounded half-yearly as for Canadian fixed-rate mortgages.
documents.keywords: First-time home buyers’ GST rebate on a new home: up to CAD 50,000 back, a 15% marginal tax between CAD 1 million and 1.5 million, and what an upgrade really costs Work out the GST (or federal part of the HST) still payable on a new home bought from a builder after the first-time home buyers’ rebate and the new housing rebate, why each extra dollar of price costs 15 cents of federal tax inside the CAD 1 million to 1.5 million phase-out, how the five-year look-back decides who is a first-time buyer, and what the PBO projects for the number of rebates.
